t: Built-in data structures and their complexity
sum: How list, tuple, dict and set are built inside CPython, what each operation really costs and why, and when to reach for deque, heapq, bisect, Counter, defaultdict or NumPy instead.
prereq: py1
Variables and container slots hold references to objects, and dict keys and set members must be hashable: their hash never changes and equal objects hash equally.
why:
A data engineer writes a script to remove duplicate user ids from a list of a million records while keeping the original order. The logic is obviously correct:

out = []
for uid in ids:
    if uid not in out:
        out.append(uid)

On the 1,000-record test file it finishes instantly. On the real file it runs for hours. Nothing is wrong with the logic; the problem is that uid not in out on a list compares uid against every element already collected. The loop does that a million times against a list that grows to a million, which is on the order of half a trillion comparisons. Changing one line — keep a set of seen ids next to the list — makes the whole thing finish in well under a second.

This is the most common kind of performance bug in Python, and it is not about clever algorithms. It comes from not knowing what the built-in containers cost. Python makes every container look equally convenient: in, indexing, append and pop work on nearly everything. Under the hood they are very different machines. A list is an array, so it is fast at the end and slow at the front; a dict is a hash table, so it is fast at finding a key but uses more memory; a deque is fast at both ends but slow in the middle. Picking the wrong one does not raise an error. It just makes your program a thousand times slower once the data is real.

Interviewers probe this constantly, both directly ("what does x in list cost?") and inside coding questions, where using a list as a queue or sorting to find a maximum quietly turns an O(n) solution into O(n²).

This lesson starts by defining big-O notation, then opens up each container in turn: how a list is laid out in memory and why appending is cheap but inserting at the front is not; what a tuple adds; how a hash table works and how CPython's dict and set implement one; and the standard-library structures — deque, heapq, bisect, Counter, defaultdict, OrderedDict — built for the jobs the basic four do badly. It finishes with memory: why a million Python ints take far more space than a million numbers should, and what NumPy does differently. All timings and sizes were measured on CPython 3.12.10, 64-bit Windows.
primer:
Cost that grows with size: big-O in one page

We need a way to talk about how expensive an operation is without timing it on every machine. Big-O notation describes how the cost grows as the number of elements, n, grows, ignoring constant factors:

  • O(1), constant: the cost does not depend on n. Reading xs[5] takes the same time for a list of ten items or ten million.
  • O(log n), logarithmic: the cost grows by one step each time n doubles. Binary search over a million sorted items needs about 20 steps.
  • O(n), linear: the cost grows in proportion. Scanning a list twice as long takes twice as long.
  • O(n log n): the cost of a good sort.
  • O(n²), quadratic: usually an O(n) operation inside a loop over n items. Double n and the time quadruples.

One more term: amortised cost is the average per operation over a long run. An operation that is usually trivial but occasionally expensive can still be "amortised O(1)" if the expensive cases are rare enough.

Four containers, four machines

Think of the built-in containers as different ways to organise a filing room.

A list is a row of numbered pigeonholes. Going straight to pigeonhole 500 is instant. Adding a folder at the end of the row is instant as long as there is an empty hole. Inserting one at the front means shuffling every folder one hole to the right. Finding "the folder labelled Smith" means checking holes one by one.

A tuple is the same row of pigeonholes, sealed: you cannot add, remove or swap folders, which makes it safe to share and usable as a label itself.

A dict is a room with a clerk who has a rule for turning any label into a pigeonhole number — that rule is the hash. Asking for "Smith" means computing the number and walking straight there. That is why finding by key is fast no matter how many folders there are, and why the label must never change (py1): if it did, the clerk would compute a different number and look in the wrong place.

A set is the same room with labels but no folders: it answers "do we have Smith?" and nothing more.

The rule of thumb

Ask what your code does most. Iterating in order and indexing by position: list. Fixed record or composite key: tuple. Looking up by key or checking membership: dict or set. Adding and removing at both ends, as in a queue: deque. Repeatedly taking the smallest or largest item: heapq. Keeping things sorted and searching them: bisect. The rest of the lesson explains why each of those is the right machine.

Where the filing-room analogy breaks: pigeonholes in a Python list do not contain the folders, only notes saying where each folder is (py1: containers hold references). That is why a list can mix types, and why a list of a million numbers takes far more memory than a million numbers would.
body:
1. list: a dynamic array of references

In CPython a list object has a small header (its reference count, its type, its length and its capacity) and a pointer to a separate block of memory holding an array of references, one 8-byte pointer per slot on a 64-bit machine. Because the slots are contiguous and equally sized, the address of slot i is just start + 8 × i, which is why xs[i] is O(1) regardless of length.

A plain array has a fixed size, but a list can grow, so it is a dynamic array: it allocates more slots than it currently uses. The number of slots in use is the length; the number allocated is the capacity. When an append finds a free slot, it just writes the pointer and increments the length. When the array is full, CPython allocates a bigger block, copies the pointers across and frees the old block. The CPython 3.12 source computes the new capacity as roughly newsize + newsize/8 + 6, rounded down to a multiple of 4 — about 12.5 percent headroom plus a little. You can watch it happen with sys.getsizeof, which reports the header plus the pointer array:

import sys
lst = []
print(sys.getsizeof(lst))            # 56   (header only, no array yet)
for i in range(40):
    lst.append(i)
    # print whenever the size jumps:
# len=1  size=88  capacity=4
# len=5  size=120 capacity=8
# len=9  size=184 capacity=16
# len=17 size=248 capacity=24
# len=25 size=312 capacity=32
# len=33 size=376 capacity=40

Capacity is (size − 56) / 8. Thirty-three appends caused only six reallocations. Because each reallocation adds room proportional to the current size, the total copying across n appends adds up to a constant multiple of n, so each append is amortised O(1).

The same layout explains the expensive operations. insert(0, x) and pop(0) must move every other pointer one slot, which is O(n). remove(x) and x in lst must search from the start, O(n). Slicing lst[a:b] copies b − a pointers, O(k). lst.sort() is O(n log n). Here is what that means in real time for a million integers:

ids_list = list(range(1_000_000))
ids_set = set(ids_list)
999_999 in ids_list    # measured: about 12.5 ms per check
999_999 in ids_set     # measured: about 0.14 µs per check (including call overhead)

A factor of nearly 100,000. Inside a loop of a million iterations, the list version is the "runs for hours" script from the introduction.

2. Sorting

sorted(iterable) returns a new list; lst.sort() sorts in place and returns None (the "mutate and return None" convention from py1). Both accept key=, a function called once per element to produce the value to compare, and reverse=True. Python's sort is stable: items with equal keys keep their original relative order, which lets you sort by several fields in passes (sort by secondary key, then by primary key):

sorted([("b", 2), ("a", 2), ("c", 1)], key=lambda t: t[1])
# [('c', 1), ('b', 2), ('a', 2)]   — 'b' still precedes 'a' among the 2s

The algorithm is a merge sort that first finds already-sorted stretches ("runs") in the data and then merges them. It was Timsort from Python 2.3; since 3.11 CPython uses the Powersort rule for deciding which runs to merge. Either way it is O(n log n) in general and close to O(n) when the input is already mostly sorted, which is common in real data.

3. tuple: a sealed array

A tuple has the same idea as a list — a header plus an array of references — but the array is allocated inline with the header at exactly the right size, because it can never grow. That makes it a little smaller (sys.getsizeof((1, 2, 3)) is 64 bytes versus 88 for the equivalent list) and slightly cheaper to create. More important than the bytes: a tuple is immutable and therefore hashable if its contents are, so it can be a dict key or set member. That makes tuples the natural representation of composite keys, such as (user_id, date), and of fixed records returned from functions. When positional access becomes unreadable, typing.NamedTuple adds field names while staying a tuple.

4. Hash tables: the idea

We want to find an item by its key without scanning. The trick is to turn the key into a slot number. A hash table is an array of slots; to store a key, compute hash(key) (an integer, py1), reduce it to a slot index, and put the entry there. To look it up later, compute the same index and look in one place.

Two different keys will sometimes produce the same slot; that is a collision. CPython resolves collisions with open addressing: if the slot is taken by a different key, it computes the next slot to try from a fixed probe sequence and keeps going until it finds the key or an empty slot. An empty slot means "not present", which is why the table must always have some empty slots.

The fuller the table, the more collisions and the longer the probes. So the table is resized — to a bigger array, with every entry reinserted — before it gets too full. The fraction in use is the load factor; CPython keeps dicts at most two-thirds full. As with list growth, resizing is proportional to size and happens rarely, so insertion is amortised O(1), and with a low load factor most lookups succeed on the first or second probe.

5. dict: CPython's compact hash table

Here is the actual lookup, step by step, for d["cat"]:

  1. Compute h = hash("cat"), a 64-bit integer.
  2. The table size is a power of two, say 8. Take the low bits: i = h & 7, giving a slot between 0 and 7. Taking low bits is a single fast machine instruction.
  3. Look at slot i. If it is empty, the key is absent: raise KeyError.
  4. If it holds an entry, compare the stored hash with h. If they differ, it cannot be our key. If they match, check stored_key is "cat" or stored_key == "cat". On success, return the value.
  5. Otherwise, compute the next slot with the recurrence from CPython's source, i = (5*i + 1 + perturb) mod size, where perturb starts as the full hash and is shifted right by 5 bits each step. Mixing in the high bits spreads out keys whose low bits collide. Go back to step 3.

Storing the hash in each entry means collisions are usually rejected by comparing two integers, without calling a possibly slow __eq__, and a resize can reinsert everything without recomputing any hashes.

The memory layout is the clever part. Since Python 3.6 a dict holds two arrays. The entries array is dense and stores (hash, key, value) triples in the order they were inserted. The indices array is the actual hash table: a sparse array of small integers, each either "empty" or a position in the entries array. The load-factor slack now costs only one to eight bytes per empty index slot rather than a 24-byte empty entry. And because entries are appended in order, iterating the dict walks the dense array in insertion order — which is why, since 3.7, insertion order is a language guarantee, not a coincidence.

A few behaviours follow from this design. Reassigning an existing key updates its entry in place, so it keeps its original position: d = {"b": 1, "a": 2}; d["c"] = 3; d["b"] = 9 iterates as ['b', 'a', 'c']. Deleting a key marks its entry as a dummy rather than shifting the array, so probe sequences through that slot keep working; the space is only reclaimed at the next resize, and a dict never shrinks just because you delete. Adding or removing keys while iterating would invalidate the walk, so CPython detects it: RuntimeError: dictionary changed size during iteration. Iterate over list(d) if you need to modify.

The views returned by d.keys() and d.items() are live (they reflect later changes) and support set operations: d.keys() & {"a", "z"} gives {'a'}. And because keys are compared by hash and ==, keys that are equal are the same key even if their types differ: {1: "int", 1.0: "float"} evaluates to {1: 'float'}, since 1 == 1.0 and hash(1) == hash(1.0).

6. set and frozenset

A set is a hash table of keys with no values, so membership, add and remove are O(1) on average. Sets use their own table (not the compact dict layout), which is why they are not ordered. They shine at two jobs. The first is fast membership, the fix for the deduplication script: keep seen = set() and test uid not in seen. (If you just need order-preserving deduplication, list(dict.fromkeys(items)) does it in one line, using a dict's keys as an ordered set: list(dict.fromkeys([3, 1, 3, 2, 1])) is [3, 1, 2].) The second is set algebra, where each operation costs time proportional to the sizes involved:

{1, 2, 3} | {3, 4}      # union:        {1, 2, 3, 4}
{1, 2, 3} & {2, 3, 9}   # intersection: {2, 3}
{1, 2, 3} - {1}         # difference:   {2, 3}
{1, 2} ^ {2, 3}         # symmetric difference: {1, 3}

frozenset is the immutable, hashable version, usable as a dict key — for example, a key representing an unordered pair of users.

7. collections.deque: a queue that is fast at both ends

For a first-in, first-out queue you need to add at one end and remove at the other. A list can only do one of those cheaply. collections.deque ("double-ended queue", pronounced "deck") is implemented as a doubly linked list of fixed-size blocks, each holding 64 references. Adding or removing at either end touches only the end block, and allocates or frees a block occasionally, so append, appendleft, pop and popleft are all O(1). The cost is that reaching the middle means walking blocks: dq[i] is O(1) near the ends but O(n) toward the middle.

The difference is dramatic, and grows with n because pop(0) is O(n) per call and therefore O(n²) to drain:

from collections import deque
# drain a queue of n items; measured on 3.12
# n = 10,000:  list.pop(0)   12.3 ms   deque.popleft   1.5 ms
# n = 100,000: list.pop(0) 1488.7 ms   deque.popleft  10.7 ms

Ten times more items made the list version 120 times slower — the signature of O(n²). A deque with maxlen is also a ready-made ring buffer that discards from the opposite end when full: after appending 0 to 4 into deque(maxlen=3) it holds deque([2, 3, 4], maxlen=3), perfect for "the last N events".

8. heapq: always know the smallest item

A heap is a binary tree in which every parent is less than or equal to its children, so the smallest item is always at the root. heapq stores this tree in a plain list with no pointers: the children of index i are at 2i + 1 and 2i + 2. Pushing appends at the end and "sifts up", swapping with the parent while smaller; popping takes the root, moves the last item to the root and "sifts down". Each walk is at most the tree's height, log₂ n, so push and pop are O(log n) and peeking at heap[0] is O(1). heapify(list) builds a heap in O(n).

Two practical patterns. First, heapq is a min-heap only, so for a max-heap push negated priorities. Second, if you push (priority, item) tuples and two priorities tie, Python compares the items, which fails for unorderable items like dicts (TypeError: '<' not supported between instances of 'dict' and 'dict'). The standard fix is (priority, next(counter), item) with counter = itertools.count(), which breaks ties by insertion order. heapq.nlargest(k, iterable) and nsmallest keep a heap of only k items, making "top k of a huge stream" O(n log k) time and O(k) memory: heapq.nlargest(2, [5, 1, 9, 3]) is [9, 5].

9. bisect: binary search on a sorted list

If a list is sorted you can find where a value belongs by binary search: compare with the middle element and discard the half it cannot be in, repeating until one position remains — O(log n). bisect.bisect_left(a, x) returns the leftmost position where x could be inserted keeping order, bisect_right the rightmost: for [1, 3, 5, 7] and x = 5 they return 2 and 3. bisect.insort(a, x) inserts in order. Searching is O(log n), but inserting still shifts elements, so it is O(n) overall. Use bisect for lookup tables (grade boundaries, time-bucketing) and mostly-read sorted data; for heavy inserts into a sorted collection, the third-party sortedcontainers package is the usual answer. Since Python 3.10 the bisect functions accept key=.

10. The dict variants in collections

  • Counter counts hashable items: Counter("mississippi").most_common(2) gives [('i', 4), ('s', 4)]. It supports addition and subtraction of counts.
  • defaultdict(factory) calls factory() to create a value for a missing key, so grouping becomes groups[key].append(item) with no existence check. Beware that merely reading a missing key inserts it.
  • OrderedDict is mostly superseded by ordered dicts, but keeps two useful methods: move_to_end(key) and popitem(last=False), which together implement a least-recently-used (LRU) cache in a few lines. With od built from "abc", od.move_to_end("a") gives order ['b', 'c', 'a'] and popitem(last=False) removes 'b'.
  • ChainMap searches several dicts in order without merging them — command-line overrides over environment settings over defaults. ChainMap({"debug": True}, {"debug": False, "port": 80}) returns True for "debug" and 80 for "port".

11. Memory: why Python containers are big

Every Python object carries a header. An int is 28 bytes for small values, more for big ones (sys.getsizeof(10**100) is 72). A list of a million ints is therefore about 8 MB of pointers plus about 28 MB of int objects (small cached ints aside). An empty dict is 64 bytes and a one-key dict 184. Millions of small dicts or objects add up to gigabytes.

When the data is numeric and homogeneous, store raw values instead of objects. The standard library's array.array('d', ...) stores C doubles contiguously at 8 bytes each. NumPy does the same and adds fast vectorised maths implemented in C, typically several to tens of times smaller and faster than lists of Python numbers. For record-like data, __slots__ classes (py6), NamedTuples, or columnar tools such as pandas, Polars and Arrow remove the per-record dictionary. py11 returns to measuring and fixing these costs.
deep:
The probe sequence and why low bits are enough

CPython's hash for small integers is the integer itself, which looks like a terrible hash: hash(5) == 5. The source comments in dictobject.c argue that it is actually good: for a contiguous range of int keys, taking the low bits gives zero collisions, better than random. The weakness appears when keys share low bits (for example all multiples of 65,536). That is handled by the probe recurrence j = (5*j + 1 + perturb) mod 2**i with perturb >>= 5 on each step: the first few probes mix in progressively higher bits of the hash, and once perturb reaches zero the 5*j + 1 recurrence alone visits every slot of a power-of-two table, guaranteeing termination because at least one slot is always empty.

Load factor, growth and the never-shrinking dict

USABLE_FRACTION(n) in the 3.12 source is (2n)/3: a table of 8 index slots holds at most 5 entries before resizing. When it resizes, the new size is based on GROWTH_RATE = used × 3, rounded up to a power of two, so a table roughly doubles or quadruples. Deletions only turn entries into dummies and decrement the used count; the table is compacted only when an insertion triggers a resize. Consequence: a dict used as a cache that once held millions of entries and has since been emptied with del still occupies its peak memory. d.clear() releases the table, and rebuilding with dict(d) creates a right-sized copy.

Key-sharing dictionaries for instances

Most objects store their attributes in a per-instance __dict__. Since Python 3.3 (PEP 412), instances of the same class share a single keys table and each instance stores only its values array, because objects of one class usually have the same attribute names set in the same order in __init__. 3.11 went further and stores those values inline in the object, creating a real dict only if someone asks for __dict__. This is why setting attributes in a consistent order in __init__ is slightly better for memory, and why adding attributes dynamically outside __init__ can make an instance fall back to a private dict.

The list growth pattern and pre-sizing

The 3.12 formula (newsize + (newsize >> 3) + 6) & ~3 gives capacities 0, 4, 8, 16, 24, 32, 40, 52, 64, 76 and so on — about 1.125× per step once large. Growth is deliberately mild to avoid wasting memory, relying on the system allocator to extend blocks in place where possible. Building a list with a comprehension or list(iterable) lets CPython size it once when the length is known, which is faster than repeated appends; [None] * n preallocates when you will fill by index. When a list shrinks below half its capacity, the next resize reallocates smaller.

Sorting internals and key functions

The sort first finds natural runs — maximal ascending or strictly descending stretches, which it reverses — and extends short runs to a minimum length with binary insertion sort. It then merges runs using "galloping" (exponential search) when one run repeatedly wins, which makes merging data with long pre-sorted stretches very cheap. The merge policy decides which adjacent runs to merge; Python 3.11 adopted Munro and Wild's Powersort policy, which is provably near-optimal in the pattern of run lengths. The key= function is evaluated exactly once per element and the results are cached alongside the items, so an expensive key such as a regex extraction costs n calls, not n log n. Sorting also only uses <, so a class needs only __lt__ to be sortable.

Hash-flooding and SipHash

If an attacker can predict hashes, they can post a request with thousands of keys that all collide, forcing every dict insert to probe past all previous colliding keys: O(n²) work for one request. Since Python 3.4 (PEP 456), str and bytes hashes use SipHash, a keyed hash function, with a key chosen randomly at startup (Python 3.11 switched to the faster SipHash-1-3 variant). Without the key, collisions cannot be precomputed. The cost is that string hashes and therefore set iteration order differ from run to run, which occasionally breaks tests that assumed an order.

Thread safety and the free-threaded build

With the GIL (the Global Interpreter Lock, covered in py8, which lets only one thread execute Python bytecode at a time), individual operations on built-in containers implemented as a single C call — append, d[k] = v, deque.popleft — appear atomic. Read-modify-write sequences like d[k] += 1 or "check if key exists, then insert" are several bytecodes and can interleave, losing updates. The free-threaded build (PEP 703; experimental in 3.13, officially supported but still optional in 3.14 per PEP 779) removes the GIL and protects each list and dict with a lightweight per-object lock, so single operations remain safe, but compound ones still need threading.Lock. queue.Queue and collections.deque's append/popleft are the documented thread-safe choices for producer-consumer patterns.
prod:
Accidental quadratic behaviour

The characteristic production symptom is a job that is fine in staging and times out in production, with run time growing much faster than data volume: 10× the rows, 100× the time. The usual culprits are membership tests against a list inside a loop, list.pop(0) or insert(0, ...) queues, building strings with += in a loop (each concatenation can copy the whole string; use "".join(parts)), and repeatedly sorting a list to get its maximum. A profiler (py11) points straight at them: the hot line will be a single in, pop or sort with a huge call count or time.

Memory blow-ups from object overhead

Loading a 1 GB CSV into a list of dicts commonly consumes 5-10 GB of RAM, because each row becomes a dict of Python strings and ints, each with its own header and hash table. The fixes, in order of effort: read in chunks and stream instead of materialising; use tuples or __slots__ objects; load into pandas, Polars or Arrow, which store each column as one typed buffer. Measure with tracemalloc rather than sys.getsizeof, which ignores referenced objects (py1).

Caches that never shrink

An unbounded dict used as a cache grows until the process is killed for exceeding its memory limit, and, because dicts do not shrink on delete, even a cache that evicts by deleting keys keeps its peak table size. Use functools.lru_cache(maxsize=...) or an OrderedDict-based LRU with a bound, or a library such as cachetools with TTL (time-to-live) expiry. Watch the process's resident memory (RSS) over days, not minutes: slow leaks from caches are the classic "restarts fix it" bug.

Order-dependent bugs

Code that iterates a set of strings and relies on the order — writing output files, generating ids, choosing the first match — produces different results on each run because of hash randomisation. It passes locally by luck and fails in CI (continuous integration) or differs between replicas. Sort explicitly (sorted(s)) wherever order is observable. The inverse surprise: dicts built from sets inherit the set's arbitrary order.

Choosing structures under concurrency

Worker pools that share a plain list or dict as a work queue lose or duplicate items under load because check-then-act sequences interleave. Use queue.Queue for threads, multiprocessing.Queue for processes, and asyncio.Queue for coroutines (py9). These have blocking get, bounded sizes for backpressure, and correct locking.

A common AI-engineering case: embeddings and vocabularies

Storing a million 768-dimensional embeddings as a list of Python lists of floats costs roughly 24 bytes per float object plus an 8-byte pointer, around 25 GB, and every similarity computation runs in the interpreter one float at a time. The same data as a single NumPy float32 array is about 3 GB and a matrix multiply runs in optimised C. Conversely, a tokenizer's vocabulary (token string to integer id) is exactly what a dict is for: a few hundred thousand keys with O(1) lookups. Knowing which side of that line your data sits on is most of the performance work in data-heavy Python services.

Seeing it

Useful tools: timeit for micro-benchmarks of alternatives; cProfile and py-spy for finding hot lines in real workloads; tracemalloc and memray for memory; and the Python wiki's TimeComplexity page as the reference for what each operation costs. A good habit in code review is to ask, for every loop, "what is the cost of the operations inside it, and how large can n get?"
myths: Dicts are unordered, so never rely on their order.

Since Python 3.7 the language guarantees that dicts iterate in insertion order (CPython 3.6 already did it as an implementation detail). Sets, however, really are unordered, and their iteration order can change between runs.
x in my_list and x in my_set are about the same speed.

A list check compares against every element until it finds a match, so its cost grows with the list; a set check hashes the value and looks in one slot. On a million elements the measured gap in this lesson was about 12 milliseconds versus about a tenth of a microsecond.
Appending to a list is sometimes slow because it has to copy the whole list.

It does occasionally copy, but the list over-allocates spare capacity in proportion to its size, so copies become rarer as it grows. Averaged over many appends the cost per append is constant; this is what amortised O(1) means.
A list works fine as a queue.

Appending to the end is cheap, but pop(0) shifts every remaining element one slot left, which costs O(n) per pop. Draining 100,000 items took about 1.5 seconds with pop(0) and about 11 milliseconds with deque.popleft() in this lesson's run.
O(1) means fast, O(n) means slow.

Big-O describes how cost grows with size, not the cost itself. A dict lookup has a large constant (hash the key, probe, compare) and a list scan of five elements can beat it. Complexity matters when n is large or the operation sits inside a loop.
Deleting keys from a dict frees its memory.

Deleting leaves a placeholder (a 'dummy' entry) in the table and never shrinks it. A dict that once held a million keys keeps its large table until it is rebuilt, for example with d = dict(d) or d = {k: v for k, v in d.items()}.
lab:
About 15 minutes with plain Python 3.10+; the numbers below are from CPython 3.12.10 on a laptop and yours will differ, but the ratios should be similar.

  1. Watch a list grow. 
    import sys
lst, last = [], sys.getsizeof([])
for i in range(70):
    lst.append(i)
    s = sys.getsizeof(lst)
    if s != last:
        print(len(lst), (s - 56) // 8)
        last = s

    Expect capacities 4, 8, 16, 24, 32, 40, 52, 64, 76 as length crosses each boundary. What it proves: reallocation is rare and proportional, so append is amortised O(1).

  2. Time in on list versus set. 
    import timeit
setup = "L = list(range(1_000_000)); S = set(L)"
print(timeit.timeit("999_999 in L", setup, number=20) / 20)
print(timeit.timeit("999_999 in S", setup, number=100_000) / 100_000)

    Expect milliseconds versus tens of nanoseconds. Try 0 in L: fast, because the scan stops at the first element — O(n) is the worst case.

  3. Show quadratic growth. Time draining a list with pop(0) for n = 10,000, 20,000 and 40,000. Each doubling should roughly quadruple the time. Repeat with deque.popleft() and see it roughly double.
  4. Break a heap with ties, then fix it. 
    import heapq, itertools
h = []
heapq.heappush(h, (1, {"x": 1}))
heapq.heappush(h, (1, {"y": 2}))   # TypeError: '<' not supported ... 'dict'
c = itertools.count()
h = []
heapq.heappush(h, (1, next(c), {"x": 1}))
heapq.heappush(h, (1, next(c), {"y": 2}))
print(heapq.heappop(h))            # (1, 0, {'x': 1})
  5. See insertion order and equal keys. Evaluate {1: "int", 1.0: "float", True: "bool"} and explain the result ({1: 'bool'}: all three keys are equal and hash equally, so the first key is kept and the last value wins).
  6. Measure a dict's memory not shrinking. 
    import sys
d = {i: i for i in range(100_000)}
print(sys.getsizeof(d))
for i in range(99_990): del d[i]
print(len(d), sys.getsizeof(d))      # 10 entries, same big size
print(sys.getsizeof(dict(d)))         # rebuilt: small

Afterwards, rewrite the dedupe loop from the introduction with a set and time both versions on 20,000 random ids.
recap: Big-O notation describes how an operation's cost grows with the number of elements n; O(1) does not grow, O(log n) grows very slowly, O(n) grows in proportion.
A list is a dynamic array of references with spare capacity, so indexing and append are O(1) (append amortised) while inserting, deleting or searching anywhere but the end is O(n).
A tuple is a fixed-size immutable array; it is a little smaller than a list, is hashable when its contents are, and is the natural type for fixed records and composite dict keys.
A dict is a hash table: it hashes the key, uses the low bits to choose a slot, probes further on collision, and keeps the table at most two-thirds full, giving O(1) average lookup, insert and delete.
CPython's compact dict stores entries in a dense array in insertion order plus a sparse index table, which saves memory and is why dicts are ordered since 3.7.
A set is a hash table of keys without values, giving O(1) average membership and fast union, intersection and difference; it is unordered.
collections.deque gives O(1) appends and pops at both ends and is the right queue; heapq gives O(log n) push and pop of the smallest item; bisect searches a sorted list in O(log n).
Counter, defaultdict, OrderedDict and ChainMap are dict variants that remove boilerplate for counting, grouping, LRU ordering and layered lookups.
Every Python object carries a header, so a million small ints in a list cost tens of megabytes; NumPy or array store raw numbers contiguously and are several times smaller and faster.
The most common performance bugs are membership tests on lists inside loops, list.pop(0) queues, and sorting everything to get the top few items.
glossary: Amortised cost
The average cost per operation over a long sequence of operations, which can be low even if a few individual operations are expensive.
Big-O notation
A way of describing how an algorithm's time or memory grows as the input size n grows, ignoring constant factors.
Bisect
Binary search: repeatedly halving a sorted range to find where a value belongs, taking O(log n) steps.
Capacity
The number of slots a list has allocated, which is at least its length; the extra slots let appends avoid reallocating.
Collision
Two different keys whose hashes select the same slot in a hash table, so one must be placed elsewhere.
Compact dict
CPython's dict layout since 3.6: a dense entries array in insertion order plus a small sparse index table pointing into it.
Deque
A double-ended queue; in CPython a linked list of fixed-size blocks that supports O(1) operations at both ends.
Dummy entry
A placeholder left in a hash table slot when a key is deleted, so that probing for other keys still works.
Dynamic array
An array that grows by allocating a larger block and copying when it runs out of room; Python's list is one.
GIL
Global Interpreter Lock: CPython's lock that lets only one thread run Python bytecode at a time (py8).
Hash table
A structure that stores items in slots chosen from each key's hash, giving average constant-time lookup.
Heap
A binary tree stored in an array where every parent is no larger than its children, so the smallest item is always at index 0.
Load factor
The fraction of a hash table's slots that are in use; CPython resizes a dict before it passes two-thirds.
LRU cache
A cache that, when full, evicts the least recently used entry first.
Open addressing
A collision strategy where a colliding key is stored in another slot of the same array, found by a fixed probe sequence.
Probe sequence
The order of slots a hash table visits when the first-choice slot is taken.
RSS
Resident set size: the amount of physical memory a process is actually using, the number memory limits are enforced against.
Stable sort
A sort that keeps items with equal keys in their original relative order.
Time complexity
How the running time of an operation scales with input size, usually written in big-O notation.
TTL
Time to live: how long a cached entry stays valid before it expires.
drill:
Fix the complexity 
# 1. dedupe while keeping order
out = []
for x in items:                # n = 1,000,000
    if x not in out:
        out.append(x)

# 2. process a work queue
queue = [start]
while queue:
    node = queue.pop(0)
    queue.extend(neighbours(node))

# 3. top 10 scores from 50M records streamed from disk
scores = sorted(read_all(), reverse=True)[:10]
Answer

1. x not in out scans a list, O(n), inside a loop of n, so the whole thing is O(n²) — hundreds of billions of comparisons at a million items. Keep a set for membership next to the output list: seen = set(), and append only when x not in seen, adding it to seen. That is O(n) overall. A one-liner that keeps order: list(dict.fromkeys(items)), because dict keys are unique and ordered.

2. list.pop(0) shifts every remaining pointer, O(n) per pop. Use collections.deque and popleft(), O(1). Also, a breadth-first search over a graph needs a visited set; without one, any cycle makes the loop run forever.

3. Sorting 50 million items is O(n log n) time and needs all of them in memory at once. heapq.nlargest(10, stream) keeps only a 10-element heap: O(n log 10) time and O(10) memory, and it consumes a generator that reads the file lazily.
qa: E
What is the time complexity of x in some_list versus x in some_set?

O(n) for a list, because it compares x against each element in turn, and O(1) on average for a set or dict, because it hashes x and inspects one slot (plus a few probes on collision). Converting a list to a set before repeated membership tests is one of the most common Python performance fixes.
Follow-up: When would you not convert? — When you test membership only once or twice, since building the set is itself O(n), or when the elements are unhashable.
E
Are Python dicts ordered? Are sets?

Dicts are: since Python 3.7 the language guarantees iteration in insertion order, and reassigning an existing key keeps its position. Sets are not ordered, and their iteration order depends on hash values, which for strings change between runs because of hash randomisation.
E
Why does list.append run in amortised O(1) time?

The list allocates more slots than it needs, roughly an extra eighth plus a small constant each time it grows. Most appends just fill a spare slot; only occasionally does it reallocate and copy. Because the extra room is proportional to the size, the total copying over n appends is O(n), so the average per append is constant.
M
How do you get a max-heap with heapq, and why add a counter to heap entries?

heapq only implements a min-heap, so push negated priorities, e.g. (-score, item). Push (priority, counter, item) tuples where counter comes from itertools.count(): equal priorities are then broken by the counter, so Python never compares the items themselves, which may be unorderable (dicts raise TypeError) or expensive to compare. The counter also makes ties first-in first-out.
Follow-up: How do you change an item's priority? — Mark the old entry as removed (lazy deletion) and push a new one; skip removed entries when popping, as the heapq docs describe.
M
Walk through how a dict looks up a key.

It computes hash(key), takes the low bits as a starting index into its index table, and reads that slot. If the slot points to an entry whose stored hash equals the key's hash and whose key is the same object or compares ==, that is the match. If the slot is empty the key is absent. Otherwise it collided, so it moves to the next slot in a pseudo-random probe sequence that mixes in higher hash bits, and repeats.
Follow-up: Why store the hash in the entry? — So collisions can be rejected by comparing integers before calling a possibly expensive __eq__, and so resizing never needs to rehash keys.
M
What's the difference between a list, a tuple and a NamedTuple or dataclass for a record?

A list is mutable and variable-length, suited to collections of similar items. A tuple is immutable, slightly smaller and hashable, suited to fixed records and dict keys, but fields are accessed by position. A NamedTuple is a tuple with named fields, keeping immutability and hashability. A dataclass is a regular class with generated methods, better when you need mutability, defaults, methods or validation.
M
Why is collections.deque better than a list for a queue, and when is it worse?

list.pop(0) and insert(0, x) shift every other element, O(n) each, while deque stores items in a linked list of fixed-size blocks and supports append, appendleft, pop and popleft in O(1). But indexing into the middle of a deque is O(n), since it must walk blocks, whereas a list indexes in O(1). Use deque for FIFO queues, BFS and sliding windows; use a list when you need random access.
M
How would you find the 10 largest values in a stream of 50 million numbers?

Use heapq.nlargest(10, stream), which keeps a min-heap of the 10 best seen so far and replaces the smallest when a larger value arrives. That is O(n log k) time with k = 10 and O(k) memory, and it works on a generator, so the data never has to fit in memory. Sorting would be O(n log n) and need all 50 million values in memory.
M
Two keys 1 and 1.0 go into the same dict. What happens?

They are equal and have the same hash, so the dict treats them as the same key: {1: 'int', 1.0: 'float'} produces {1: 'float'}. The first key object inserted is kept and only the value is replaced. This follows directly from the hash/eq contract: equal objects must hash equally, and the dict relies on equality to decide identity of keys.
H
Why can a dict lookup degrade to O(n), and what does Python do about it?

If many keys land on the same probe sequence, each lookup must walk past all of them. With a good hash this is rare, but an attacker who can predict hashes can craft thousands of colliding keys, for example in JSON request bodies, turning each insert into a scan and the whole request into O(n²) work. Python randomises the hash of str and bytes with a per-process secret key (SipHash) so collisions cannot be precomputed. Integers are not randomised, which is fine because their hashes are trivially predictable but also well distributed for normal data.
Follow-up: Does randomisation affect you in tests? — Set iteration order of strings changes between runs, so tests must not depend on it; PYTHONHASHSEED=0 makes it reproducible when debugging.
H
Explain CPython's compact dict layout and why it saved memory.

Before 3.6 a dict was one sparse array of (hash, key, value) entries, a third of which was always empty because of the two-thirds load factor, so a third of 24-byte entries was wasted. The compact layout keeps a dense entries array of those triples in insertion order and a separate sparse index array of small integers (1, 2, 4 or 8 bytes depending on size) that point into it. The emptiness is now in the tiny index array, which saved 20 to 25 percent of memory, made iteration faster (it walks a dense array) and gave insertion order for free.

Follow-up: What about instance __dict__s? — Since 3.3 (PEP 412) instances of the same class can share one keys table and only store their values, and 3.11 and later inline values further; __slots__ removes the dict altogether.
H
Your service holds 20 million small records as dicts and uses 12 GB. How would you shrink it?

Each dict carries its own header and hash table, easily 200+ bytes before the values. Options in increasing effort: classes with __slots__ or NamedTuples, which store fields in a fixed array and drop the per-object table; interning repeated strings; storing columns instead of rows, e.g. one array or NumPy array per field, which removes per-object headers entirely; or moving to Arrow, pandas or Polars, which store typed columns contiguously. Measure with tracemalloc before and after, since getsizeof does not count referenced objects.
Follow-up: What do you lose with a columnar layout? — Convenient per-record objects and cheap single-record mutation; you gain vectorised operations and often 5-10x less memory.
H
Is list.append thread-safe? Is d[k] += 1?

On the standard GIL build each individual list or dict operation implemented in C runs without interruption, so a single append from several threads will not corrupt the list. d[k] += 1 is a read, an add and a write as separate steps, and a thread switch between them loses updates. The free-threaded build (optional since 3.13, officially supported in 3.14) keeps single operations safe with per-object locks, but compound operations still need a threading.Lock or a thread-safe structure such as queue.Queue. Relying on implicit atomicity is fragile either way.

sum: What def really creates, how arguments are matched to parameters (positional, keyword, *args, **kwargs, / and *), how Python decides which variable a name means (LEGB), and how closures keep variables alive, including the late-binding trap.
prereq: py1
Names are bound to objects in namespaces; assignment binds and never copies; default arguments are evaluated once when def runs.
why:
A developer is wiring up a small dashboard. For each of three data sources they create a button, and each button's click handler should refresh its own source. The code is a tidy loop:

handlers = []
for source in ["sales", "users", "errors"]:
    handlers.append(lambda: refresh(source))

Every button refreshes "errors". Nothing is misspelled and there is no exception. The bug comes from how Python decides what the name source means inside the lambda, and when it looks up its value.

A second developer adds a request counter to a module: count = 0 at the top, and count += 1 inside the handler function. The first request crashes with UnboundLocalError: cannot access local variable 'count' — even though count is right there, one screen up, with a value of zero. A third adds a flag to a widely used function, def connect(host, port, timeout, retries, verify), and six months later a caller swaps the two middle numbers and nobody notices until production retries for five minutes instead of five seconds.

Functions are the first abstraction every Python programmer learns, and these bugs show that "I can write a function" and "I know what a function does" are different things. The rules involved are small — how arguments are matched to parameters, which scope a name belongs to, and what a closure captures — but they are precise, and getting them slightly wrong produces exactly this kind of quiet misbehaviour. They also underpin everything that comes later in this track: decorators (py4) are closures, generators (py5) are suspended function frames, and frameworks like pytest and FastAPI read your function signatures to decide what to pass in.

This lesson starts from what a def statement actually creates, then walks through calling: how Python matches arguments to parameters, defaults, *args and **kwargs, and the / and * markers. Then scope: namespaces, the LEGB lookup order, the compile-time rule behind UnboundLocalError, global and nonlocal, and the special cases of class bodies and comprehensions. Then closures: what a cell is, how state survives after a function returns, and why the loop above breaks. It ends with functions as values — higher-order functions, lambdas and functools.partial. Everything was run on CPython 3.12.10; version-specific behaviour is marked.
primer:
A function is an object that holds a recipe

Think of a def statement as writing a recipe card and filing it under a name. Writing the card does not cook anything. Later, each call takes the card, sets out a fresh, empty kitchen counter, puts the ingredients you handed over onto it with labels, follows the steps, hands back the result, and wipes the counter clean.

In Python terms: def runs like any other statement and creates a function object — containing the compiled code, the default values and a reference to the module's global namespace — and binds it to a name (py1: binding). Each call creates a call frame, a fresh record holding that call's local namespace, and binds each parameter (the names in the definition) to the matching argument (the values at the call site). When the function returns, the frame is discarded along with its local names, unless something still refers to them.

def greet(name, greeting="Hello", *, punctuation="!"):
    return f"{greeting}, {name}{punctuation}"

greet("Asha")                     # 'Hello, Asha!'
greet("Asha", "Hi")               # 'Hi, Asha!'
greet("Asha", punctuation=".")    # 'Hello, Asha.'
greet("Asha", "Hi", ".")          # TypeError: greet() takes from 1 to 2 positional arguments but 3 were given

Arguments can be passed by position or by name (keyword arguments). Parameters can have defaults. The bare * in the definition means everything after it must be passed by name, which is why the last call fails.

Which variable does a name mean?

Inside a function, a name could refer to a local variable, a variable of an enclosing function, a module-level variable, or a built-in like len. Python searches in that order — Local, Enclosing, Global, Built-in, "LEGB" — and uses the first match. The twist is that Python decides whether a name is local before the function ever runs: if the function assigns to the name anywhere, it is local everywhere in that function.

Functions that remember

A function defined inside another function can use the outer function's variables — and keeps them alive after the outer function has returned. That combination is a closure:

def make_multiplier(n):
    def multiply(x):
        return x * n        # n belongs to make_multiplier
    return multiply

double = make_multiplier(2)
double(5)                   # 10 — n is still 2, long after make_multiplier returned

This is how Python functions carry configuration and state without a class, and it is the mechanism behind decorators in the next lesson. The one thing to remember now: the closure remembers the variable, not a snapshot of its value, which is the root of the loop bug in the introduction.

Where the recipe analogy breaks: the kitchen counter is not always wiped clean. If a closure still refers to some of the frame's variables, those survive. And unlike a paper recipe, the function object is a live Python object you can inspect, pass around, store in a dict and even attach attributes to.
body:
1. What def creates

Python code is first compiled into bytecode, a compact list of instructions for the interpreter. When the compiler meets a function, it produces a code object for the body. Then, when the module actually runs and reaches the def line, Python executes it: it evaluates the default values, builds a function object that bundles the code object, the defaults, the module's global namespace and any captured variables, and binds the function's name to it.

def f():
    pass

print(f(), f.__name__, type(f.__code__))
# None f <class 'code'>

Three consequences follow. A function with no return (or a bare return) returns None. A def inside an if or inside another function creates a new function object every time that line runs. And defaults are evaluated once, at def time — the mutable-default trap from py1.

2. Matching arguments to parameters

When you call a function, Python must decide which argument goes into which parameter. The algorithm is mechanical, and knowing it explains every argument-related TypeError:

  1. Positional arguments fill positional parameters left to right. If there are more positional arguments than positional parameters, the extras go into *args if the function has it, and otherwise raise "takes N positional arguments but M were given".
  2. Keyword arguments are matched by name. If the named parameter was already filled in step 1, Python raises "got multiple values for argument". If no parameter has that name, it goes into **kwargs if present, and otherwise raises "got an unexpected keyword argument".
  3. Defaults fill any parameters still empty.
  4. Anything still empty raises "missing required argument".
def g(a, b, c=3):
    return (a, b, c)

g(1, c=5, b=2)     # (1, 2, 5)  — a by position, b and c by name
g(1, 2, a=3)       # TypeError: g() got multiple values for argument 'a'
g(1)               # TypeError: g() missing 1 required positional argument: 'b'

2a. Returning values and unpacking them

A function returns exactly one object. "Returning several values" is really returning one tuple: return a, b, c builds the tuple (a, b, c), because commas, not parentheses, make a tuple. The caller can keep the tuple or unpack it into several names in one assignment:

def stats(xs):
    return min(xs), max(xs), sum(xs) / len(xs)

r = stats([3, 1, 2])            # (1, 3, 2.0)  — one tuple
lo, hi, mean = stats([3, 1, 2]) # 1 3 2.0      — unpacked into three names

Unpacking requires the counts to match: a, b = [1, 2, 3] raises ValueError: too many values to unpack (expected 2). A starred name absorbs "the rest" as a list, which is handy for head/tail splits: first, *rest = [10, 20, 30, 40] gives 10 and [20, 30, 40], and *init, last = "abc" gives ['a', 'b'] and 'c'. When a function returns more than three or four values, callers start mixing up positions; return a NamedTuple or dataclass instead so each field has a name.

2b. Docstrings and annotations

Two optional parts of a def are stored on the function object for tools and readers. A string literal as the first statement of the body is the docstring, available as f.__doc__ and shown by help(f) and editors. Annotations after parameters and after -> record intended types:

def area(w: float, h: float = 1.0) -> float:
    """Return the area of a w-by-h rectangle."""
    return w * h

area.__annotations__   # {'w': <class 'float'>, 'h': <class 'float'>, 'return': <class 'float'>}
area("ab", 2)          # 'abab' — annotations are not enforced at runtime

The last line matters: Python itself ignores annotations when calling the function, so a string multiplied by 2 happily returns 'abab'. They are checked by separate tools such as mypy and Pyright, and read by frameworks such as FastAPI and Pydantic. py10 covers type hints properly; for now, read them as documentation that tools can verify.

3. Collecting and unpacking: *args and **kwargs

A parameter written with one star collects every surplus positional argument into a tuple; one with two stars collects every surplus keyword argument into a dict. The names args and kwargs are just convention.

def v(*args, **kwargs):
    return args, kwargs

v(1, 2, x=3)       # ((1, 2), {'x': 3})

At a call site the same symbols do the reverse, unpacking a sequence into positional arguments and a mapping into keyword arguments:

nums = [1, 2, 3]
opts = {"sep": "-"}
print(*nums, **opts)     # same as print(1, 2, 3, sep="-")  → 1-2-3

Put together, def wrapper(*args, **kwargs): return inner(*args, **kwargs) forwards any call unchanged to another function. That one line is the skeleton of nearly every decorator in py4.

4. Positional-only and keyword-only parameters

Two markers in a parameter list restrict how parameters may be passed. Everything after a bare * (or after *args) is keyword-only: callers must use the name (PEP 3102, Python 3.0). Everything before a / is positional-only: callers must not use the name (PEP 570, Python 3.8). The general shape is:

def f(pos_only, /, normal, *, kw_only): ...
def pos(a, b, /, c, *, d):
    return a, b, c, d

pos(1, 2, 3, d=4)          # (1, 2, 3, 4)
pos(1, 2, c=3, d=4)        # (1, 2, 3, 4)
pos(a=1, b=2, c=3, d=4)    # TypeError: pos() got some positional-only arguments passed as keyword arguments: 'a, b'
pos(1, 2, 3, 4)            # TypeError: pos() takes 3 positional arguments but 4 were given

Why would you want either? Keyword-only parameters make call sites self-describing and robust: connect("db", 5432, timeout=5, retries=3) cannot be silently swapped, and you can later add or reorder options without breaking anyone. Positional-only parameters do the opposite job: the parameter name is not part of the public contract, so the author can rename it, and the name never collides with a key a caller passes through **kwargs. Many built-ins are positional-only for that reason; len(obj=[1]) fails.

5. Namespaces and the LEGB rule

Recall from py1 that a namespace maps names to objects. When a function runs there are several namespaces in play: the call's local namespace, the local namespaces of any enclosing functions, the module's global namespace, and the built-in namespace (the builtins module, home of len, print and the exception classes). The region of code in which a binding is visible is its scope. Name lookup searches Local, then Enclosing (innermost first), then Global, then Built-in:

x = "global"
def outer():
    x = "enclosing"
    def inner():
        return x
    return inner()

outer()     # 'enclosing'

Because built-ins come last, a module that defines its own len or a function with a parameter called list shadows the built-in in that scope. Linters warn about this for good reason.

6. Scope is decided at compile time

Here is the rule that produces UnboundLocalError. When the compiler processes a function body, it collects every name the function assigns to — by =, augmented assignment like +=, for targets, import, def, with ... as, except ... as. Those names are local for the whole body, and the compiler emits "load local" instructions for every use of them. There is no runtime fallback to the global.

total = 0
def add(x):
    total += x          # reads local total, which has no value yet
    return total

add(1)
# UnboundLocalError: cannot access local variable 'total' where it is not associated with a value

Walk through it: total += x means "load total, add x, store total". The store makes total local. At runtime the load looks in the local slot, finds it empty, and raises. The global total is never consulted.

Two declarations change the rule for a name. global total says: in this function, total means the module-level variable, and assignments rebind it there. nonlocal n says: n means the variable in the nearest enclosing function, and assignments rebind it there. Note what does not need a declaration: mutating an object through a name (items.append(1), config["k"] = v) is not an assignment to the name, so it works on a global or enclosing object without global or nonlocal (py1: mutation versus rebinding).

Idiomatic code rarely uses global. Module-level mutable state is hard to test and unsafe to share between threads; returning values, passing objects in, or keeping state on an instance are all clearer.

7. The two scope exceptions: class bodies and comprehensions

A class body runs in its own namespace, which becomes the class's attributes. But it is not an enclosing scope for functions defined inside it. A method looking up a bare name skips the class and goes straight to the module:

class C:
    y = 10
    def m(self):
        return y            # NameError: name 'y' is not defined

# write self.y or C.y instead

This is deliberate: methods are called later, from anywhere, and would otherwise depend on class-body variables in confusing ways. The same rule catches comprehensions in class bodies. A comprehension has its own scope, and its expression cannot see class attributes. Only its first (outermost) iterable is evaluated in the class scope:

class D:
    n = 3
    vals = [k for k in range(n)]      # OK: range(n) is evaluated in the class scope → [0, 1, 2]

class E:
    y = 10
    vals = [k * y for k in range(3)]  # NameError: name 'y' is not defined

In ordinary functions, the comprehension's own scope is what stops its loop variable from leaking: after i = 99; [i for i in range(3)], i is still 99. Since Python 3.12 (PEP 709) comprehensions are compiled inline rather than as hidden nested functions, which makes them faster, but the isolation of the loop variable is preserved.

8. Closures and cells

Normally a function's locals live in its frame and vanish when the call returns. But if an inner function references an outer function's variable, that variable must outlive the outer call. The compiler handles it by storing such variables in a cell: a tiny object that holds one reference. Both the outer frame and the inner function point at the same cell. The inner function keeps its cells in __closure__, and its code object lists their names in co_freevars (a free variable is one used in a function but defined in an enclosing one).

def counter():
    n = 0
    def inc():
        nonlocal n
        n += 1
        return n
    return inc

c1 = counter()
c1(); c1()
print(c1(), c1.__code__.co_freevars, c1.__closure__[0].cell_contents)
# 3 ('n',) 3
c2 = counter()
print(c2())      # 1 — a separate call to counter() made a separate cell

Two points to notice. First, nonlocal is required here because n += 1 rebinds n; without it, n would be local to inc and you would get UnboundLocalError. Second, several inner functions defined in the same call share the same cells — a getter and a setter returned together see each other's changes, which is a tiny object with private state.

The bytecode shows the machinery directly. On 3.12, dis of an outer function that creates a closure shows MAKE_CELL for the variable, STORE_DEREF to assign it, and LOAD_CLOSURE plus MAKE_FUNCTION ... (closure) to build the inner function; the inner function uses COPY_FREE_VARS and LOAD_DEREF ("dereference the cell") instead of the ordinary LOAD_FAST.

9. Late binding: the loop trap explained

A closure reads a cell's current contents each time it runs. When closures are created in a loop, they all share the single cell for the loop variable, and by the time any of them runs the loop has finished:

fns = [lambda: i for i in range(3)]
print([f() for f in fns])              # [2, 2, 2]

This is late binding: the name is looked up when the function is called, not when it is created. The dashboard bug in the introduction is exactly this: every handler reads source after the loop ended, when it was "errors".

Two fixes capture the value at creation time. A default argument is evaluated when the lambda is created (section 1), so lambda i=i: i stores the current value in the function's defaults. Or use functools.partial, which stores the argument in the partial object:

fns = [lambda i=i: i for i in range(3)]
print([f() for f in fns])                               # [0, 1, 2]

import functools
fns = [functools.partial(lambda i: i, i) for i in range(3)]
print([f() for f in fns])                               # [0, 1, 2]

The default-argument trick has one downside: the function now accepts an i argument that a caller could override by accident. partial or a small factory function (def make(i): return lambda: i, where each call creates a new cell) avoids that.

10. Functions as values

Because functions are first-class objects (py1), you can pass them to other functions. A function that takes or returns a function is a higher-order function. The everyday examples are sorted(rows, key=...), max(items, key=...), map and filter, and callback registration.

A lambda is an expression that creates a function whose body is one expression. It is the same kind of function object as one made by def, just anonymous: (lambda x: x * x).__name__ is '<lambda>', which is what appears in tracebacks. Use it for short key functions; use def for anything worth naming.

The operator module provides ready-made key functions that are faster and clearer than lambdas for common cases: sorted(rows, key=itemgetter(1)) sorts by the second field, attrgetter("name") by an attribute. functools.partial performs partial application: it fixes some arguments of a function and returns a new callable. cube = functools.partial(pow, exp=3) gives a function where cube(2) returns 8 (using the built-in pow, whose second parameter is called exp).

11. Recursion and its limit

A function may call itself. Each call creates a new frame, and CPython caps the depth of nested Python calls with a recursion limit, 1000 by default (sys.getrecursionlimit()). Exceeding it raises RecursionError: maximum recursion depth exceeded. CPython does not perform tail-call optimisation (reusing the frame when a function's last action is a call), so even tail-recursive code is limited. Recursion is natural for trees of known, modest depth; for arbitrary-depth input, use a loop and an explicit stack (a list you append to and pop from).
deep:
How the compiler chooses load instructions

The scope decision is visible in the bytecode. Locals use LOAD_FAST/STORE_FAST, which index directly into an array in the frame — no dictionary lookup at all, which is why local variable access is the fastest in Python. Globals and built-ins use LOAD_GLOBAL, which checks the module dict and then the builtins dict. Cell and free variables use LOAD_DEREF/STORE_DEREF through the cell. Since 3.11, the specialising adaptive interpreter (PEP 659) rewrites LOAD_GLOBAL at runtime into a specialised form that caches the lookup and checks a version number on the dicts, so repeated global lookups are cheap too; the old advice to copy globals into locals for speed now rarely matters.

Cheaper calls since 3.11

Before 3.11, every Python-to-Python call went through the C function that evaluates frames, recursing on the C stack and allocating a frame object on the heap. 3.11 made frames lightweight structs allocated in a contiguous per-thread stack and inlined Python-to-Python calls inside the interpreter loop, so a call no longer consumes C stack. Heap frame objects are only created if someone asks for them (a traceback, sys._getframe, a debugger). Calls still cost tens of nanoseconds — orders of magnitude more than a C function call — so in hot numeric loops vectorisation (py11) still beats factoring code into many tiny functions.

Recursion limits after the 3.11 changes

Because Python calls no longer recurse on the C stack, 3.12 made sys.setrecursionlimit apply to Python code only; recursion through C code (deep repr of nested structures, C extensions calling back into Python) is protected by a separate mechanism. Raising the Python limit is therefore much safer than it used to be, but it is still a smell: a limit of 100,000 frames means 100,000 frames of memory, and a recursion that deep over user-controlled input is a denial-of-service vector. Explicit stacks remain the robust answer.

locals(), exec and PEP 667 (3.13)

In a function, locals() historically returned a dict that was a cached, partially synchronised copy of the fast locals array; writing to it sometimes appeared to work and sometimes did not. PEP 667 in Python 3.13 made it well defined: in functions, generators, coroutines and comprehensions, each locals() call returns a fresh independent snapshot, and exec/eval without an explicit namespace run against such a snapshot, so assignments inside them never create real local variables. Debuggers use frame.f_locals, which is now a write-through proxy. If you need dynamic names, use a dict explicitly.

Comprehension inlining (PEP 709, 3.12)

Until 3.11, each list, dict or set comprehension compiled into a hidden nested function that was created and called on every evaluation. 3.12 inlines the comprehension's bytecode into the containing function, saving the function creation and call (up to about twice as fast for small comprehensions per the PEP), while pushing and popping the iteration variable so it still does not leak. Visible differences are small: tracebacks no longer show a separate <listcomp> frame, and locals() inside a comprehension now includes the enclosing function's variables. Generator expressions are not inlined, since they must suspend (py5).

Signatures as an API: inspect and frameworks

inspect.signature(pos) returns (a, b, /, c, *, d), a structured object listing each parameter's kind, default and annotation. Frameworks build on it: pytest injects fixtures by matching parameter names, FastAPI reads parameter names, defaults and type annotations to decide what comes from the URL path, the query string or the body, and Typer and Click-like tools build command-line interfaces from signatures. This is why renaming a parameter in such code is a behaviour change, and why decorators must preserve signatures with functools.wraps (py4).

Closures, pickling and processes

To send a callable to another process, multiprocessing and most task queues pickle it, and pickle stores functions by module and qualified name, to be re-imported on the other side. Lambdas and nested functions have names like <lambda> or outer.<locals>.inner that cannot be imported, so they fail to pickle. functools.partial of a module-level function pickles fine because it stores the function reference and the arguments. This is a common reason to prefer partial or a small class over a closure in data pipelines (py9).

Closures versus classes

A closure is the smallest possible object: private state (its cells) and exactly one behaviour. It avoids the ceremony of a class for callbacks and factories, and attribute lookups on self are replaced by fast cell loads. The trade-offs are that the state is invisible to debuggers and repr, cannot be reset or inspected without hacks, and cannot be pickled. A rule of thumb that interviewers accept: closure for one behaviour and a little state, class once there are two or more operations or the state needs to be observed.
prod:
Callbacks registered in loops

The late-binding bug shows up wherever code builds callbacks in a loop: GUI and dashboard handlers, asyncio loop.call_later calls, retry hooks, route registration, and executor.submit(lambda: work(item)) in thread pools. The symptom is that "every task processed the last item", often only under load, when the loop finishes before the callbacks run. Code review rule: a lambda inside a for loop that references the loop variable is a bug until proven otherwise. executor.submit(work, item) passes the value directly and avoids the closure entirely.

Signatures as contracts in shared code

In a library or a shared internal package, parameter names and order are part of the public API. Making optional parameters keyword-only from the start lets you add, reorder and deprecate them without breaking callers; retrofitting it later is itself a breaking change. The opposite failure is **kwargs swallowing typos: a function that accepts **kwargs and forwards them selectively will silently ignore timeuot=5. Validate unknown keys or avoid catch-all **kwargs in public functions.

Module-level mutable state

Functions that update globals — counters, caches, registries, "current user" variables — are a source of bugs under concurrency (lost updates between threads, py9) and in tests (state leaking from one test to the next, py12). In web services, request-specific data belongs in parameters, in a request object, or in contextvars, which give each thread or asyncio task its own value. Global configuration should be read-only after startup.

Closures that pin memory

A handler registered with an event bus, a cache of partially applied functions, or a long-lived lru_cache-decorated nested function keeps its cells, and those cells keep whatever they reference. In data pipelines it is easy to close over a large DataFrame or model object "just for logging", and the object then lives as long as the callback is registered. Memory profilers show the object held by a cell; the fix is to capture only small values (an id, a length) or to deregister callbacks when done.

Recursion on untrusted input

Recursive parsers and tree walkers (for example over ASTs, abstract syntax trees, the tree form of parsed code) work in tests and crash in production when a user sends a structure nested 5,000 levels deep, producing RecursionError (a 500 error at best). Services that process arbitrary JSON, ASTs or nested configs should either cap depth explicitly or iterate with an explicit stack. The standard library's json module itself raises RecursionError on very deeply nested input, so validate size and depth at the edge.

Notebooks and stale globals

Jupyter notebooks, the everyday tool of data and AI work, run every cell in one shared global namespace. A function defined in cell 3 that reads a global df or model sees whatever value that name has when the function runs, which depends on which cells you ran and in what order, not on the order they appear on screen. The classic result is a notebook that works for its author and fails for everyone who runs it top to bottom, or a training function that silently uses a stale, differently filtered DataFrame. The fix is the same discipline as elsewhere in this lesson: pass data in as parameters instead of reading globals, and regularly use "restart kernel and run all" to prove the notebook works from a clean state.

Tooling

Linters catch most of this lesson statically: Ruff/flake8-bugbear's B006 (mutable defaults), B023 (function definition in a loop that uses the loop variable — the late-binding rule), A001/A002 (shadowing built-ins), and PLW0603 (use of global). Type checkers (py10) catch wrong argument counts and names at call sites before they reach production.
myths: A function can read a global and then assign to it, as long as the read comes first.

Python decides whether a name is local when it compiles the function, by looking for any assignment to it anywhere in the body. If there is one, the name is local for the entire function, so a read before the assignment raises UnboundLocalError even though a global with that name exists.
A closure remembers the value a variable had when the inner function was created.

A closure remembers the variable itself, stored in a shared cell, and reads its current value when the inner function runs. That is why lambdas created in a loop all see the loop variable's final value.
*args and **kwargs are special keywords.
Only the * and ** matter; args and kwargs are conventional names. def f(*values, **options) works identically.
Methods can see class attributes by their bare names, like Java fields.

A class body is not an enclosing scope for the functions defined in it. Inside a method, y does not find the class attribute y; you must write self.y or ClassName.y. The same rule makes a class attribute invisible inside a comprehension's expression in the class body.
Python optimises tail recursion, so deep recursion is fine.

CPython performs no tail-call optimisation. Each call uses a frame, and the default recursion limit is 1000, after which RecursionError is raised. Deep recursion over user data (nested JSON, long linked structures) should be rewritten as a loop with an explicit stack.
Lambdas are faster or more 'functional' than def.

A lambda creates exactly the same kind of function object as def; it is just limited to one expression and has the unhelpful name <lambda> in tracebacks. Use it for short throwaway key functions and def for anything you would want to name, test or read in a stack trace.
