recap: CPython frees most objects by reference counting: every reference added or removed updates a counter, and the object is freed the moment it reaches zero.
Reference counting cannot free cycles, so a cyclic garbage collector periodically looks at container objects, finds groups that are only referenced by each other, and frees them.

The collector is generational: new objects are checked often and survivors less often, with collection triggered by allocation counts (thresholds 700, 10, 10 on 3.12 and 3.13, and again from 3.14.5 after 3.14.0-3.14.4 briefly used an incremental collector).
Small objects are allocated by pymalloc from arenas, which are returned to the operating system only when completely empty, so resident memory can stay high after objects are freed.

Real-world Python leaks are almost always unintended references: unbounded caches, growing globals, listeners never removed, closures or tracebacks holding large objects; tracemalloc snapshots and diffs find them by line.
Weak references let caches and observers refer to objects without keeping them alive.
The Global Interpreter Lock lets only one thread execute Python bytecode at a time; it exists mainly to keep reference counts and interpreter internals consistent cheaply.
Because the GIL is released during blocking I/O and inside many C extensions, threads speed up I/O-bound work and some native work, but not pure-Python CPU-bound work.
The GIL does not make compound operations atomic, so shared mutable state still needs locks or queues.

For CPU-bound parallelism use processes, vectorised native libraries, sub-interpreters (concurrent.interpreters and InterpreterPoolExecutor in 3.14), or the free-threaded build (officially supported in 3.14, about 5-10% single-thread cost).
glossary: Arena
A large block of memory (1 MiB on 64-bit builds since 3.10, 256 KiB on 32-bit builds) that pymalloc carves into pools and blocks for small objects.
Copy-on-write
An operating-system optimisation where a forked child shares its parent's memory pages until one of them writes to a page, which is then copied.
CPU-bound
Limited by computation; the program would go faster with a faster or additional processor.
Cyclic garbage collector
The part of CPython that finds and frees groups of objects that reference each other but are unreachable from the program.
Free-threaded build
A separate CPython build (PEP 703; experimental in 3.13, officially supported in 3.14) without the GIL, where threads run Python code in parallel.
Generation
A group of tracked objects of similar age; younger generations are collected more often because most objects die young.
GIL
Global Interpreter Lock: the lock in standard CPython that allows only one thread at a time to execute Python bytecode.
I/O-bound
Limited by waiting for input/output such as network, disk or a database, rather than by computation.
Memory leak
Memory that a program keeps using even though it no longer needs the data; in Python usually objects still referenced by mistake.
OOM killer
The Linux kernel mechanism that kills a process when the system or container runs out of memory; containers report exit code 137.
pymalloc
CPython's allocator for small objects (up to 512 bytes), which is faster than the system allocator for Python's many small allocations.
Race condition
A bug where the result depends on the timing of threads, such as two threads reading the same value and both writing back value plus one.
Reference count
The number of references pointing at an object; CPython frees the object when it reaches zero.
RSS
Resident set size: physical memory currently used by a process, the number dashboards and memory limits usually track.
Sub-interpreter
An additional, isolated Python interpreter inside the same process; since 3.12 each can have its own GIL, and 3.14 exposes them via concurrent.interpreters.
tracemalloc
A standard-library module that records where each allocation happened, so snapshots can be compared to find growth by source line.
Unreachable
Not reachable by following references from the program's roots (globals, stacks); unreachable objects are garbage.
Weak reference
A reference that does not increase an object's reference count, so it does not keep the object alive; created with the weakref module.
drill:
Diagnose it

A Flask service's memory grows from 300 MB to 3 GB over two days and is then killed by the OOM killer. CPU is normal. Code includes:

_seen_users = {}

@app.get("/profile/<uid>")
def profile(uid):
    _seen_users[uid] = load_profile(uid)     # "cache"
    return render(_seen_users[uid])

class Report:
    @functools.lru_cache(maxsize=None)
    def rows(self, day): ...

How do you confirm the cause, and fix it?

Answer

Confirm: the memory graph climbs with traffic rather than plateauing, which rules out allocator fragmentation. Take tracemalloc snapshots an hour apart (or attach memray to a canary) and compare top allocations by line; growth attributed to load_profile and to the rows cache confirms it. len(_seen_users) and Report.rows.cache_info() exposed as metrics are even cheaper checks.

Causes: (1) _seen_users is an unbounded module-level dict: every distinct user ever seen stays in memory forever, separately in each worker process. (2) lru_cache(maxsize=None) on a method is unbounded and includes self in every key, so every Report instance and all its rows are kept alive.

Fixes: replace the dict with a bounded cache with expiry (cachetools.TTLCache(maxsize=10_000, ttl=300)), or move shared caching to Redis so it is not duplicated per process. For rows, use a bounded cache keyed on day only, or functools.cached_property if the value is per instance. Add a memory alert, and consider max_requests worker recycling in gunicorn as a safety net — a net, not the fix. Note that this is not the GIL or the garbage collector: every one of these objects is still referenced, so no collector may free it.
qa: E
Does the GIL make Python code thread-safe?

No. It guarantees only that one thread runs bytecode at a time; the interpreter can switch threads between any two bytecode instructions, so read-modify-write sequences on shared data can interleave and lose updates. Individual operations on built-in types implemented in C, such as list.append, happen to be atomic, but your logic usually spans several of them. Protect shared mutable state with a lock, or confine it to one thread and communicate through a queue.

Follow-up: Why did counter += 1 on four threads give the right answer in the lesson's test? — Since 3.10 the interpreter only switches threads at certain instruction boundaries, so that particular race became rare in practice; it is still not guaranteed, and it is common on the free-threaded build.
E
How does CPython decide when to free an object?

Primarily by reference counting: each object stores how many references point at it, the count changes whenever a reference is created or dropped, and when it reaches zero the object is freed immediately, running __del__ and releasing anything it references. Objects stuck in reference cycles are freed later by the cyclic garbage collector.
E
Why do threads speed up I/O-bound Python but not CPU-bound Python?

The GIL is released while a thread waits in a blocking system call — a socket read, a file read, time.sleep — so other threads run during that wait. Pure-Python computation holds the GIL, so CPU-bound threads just take turns. In the lesson's measurement, four CPU-bound tasks took 2.37 s sequentially and 2.38 s on four threads, but 1.00 s on four processes.
M
If CPython uses reference counting, why does it also need a garbage collector?

Reference counting cannot reclaim reference cycles: if a points to b and b points to a, both counts stay at least one even when nothing else can reach them. Cycles are common — parent and child pointers, objects referencing their own bound methods, exceptions referencing frames that reference the exception. The cyclic collector periodically examines container objects, subtracts references that come from inside the examined set, and frees groups whose remaining count is zero.

Follow-up: Can you turn the collector off? — Yes, with gc.disable(), and some services do so for latency, relying on reference counting and occasional manual gc.collect(); any cycles then accumulate until collected, so it needs monitoring.
M
How would you find a memory leak in a long-running Python service?

First confirm it: plot RSS over time and correlate growth with traffic, then check whether it plateaus (allocator behaviour, not a leak) or grows without bound. Then take tracemalloc snapshots some time apart, or run memray on a canary, and compare the top allocation sites by line. Look for the classic causes at those lines — unbounded dicts or caches, lru_cache on methods, callbacks never removed — and use gc.get_referrers or objgraph to see what keeps the suspicious objects alive. Expose the size of suspect caches as metrics.
M
What is the cyclic collector's generational scheme, and why generations?

Tracked container objects start in the youngest generation. A collection of generation 0 is triggered when allocations minus deallocations exceed a threshold (700 by default on 3.12); survivors move to an older generation, which is collected less often (after 10 young collections, and so on). It works because most objects die young, so scanning young objects often finds most garbage while rarely paying to scan the large, long-lived heap.
M
What is a weak reference and when would you use one?

A weak reference points at an object without increasing its reference count, so it does not keep the object alive; calling it returns the object or None once it has been freed. Use weakref.WeakValueDictionary for caches that should not keep entries alive by themselves, WeakKeyDictionary to attach data to objects you do not own, and weakref.WeakMethod or weak sets for observer lists so that listeners that go away are dropped automatically.
M
Why does process memory stay high after a large data structure is freed?

CPython's small-object allocator, pymalloc, takes memory from the operating system in arenas and splits them into pools of fixed-size blocks. Freed blocks are reused by later allocations, but an arena can be returned to the OS only when every block in it is free, and a few surviving objects scattered across arenas keep them pinned. The system allocator used for larger objects behaves similarly. So RSS reflects peak usage; the fix is to avoid the peak (stream data), or to do the memory-heavy work in a short-lived subprocess.
M
How do you get CPU parallelism in Python?

Use multiple processes (ProcessPoolExecutor or multiprocessing), each with its own interpreter and GIL, paying for process start-up and for pickling data between processes. Or push the work into native code that releases the GIL: NumPy, PyTorch, Polars, hashlib and compression libraries parallelise under threads. On 3.14 there are two newer options: sub-interpreters via InterpreterPoolExecutor, lighter than processes but with limited object sharing and extension support, and the free-threaded build, where plain threads run Python code in parallel at a single-thread cost of roughly 5-10%.
H
Why does CPython have a GIL at all?

Reference counts change on almost every operation, so without a lock every increment and decrement would need to be atomic, which is expensive, and many interpreter internals and C extensions assume exclusive access. One global lock made the interpreter simple, single-threaded code fast, and C extensions easy to write. The cost is that pure-Python threads cannot run in parallel. PEP 703 removes it by using biased reference counting (cheap non-atomic updates by the owning thread, atomic ones by others), immortal objects, deferred counting for some objects, per-object locks for containers, and the mimalloc allocator.

Follow-up: What happens if a free-threaded interpreter imports an incompatible C extension? — Unless the extension declares support, the interpreter re-enables the GIL for the process and warns; PYTHON_GIL=0 or -X gil=0 forces it off.
H
What is gc.freeze() for?

Pre-fork servers such as gunicorn load the application in a parent process and fork workers, which share the parent's memory pages via copy-on-write. Reference-count updates and GC scans write to object headers, which makes the kernel copy those pages into each worker, so shared memory quietly becomes private. gc.freeze() moves all current objects into a permanent generation that the collector ignores, avoiding writes from GC scans; the documented pattern is gc.disable() early in the parent, gc.freeze() just before fork, gc.enable() in the children. Immortal objects in 3.12 remove the refcount writes for the most shared objects.
H
What happened to the garbage collector in Python 3.14?

3.14.0 shipped an incremental collector with only young and old generations, which scanned the old generation in increments to cut maximum pause times on large heaps by an order of magnitude. Production users reported significant memory pressure, because garbage in the old generation was reclaimed more slowly, and 3.14.5 reverted to 3.13's three-generation collector: gc.collect(1) again collects the middle generation and threshold2 is honoured. The lesson is that GC behaviour can change between patch releases, so pin versions and watch memory when upgrading.
H
What does __del__ guarantee, and why is it a poor place for cleanup?

__del__ runs when the object is about to be destroyed, which for CPython is usually immediately at refcount zero, but may be delayed until a GC pass if the object is in a cycle, delayed indefinitely if a traceback or cache holds it, and not run at all for objects alive at interpreter shutdown in some cases. Since 3.4 (PEP 442) objects with __del__ in cycles can be collected, but the order is undefined. Use context managers for deterministic cleanup and weakref.finalize for 'run this when the object goes away' callbacks.

sum: Choosing between threads, processes and asyncio for I/O-bound and CPU-bound work; concurrent.futures; how the asyncio event loop, coroutines and tasks actually run; TaskGroup, timeouts, cancellation and backpressure; race conditions without and with the GIL; and what changed up to Python 3.14.
prereq: py5
Generators pause at yield and resume on request; async generators and async for exist; a coroutine is a pausable function.
py7
Exceptions propagate up the stack; context managers guarantee cleanup; ExceptionGroup and except* handle several failures at once.
py8
The GIL lets one thread run Python bytecode at a time but is released during blocking I/O and in many C extensions; processes each have their own GIL.
net13
A socket is a kernel object; an event loop uses non-blocking sockets and epoll/kqueue/IOCP to wait on many at once; connection pools bound concurrency.
why:
An AI team builds a service that enriches documents: for each incoming document it calls an embedding API, a moderation API and a vector database, then combines the results. Each call takes about 200 ms. Written as ordinary sequential Python, one document takes 600 ms and the service handles fewer than two documents per second per worker, while the CPU sits almost entirely idle. The program is not slow; it is waiting, one call at a time.

A developer rewrites it with async def and sprinkles await in front of every call. Nothing gets faster. Then someone notices that one helper still uses the synchronous requests library, and under load the whole service's latency climbs to seconds, even for the health check. A second developer adds a thread pool for a slow text-cleaning step that is pure Python, and that gets no faster either. A third fixes the first problem by firing all 10,000 API calls at once with asyncio.gather, and the embedding provider starts returning 429 "too many requests" errors.

Each of these is a different misunderstanding of concurrency in Python. Python offers three models — threads, processes and asyncio — and they are good at different things because of the GIL (py8) and because of how each one waits. Choosing the wrong one gives no speed-up; using the right one wrongly (sequential awaits, a blocking call on the event loop, unbounded fan-out, lost exceptions) gives outages. For AI engineers this is daily work: almost every LLM application is dominated by network waits on model APIs, vector stores and databases, and streaming responses and batching requests are concurrency problems.

This lesson starts with the difference between concurrency and parallelism and between I/O-bound and CPU-bound work, which decides the model to use. It covers threads and concurrent.futures, then processes and their pickling and start-method rules. Most of the lesson is asyncio: what a coroutine and a task are, how the event loop runs them, how to get real concurrency with gather and TaskGroup, and the essential production controls — never blocking the loop, timeouts, cancellation, bounded concurrency and queues. It ends with race conditions in both worlds and the changes up to Python 3.14. Measurements are from CPython 3.12.10; the network-socket machinery underneath asyncio is covered in net13.
primer:
One cook, many dishes

Imagine a kitchen. A sequential cook puts pasta on to boil and stands watching the pot for ten minutes, then starts the sauce. Most of the cook's time is spent waiting. A concurrent cook puts the pasta on, starts chopping for the sauce while the water heats, checks the oven, and returns to each dish when it needs attention. There is still only one cook, but several dishes are in progress at once, and the meal is ready much sooner. Parallel cooking means hiring more cooks, who genuinely work at the same instant.

That distinction maps directly onto programs:

  • I/O-bound work spends its time waiting for something outside the CPU — a network response, a disk read, a database query. It needs concurrency: something that lets the program start other work while waiting. Threads and asyncio both do this.
  • CPU-bound work spends its time computing. It needs parallelism: more cores working at once. Because of the GIL (py8), Python threads cannot run Python code in parallel, so this needs processes, native code, or the newer options in 3.14.

The three tools

Threads are several cooks sharing one kitchen and, in standard CPython, one knife (the GIL): only one can cut at a time, but while one waits for the oven another can cut. They work with any ordinary library, which makes them the easiest way to overlap a few dozen network calls.

Processes are separate kitchens, each with its own cook and its own knife. They really do work in parallel, but ingredients must be packed up and carried between kitchens (pickling), and setting up a kitchen takes time.

asyncio is the single concurrent cook: one thread runs an event loop that juggles thousands of tasks, each of which says explicitly "I'm waiting now, go do something else" by writing await. It is the most efficient way to wait on many things at once, but it requires every step to cooperate: one task that stands staring at a pot without saying await freezes the whole kitchen.

What each one costs

The three tools also differ in price. An operating-system thread reserves memory for its own stack and is switched by the kernel, so a few hundred threads are fine but tens of thousands are not. A process costs a whole interpreter — tens of megabytes and noticeable start-up time — plus the work of copying data to and from it. An asyncio task is just a small Python object, so a single process can keep tens of thousands of them waiting at once. The trade-off runs the other way for convenience: threads and processes work with any library, while asyncio needs libraries written for it. Most real services end up combining them, for example an asyncio web server that hands CPU-heavy steps to a process pool.

Where the kitchen analogy breaks: real cooks can be interrupted at any moment, and so can threads, which is why shared data needs locks. asyncio tasks can only switch at an await, which makes it easier to reason about which code runs uninterrupted — but not immune to races, as the end of the lesson shows.
body:
1. Threads and concurrent.futures

The threading module creates operating-system threads directly, but most code should use the higher-level concurrent.futures API, which manages a pool of reusable threads (a thread pool) and hands you futures: placeholder objects for results that will arrive later. Here ten simulated 200 ms calls run sequentially and then on a pool:

import time
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor

def fetch(i):
    time.sleep(0.2)          # stands in for a network call; releases the GIL
    return i * 10

# sequential: 2.00 s
with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=10) as pool:
    results = list(pool.map(fetch, range(10)))     # 0.20 s, [0, 10, 20, ...]

The waits overlap because time.sleep, like real socket reads, releases the GIL (py8). pool.map returns results in input order. For more control, pool.submit(fn, *args) returns a Future immediately; future.result(timeout=...) waits for it; as_completed(futures) yields futures as they finish, in completion order, so you can handle fast results first:

from concurrent.futures import as_completed
with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=16) as pool:
    futures = {pool.submit(fetch_url, url): url for url in urls}
    for fut in as_completed(futures):
        url = futures[fut]
        try:
            handle(url, fut.result())
        except Exception as e:
            log.warning("failed %s: %s", url, e)

Two rules. First, an exception raised in a worker is stored in the future and re-raised only when you call result(); in the test, a pool where item 3 raised completed the with block silently, and the error appeared only when the results were collected. Never fire and forget. Second, max_workers is your concurrency limit, and it protects downstream services; the default for threads is min(32, cpu_count + 4). The with block waits for all submitted work on exit. Since 3.14, Executor.map accepts buffersize= to limit how many tasks are submitted ahead of the results you have consumed, so mapping over a huge or infinite iterable no longer submits everything up front.

For producer-consumer designs between threads, queue.Queue is the thread-safe building block: put blocks when a bounded queue (maxsize) is full, giving backpressure, and get blocks until an item is available.

2. Processes

For CPU-bound pure-Python work, ProcessPoolExecutor has the same API but runs each task in a separate process with its own interpreter and GIL. In py8's measurement, four CPU-bound tasks took 2.38 s on threads and 1.00 s on processes. The price is that everything crossing the process boundary — the function, its arguments and its result — is pickled (serialised to bytes) and unpickled on the other side. That has three consequences:

  • The function must be importable by name: module-level functions work; lambdas and nested functions do not. On 3.12, pool.map(lambda x: x, [1]) failed with AttributeError: Can't get local object 'main_sync.<locals>.<lambda>'.
  • Each task costs at least the pickling of its data plus inter-process communication, typically well under a millisecond for small data but significant for large arrays. Tasks must be large enough to amortise it; map(fn, items, chunksize=100) sends items in batches.
  • Large read-only data (a model, a lookup table) should be loaded once per worker with the pool's initializer= argument, not sent with every task.

How child processes are created is the start method. fork copies the parent process instantly (sharing memory copy-on-write, py8) but can deadlock if the parent has threads holding locks at the moment of the fork. spawn starts a fresh interpreter that re-imports your main module, slower but safe; it is the default on Windows and macOS. forkserver forks children from a clean single-threaded helper process; since Python 3.14 it is the default on Linux and other Unix systems except macOS. With spawn and forkserver, the main module is imported in each child, so code that creates the pool must be under if __name__ == "__main__":, or each child would try to create its own pool.

3. asyncio: coroutines

Threads are managed by the operating system, which can switch between them at any moment, and each costs memory for its stack; thousands of threads become expensive. asyncio takes the opposite approach: one thread, and tasks that cooperatively hand control back whenever they would wait.

The building block is the coroutine. A function defined with async def is a coroutine function; calling it runs nothing and returns a coroutine object, a paused computation much like a generator (py5). Inside it, await something means: "suspend me until something is done, and let other work run meanwhile." asyncio.run(main()) creates an event loop, runs the main coroutine to completion, and closes the loop.

import asyncio

async def fetch_a(i):
    await asyncio.sleep(0.2)      # a non-blocking wait: suspends this coroutine
    return i * 10

async def main():
    for i in range(10):
        await fetch_a(i)          # measured: 2.10 s — each await waits before the next starts

asyncio.run(main())

That loop is sequential. await waits for one thing; it does not start anything else. This is the single most common asyncio mistake: code that is async all the way down and exactly as slow as the synchronous version.

4. Tasks, gather and TaskGroup: getting actual concurrency

Concurrency comes from starting several coroutines before waiting for them. A task wraps a coroutine and schedules it on the event loop so it runs independently. Three ways to get there:

results = await asyncio.gather(*(fetch_a(i) for i in range(10)))   # 0.21 s, results in order

async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg:                               # 3.11+
    tasks = [tg.create_task(fetch_a(i)) for i in range(1000)]
# 1,000 concurrent 0.2 s waits: 0.21 s total
results = [t.result() for t in tasks]

task = asyncio.create_task(fetch_a(1))   # starts running at the next await
...                                      # do other things
value = await task

gather and TaskGroup differ in how they handle failure, which matters a lot in production. With gather, the first exception propagates to the awaiting code but the other tasks keep running in the background; with return_exceptions=True it instead returns exceptions in place of results: [0, 1, ValueError('task 2 failed'), 3]. TaskGroup implements structured concurrency: the async with block cannot exit until every task in it has finished, and if one task fails, the group cancels the others and raises all failures as an ExceptionGroup (py7). In the test, four tasks where task 2 failed after 20 ms finished in 0.08 s with the others cancelled rather than running for their full second. That makes it impossible to leak background tasks by accident, which is why TaskGroup is the default choice for new code.

One more rule about loose tasks: the event loop keeps only weak references to tasks. A task created with create_task and not stored anywhere can be garbage-collected mid-flight. Keep references (a set, with a done-callback that removes the task) or use a TaskGroup.

5. How the event loop runs all this

The event loop is a scheduler running in one thread. It keeps a queue of tasks that are ready to run and a record of what each suspended task is waiting for. Each iteration:

  1. Run each ready task until it reaches an await on something that is not finished yet (a network read, a timer, another task). The task is suspended there, and the loop records a callback to resume it.
  2. Ask the operating system which sockets are ready, using the platform's efficient readiness API (epoll on Linux, kqueue on macOS, IOCP on Windows; net13 explains these). The wait's timeout is the time until the nearest timer, such as a pending sleep.
  3. For each socket that became readable or writable and each timer that expired, mark the waiting task ready.
  4. Repeat.

Two properties follow. Waiting costs almost nothing: a suspended coroutine is a small object, not a thread with a stack, so tens of thousands of concurrent connections fit in one process. And switching is cooperative: a task runs uninterrupted between two awaits. That is what makes the next section so important.

6. Never block the loop

Anything that takes time without awaiting — time.sleep, requests.get, a synchronous database driver, reading a big file, parsing a large JSON document, a CPU-heavy loop — holds the loop in step 1, and every other task waits. We can measure it with a heartbeat task that expects to wake every 100 ms:

async def heartbeat():
    for _ in range(5):
        t = time.perf_counter()
        await asyncio.sleep(0.1)
        ticks.append(round(time.perf_counter() - t, 2))

# with time.sleep(0.5) called inside another coroutine:
#   heartbeat intervals: [0.56, 0.1, 0.11, 0.11, 0.11]   ← one tick delayed by the blocking call
# with await asyncio.to_thread(time.sleep, 0.5) instead:
#   heartbeat intervals: [0.11, 0.11, 0.11, 0.11, 0.11]

In a web server, that delayed tick is every other user's request. The fixes: use async-native libraries (httpx or aiohttp for HTTP, asyncpg or async SQLAlchemy for databases); wrap unavoidable blocking calls in await asyncio.to_thread(fn, *args) (3.9+), which runs them on a thread pool while the loop continues; and send CPU-heavy work to a process pool with await loop.run_in_executor(process_pool, fn, *args), because a thread would still hold the GIL. asyncio's debug mode (asyncio.run(main(), debug=True) or PYTHONASYNCIODEBUG=1) logs any callback that runs longer than 100 ms, which finds these calls quickly.

7. Timeouts and cancellation

Every network call needs a timeout, or one hung connection holds a task (and whatever it has locked) forever. asyncio.timeout (3.11+) is a context manager: if the block takes longer, it is cancelled and TimeoutError is raised:

try:
    async with asyncio.timeout(0.1):
        await asyncio.sleep(1)
except TimeoutError:
    print("timed out")

Under the hood, timeouts, TaskGroup failure handling and task.cancel() all use cancellation: the loop raises asyncio.CancelledError inside the task at its current await. The task should let it propagate after cleaning up:

async def worker():
    try:
        await asyncio.sleep(10)
    except asyncio.CancelledError:
        print("worker: cleaning up after cancel")
        raise                      # re-raise, or cancellation silently fails

t = asyncio.create_task(worker())
await asyncio.sleep(0.01)
t.cancel()                         # prints the cleanup line; awaiting t raises CancelledError

Since 3.8 CancelledError inherits from BaseException, so except Exception does not catch it. Code that swallows it breaks timeouts and TaskGroups in confusing ways. asyncio.shield() protects an inner operation from an outer cancellation when it must finish (such as committing a transaction), and should be used sparingly.

8. Bounding concurrency and backpressure

asyncio makes it easy to start 100,000 operations at once, which is usually a bug: it opens too many sockets, uses memory for every pending response, and floods the downstream service until it rate-limits or falls over. Bound it. A semaphore lets at most N tasks into a section:

sem = asyncio.Semaphore(3)
async def limited(i):
    async with sem:              # at most 3 inside at once
        await asyncio.sleep(0.05)
# 20 tasks via gather: measured peak concurrency 3

For long-running pipelines, a fixed set of worker tasks reading from a bounded asyncio.Queue is often better: it bounds concurrency, and when workers fall behind, await queue.put() blocks the producer — backpressure — instead of letting work pile up in memory. queue.join() waits until every item has been marked done with task_done(); in the test, three workers processed 20 items through a queue of size 10.

queue = asyncio.Queue(maxsize=10)
async def consumer():
    while True:
        item = await queue.get()
        try:
            await process(item)
        finally:
            queue.task_done()

Size the bound from the downstream limit: the API's rate limit or concurrency allowance, the database's connection pool, or the number of GPU batches the model server accepts. And share one HTTP client (one connection pool) across tasks rather than creating one per request.

9. Race conditions in both worlds

Threads can be interrupted between any two bytecodes, so shared mutable state needs threading.Lock (py8 showed a counter losing 2,295 of 4,000 updates). asyncio tasks can only be interrupted at await, so code between awaits is effectively atomic — a real simplification. But a read, an await and a write still interleave:

counter = 0
async def incr():
    global counter
    v = counter
    await asyncio.sleep(0)        # any await is a switch point
    counter = v + 1

await asyncio.gather(*(incr() for _ in range(100)))
print(counter)                    # measured: 1, not 100

All 100 tasks read 0 before any of them wrote. The asyncio fixes are the same ideas as for threads: asyncio.Lock around the check-then-act sequence, or keep the state in one task and send it messages through a queue. Note that asyncio.Lock is not thread-safe and threading.Lock must never be awaited on the loop (acquiring it would block the loop); the two worlds need their own primitives.

10. Mixing sync and async code

Real systems combine both. From async code, call blocking code with asyncio.to_thread or run_in_executor. From synchronous code, run a coroutine with asyncio.run(), which creates a new loop — but it cannot be called from inside a running loop (a common error in notebooks, where Jupyter already runs one; use await directly there). From another thread, submit a coroutine to a running loop with asyncio.run_coroutine_threadsafe(coro, loop), which returns a concurrent.futures.Future. Frameworks hide much of this: FastAPI runs plain def endpoints in a thread pool and async def endpoints on the loop, which is exactly why a blocking call inside an async def endpoint is so damaging.
deep:
Coroutines are generators with a different hat

A coroutine object implements send() and throw() like a generator (py5). When a coroutine awaits something that is not ready, the chain of awaits bottoms out in a Future, which yields itself up through every await to the task driving the coroutine. The task registers a callback on that future and returns control to the loop. When the future completes — because the selector reported the socket ready — the callback schedules the task, which calls coro.send(None) to resume the whole chain exactly where it paused. Cancellation is coro.throw(CancelledError()) at that point. This is why an await on an already-completed awaitable does not yield to the loop at all, and why await asyncio.sleep(0) is the idiom for "let other tasks run now".

Eager tasks and task factories (3.12+)

By default, create_task schedules the coroutine to start at the loop's next iteration. Python 3.12 added asyncio.eager_task_factory: with it, a new task starts running synchronously inside create_task until its first real suspension, and if it finishes without ever suspending (for example, a cache hit), no scheduling happens at all. For workloads with many tasks that often complete immediately, this measurably reduces overhead. Since 3.14, create_task passes arbitrary keyword arguments through to the task factory, so custom factories can accept extra metadata.

How asyncio talks to the operating system

On Linux and macOS the default loop uses the selectors module over epoll or kqueue: sockets are non-blocking, the loop registers interest in readability or writability, and the selector call blocks until something is ready or a timer is due (net13 covers readiness-based I/O). On Windows the default is the ProactorEventLoop over IOCP, which is completion-based: the loop submits a read and is told when it has finished. Disk files are not supported by readiness APIs, so asyncio's file-like operations and to_thread use threads for disk I/O. uvloop, a drop-in loop built on libuv, is commonly used in production for 2-4× lower loop overhead.

Thread-pool sizing and the GIL

For I/O-bound threads, the right pool size is set by the downstream resource and by latency: to sustain R requests per second with a latency of L seconds, you need about R × L in flight (Little's law). CPU-bound threads are capped by the GIL, so a large pool only adds contention; py8's convoy effect means a CPU-heavy thread also adds latency to I/O threads sharing the GIL. On the free-threaded build (3.14), thread pools can run pure-Python CPU work in parallel, and ThreadPoolExecutor becomes a viable choice for it — provided every shared structure is properly locked.

Processes: sharing without copying

Pickling large NumPy arrays into every task can dominate run time. multiprocessing.shared_memory.SharedMemory (3.8+) creates a named block of memory that several processes can map; wrap it in a NumPy array with np.ndarray(shape, dtype, buffer=shm.buf) and pass only the name between processes. Memory-mapped files (np.memmap) and Arrow buffers serve the same purpose. Worker initializers that load a model once per process, combined with chunksize batching, usually recover most of the theoretical speed-up.

fork, threads and the 3.14 default

fork() copies only the calling thread into the child, but copies the memory of all threads, including any locks they held. If another thread held, say, the logging module's lock or the allocator's lock at the instant of the fork, the child inherits a lock that nobody will ever release and deadlocks the first time it needs it. That is why 3.12 began emitting a DeprecationWarning when forking a process that has other threads, and why 3.14 switched Linux's default start method to forkserver, where children are forked from a helper process started before the application creates threads. Code that relied on children inheriting module-level state modified at runtime must now pass that state explicitly.

Structured concurrency and its origins

Nathaniel J. Smith's essay "Go statement considered harmful" argued that spawning a background task is like a goto: control flow escapes the scope that created it, so errors can be lost and resources outlive their owners. His Trio library introduced "nurseries", scopes that cannot exit until their child tasks finish, and asyncio adopted the idea as TaskGroup in 3.11 along with asyncio.timeout. The practical rule that follows: every task should have an owner that awaits it, and loose create_task calls should be rare, documented, and supervised.

Introspection in 3.14

Python 3.14 added tooling for the hardest asyncio debugging question — "what is every task waiting on?". python -m asyncio ps PID lists the tasks of a running process with their coroutine stacks and awaiter chains, python -m asyncio pstree PID draws the tree of tasks awaiting each other, and asyncio.capture_call_graph()/print_call_graph() produce the same information from inside the program. These rely on 3.14's safe external debugger interface (PEP 768).
prod:
The blocked event loop

The most common asyncio incident is a latency spike across all endpoints of a service caused by one blocking call: a synchronous SDK call, a requests.get in a helper, a large json.loads, a CPU-heavy tokenisation step, or logging to a slow disk. Symptoms: p99 latency jumps for everything, including the health check, while CPU is low. Detection: event-loop lag metrics (a heartbeat measuring its own lateness), asyncio debug mode's slow-callback warnings in staging, and py-spy dump on a stuck process. Fix: async libraries, to_thread, process pools, and linting with rules such as Ruff's ASYNC family, which flags blocking calls in async functions.

Unbounded fan-out

A batch job that does await asyncio.gather(*[call(x) for x in items]) over a million items creates a million coroutines and, as fast as the loop can go, a million requests. The provider returns 429s, the local process runs out of file descriptors ("Too many open files") or memory, and retries amplify the load. Always bound concurrency with a semaphore or worker pool, respect provider rate limits with a token bucket, and use Executor.map(..., buffersize=) (3.14) or a bounded queue so input is not materialised all at once.

Lost exceptions

Background tasks created with create_task and never awaited, thread-pool futures never collected, and gather without handling the first exception all lose errors. The only trace may be a "Task exception was never retrieved" message at garbage collection, if that. Use TaskGroups, collect every future's result, and add a done-callback that logs failures for intentionally detached tasks.

LLM applications: concurrency patterns

Typical AI workloads are almost pure I/O: calls to model APIs, embedding services and vector stores. Good patterns: an async client shared per process; a semaphore sized to the provider's concurrency limit; per-call timeouts plus an overall deadline for the user request; retries with exponential backoff and jitter on 429 and 5xx responses; streaming responses back to users as tokens arrive (py5); and batching (sending 100 texts per embedding request) wherever the API supports it, which usually beats higher concurrency for throughput and cost. Retrieval, tool calls and reranking that do not depend on each other should run concurrently in a TaskGroup rather than one after another.

Process pools in data pipelines

Feature engineering and pre-processing in pure Python are the classic candidates for process pools. Common production problems: pickling a large DataFrame into every task (use shared memory, memory-mapped files, or have workers read their own partition from storage), forgetting the __main__ guard (children re-execute the script), and worker processes silently killed by the OOM killer, which surfaces as BrokenProcessPool. Size the pool below the core count if the machine also runs other services, and set max_tasks_per_child (3.11+) to recycle workers that leak.

Graceful shutdown

Deployments restart processes constantly. A service should stop accepting work on SIGTERM, let in-flight tasks finish within a deadline, cancel the rest, and close pools and clients. asyncio.run cancels remaining tasks on exit; worker loops should treat CancelledError as "finish or checkpoint the current item and stop". Thread pools and process pools should be shut down with shutdown(wait=True, cancel_futures=True) (3.9+), and queue.Queue.shutdown() (3.13+) unblocks threads waiting on a queue.
myths: async code is faster than normal code.

No single operation gets faster. asyncio lets one thread wait on thousands of operations at once, so total time for many I/O waits overlaps; in this lesson ten 0.2-second waits took 0.21 s with gather versus 2.1 s awaited one by one. For CPU-bound work async adds overhead and nothing else.
Putting await in front of calls makes them run concurrently.

await waits for one thing to finish before moving on. A loop that awaits each call in turn is sequential. Concurrency comes from starting several operations before waiting — gather, TaskGroup, create_task.
asyncio code has no race conditions because it is single-threaded.

Tasks can only switch at await points, which makes races rarer and easier to reason about, but a read, an await, and a write on shared state still interleave. In the lesson's test, 100 tasks doing read, await asyncio.sleep(0), write left a counter at 1 instead of 100.
You can call any library from async code.

A blocking call such as requests.get, time.sleep or a synchronous database driver freezes the whole event loop and every task on it. Measured: a 0.5-second time.sleep inside a coroutine stretched a 0.1-second heartbeat to 0.56 s. Use async libraries, or run the blocking call with asyncio.to_thread.
More workers always means more throughput.

Past the point where the bottleneck (the database's cores, the API's rate limit, your CPU count for CPU work) is saturated, extra workers add queueing, memory and contention, and can trigger rate limiting. Concurrency should be bounded and sized to the downstream resource.
If a thread-pool task fails, you'll see the exception.
An exception in a concurrent.futures worker is stored in its Future and re-raised only when you call result(). If you never collect results, failures vanish silently.

recap: Concurrency means making progress on several tasks over the same period; parallelism means literally running at the same instant on several cores.
For I/O-bound work, threads or asyncio overlap the waiting; for CPU-bound pure-Python work, processes (or native code, sub-interpreters, or the free-threaded build) are needed because of the GIL.
concurrent.futures gives one API over thread and process pools: submit returns a Future, map and as_completed collect results, and result() re-raises a worker's exception.
Process pools pickle functions, arguments and results, so they need module-level functions, the __main__ guard under spawn or forkserver, and tasks large enough to amortise the overhead.
asyncio runs coroutines on a single-threaded event loop that switches between tasks only at await points and uses the operating system's readiness notifications to wait on many sockets at once.
A coroutine does nothing until awaited or wrapped in a Task; concurrency comes from gather, TaskGroup or create_task, not from await alone.
Any blocking call or long computation inside a coroutine stalls every task on the loop; use async libraries, asyncio.to_thread, or run_in_executor with a process pool.
asyncio.TaskGroup (3.11+) provides structured concurrency: it waits for all child tasks, cancels the rest if one fails, and raises an ExceptionGroup.
Timeouts (asyncio.timeout), cancellation (CancelledError, which must not be swallowed) and bounded concurrency (Semaphore or a queue of workers) are required for robust async code.
Shared mutable state races in threads and across await points in asyncio; use locks, queues or confinement to one task.
glossary: asyncio
Python's standard library for writing single-threaded concurrent code with async/await and an event loop.
Backpressure
Slowing producers when consumers cannot keep up, for example by blocking on a bounded queue, so work does not pile up without limit.
Cancellation
Asking a task to stop; asyncio does it by raising CancelledError inside the task at its next await.
Concurrency
Structuring a program to make progress on several tasks over overlapping time periods, not necessarily simultaneously.
Coroutine
The object returned by calling an async def function; it runs only when awaited or scheduled as a task, and can pause at await.
Event loop
The scheduler at the heart of asyncio that runs ready tasks, waits for I/O readiness, and resumes tasks whose operations completed.
Executor
An object that runs callables on a pool of threads, processes or interpreters and returns Futures (concurrent.futures).
Future
A placeholder for a result that is not available yet; it becomes done with a value or an exception.
Parallelism
Executing several computations at literally the same time on different CPU cores.
Pickling
Serialising Python objects to bytes with the pickle module so they can be sent to another process.
Semaphore
A counter-based lock that allows up to N holders at once; used to cap concurrency.
Start method
How multiprocessing creates child processes: fork (copy the parent), spawn (fresh interpreter) or forkserver (fork from a clean helper process).
Structured concurrency
A discipline where concurrent tasks are started within a scope that does not exit until all of them have finished or been cancelled.
Task
An asyncio object that wraps a coroutine and schedules it to run on the event loop concurrently with others.
Thread pool
A fixed set of reusable threads that execute submitted tasks, avoiding the cost of creating a thread per task.

(1) requests.get is blocking: inside a coroutine it freezes the event loop for the duration of every request, so no other task in the process runs, and because nothing is started concurrently the loop is fully sequential — about 10,000 × latency. Use an async client, run the requests concurrently, and bound the concurrency:

import asyncio, httpx

async def fetch_all(urls, limit=100):
    sem = asyncio.Semaphore(limit)
    async with httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=10) as client:
        async def one(u):
            async with sem:
                r = await client.get(u)
                r.raise_for_status()
                return r.json()
        async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg:
            tasks = [tg.create_task(one(u)) for u in urls]
    return [t.result() for t in tasks]

One shared client reuses connections (a connection pool); the semaphore protects the target service and your file descriptors; the timeout stops one hung server from holding a slot forever. Decide the failure policy explicitly: TaskGroup cancels everything on the first error, which suits "all or nothing"; gather(..., return_exceptions=True) suits "take what succeeded". For 10,000 URLs, also consider retries with backoff for transient errors.

(2) Three seconds of pure-Python CPU work on the event loop blocks every other request the server is handling for three seconds. Move it off the loop: await loop.run_in_executor(process_pool, compute_heavy_model, data), with a process pool created once at start-up, because the work is CPU-bound pure Python and a thread would still hold the GIL. Mind the pickling cost of data. Better still, vectorise the model with NumPy (which may also make a thread pool viable, since NumPy releases the GIL) or move it to a separate inference service that the handler calls asynchronously.
qa: E
Why does asyncio not help CPU-bound code?

asyncio runs all coroutines on one thread and switches only at await points. CPU-bound work never awaits, so it monopolises the loop: nothing else runs, and only one core is used. CPU-bound work belongs in processes, native code that releases the GIL, or, on 3.14, sub-interpreters or the free-threaded build.
E
When would you use threads, processes and asyncio?

Threads for I/O-bound work with ordinary blocking libraries at moderate concurrency, tens to hundreds of simultaneous waits. asyncio for I/O-bound work at high concurrency, thousands of sockets, when async-native libraries exist. Processes for CPU-bound pure-Python work, since each has its own GIL. For numeric work, vectorise with NumPy or similar first; it may make parallelism unnecessary.

Follow-up: Why not always use asyncio for I/O? — It needs async versions of every library in the call path, one blocking call anywhere stalls everything, and for a few dozen concurrent calls a thread pool is simpler and just as fast.
E
What is the difference between concurrency and parallelism?

Concurrency is about structure: several tasks are in progress over the same period, possibly interleaved on one core, like a chef switching between dishes while each simmers. Parallelism is about execution: several computations literally run at the same instant on different cores. asyncio provides concurrency without parallelism; multiprocessing provides both.
M
What happens if you call a blocking function inside an async coroutine?

It blocks the whole event loop: the loop cannot run any other task until the call returns, so every other request in that process stalls, which shows up as latency spikes in unrelated endpoints. Use an async library, or offload the call with await asyncio.to_thread(fn, ...) or loop.run_in_executor; for CPU-heavy work use a process pool executor.

Follow-up: How do you detect it in production? — asyncio debug mode (PYTHONASYNCIODEBUG=1 or asyncio.run(..., debug=True)) logs callbacks that take longer than 100 ms; a heartbeat task that measures its own lateness, or event-loop lag metrics, catch it continuously.
M
gather versus TaskGroup — what is the difference?

Both run awaitables concurrently. gather returns results in order; by default the first exception propagates to the awaiting code while the other tasks keep running, and with return_exceptions=True exceptions are returned in the result list instead. TaskGroup (3.11+) is structured: the async with block does not exit until all tasks finish, and if one fails the rest are cancelled and all failures are raised together as an ExceptionGroup. Use TaskGroup when the tasks form one unit of work; gather(return_exceptions=True) when partial results are acceptable.
M
Explain what the event loop does in one iteration.

It runs every task that is ready, each until it hits an await on something not yet done, at which point the task is suspended and its callback is registered. It then asks the operating system, through a selector such as epoll, kqueue or IOCP, which sockets are ready, with a timeout set by the nearest scheduled timer. It marks the tasks waiting on those sockets or expired timers as ready, and repeats. Only one task runs at any moment, and a task gives up control only at an await.
M
How do you limit concurrency when fetching 100,000 URLs with asyncio?

Never create 100,000 in-flight requests at once, which exhausts file descriptors, memory and the target's patience. Either wrap each request in async with semaphore where semaphore = asyncio.Semaphore(100), or start a fixed number of worker tasks that pull URLs from an asyncio.Queue with a maxsize, which also gives backpressure to the producer. Share one HTTP client so connections are pooled and reused, add per-request timeouts, and retry transient failures with backoff.
M
What goes wrong when using ProcessPoolExecutor, and how do you avoid it?

Functions, arguments and results must be pickled, so lambdas, nested functions and objects with open handles fail; on 3.12 a lambda failed with 'Can't get local object'. With spawn (Windows, macOS) and forkserver (Linux default since 3.14), children re-import the main module, so pool creation must sit under if __name__ == '__main__'. Per-task overhead is milliseconds, so batch small tasks with chunksize, and load large read-only data once per worker with an initializer rather than sending it with every task.
M
How does cancellation work in asyncio and what must your code do?

task.cancel() arranges for CancelledError to be raised inside the task at its current or next await. The task should let it propagate, running cleanup in finally blocks or async with exits. Since 3.8 CancelledError inherits from BaseException, so except Exception does not swallow it; code that catches it for cleanup must re-raise. asyncio.timeout() and TaskGroup both work by cancelling, so swallowing CancelledError breaks timeouts and structured concurrency.
H
Why can an asyncio task disappear mid-flight if you don't keep a reference?

The event loop holds only weak references to tasks. A task created with create_task and not stored anywhere can be garbage-collected before it finishes, silently stopping its work, and its exception may only surface as a 'Task exception was never retrieved' log. Keep tasks in a set and remove them in a done callback, or better, create them inside a TaskGroup, which holds them and awaits them.

Follow-up: What's the related fire-and-forget risk? — Even if kept alive, an unawaited task's exception is never raised anywhere; background tasks need a done callback that logs failures or a supervising TaskGroup.
H
How would you run CPU-heavy model inference inside an async web server?

Never on the event loop: it would block every request. For pure-Python work, submit it to a ProcessPoolExecutor via loop.run_in_executor, created once at start-up with a bounded number of workers and the model loaded in each worker's initializer. If the model runs in native code that releases the GIL (PyTorch, ONNX Runtime), a thread pool via asyncio.to_thread works and avoids pickling. At scale, move inference to a separate service with its own batching and autoscaling, and have the web tier call it asynchronously.

Follow-up: Why a separate service? — Model servers batch requests across users to use the GPU efficiently, scale independently of the web tier, and isolate memory-hungry processes from latency-sensitive request handling.
H
What changed about multiprocessing start methods, and why does it matter?

fork copies the parent process, including the state of any threads' locks, so forking a process that has threads can deadlock the child if a lock was held at the moment of fork. Python 3.12 started warning about forking multi-threaded processes, and 3.14 changed the default start method on Linux and other non-macOS Unix platforms from fork to forkserver (macOS and Windows already used spawn). Code that relied on children inheriting globals set at runtime, or on passing unpicklable objects implicitly, breaks; it must pass state explicitly or request fork explicitly with get_context('fork').
H
How do you debug a stuck asyncio service?

First find what the loop is doing: py-spy dump on the process shows the Python stacks of all threads, revealing a blocking call on the loop thread. If the loop is idle, the tasks are waiting on something: on 3.14, python -m asyncio ps PID and pstree PID list running tasks with their coroutine stacks and awaiter chains, and asyncio.print_call_graph() does the same from inside. Before 3.14, asyncio.all_tasks() with task.print_stack() in a debug endpoint serves the same purpose. Common culprits: a lock or semaphore never released, a queue nobody consumes, a missing timeout on a network call.
