why:
Friday afternoon, a routine deploy of an unchanged service fails in production with ImportError: cannot import name 'soft_unicode' from 'markupsafe'. Nobody touched the code. The requirements.txt listed flask and jinja2==2.11.3, and that pinned Jinja2 depended on MarkupSafe with no upper limit. That morning a new MarkupSafe release removed a function the old Jinja2 used, and the fresh Docker build pulled it in. This exact incident hit thousands of projects in February 2022.

Other versions of the same pain: a notebook that works for its author but not for a colleague because they have a different pandas; a test suite that passes locally and fails in CI because the tests imported the source folder instead of the installed package; a Docker image that takes twenty minutes to build because a package without a matching wheel compiles from source; an internal package name that an attacker registered on the public index. None of these are programming bugs. They are problems of environment: which code, at which version, gets loaded when your program says import.

Packaging has a reputation for confusion because Python accumulated many tools over thirty years. The modern picture is much simpler, built on a few standards: pyproject.toml to describe a project, wheels as the installable format, virtual environments for isolation, and lockfiles for reproducibility, with fast tools such as uv on top. An AI engineer meets all of it daily: GPU-specific wheels for PyTorch, conflicting versions between an LLM SDK and an older library, reproducible training environments, and container images that must build quickly.

This lesson starts from the import system — how import finds code — because everything else is about controlling that. It then covers virtual environments, pyproject.toml, how a project becomes a wheel and how installation works (with a real package built and installed along the way), the crucial difference between version ranges and lockfiles, the modern toolchain, compiled wheels, Docker images and supply-chain security. All commands were run on CPython 3.12.10 in throwaway environments, with build, hatchling and uv 0.12.
primer:
Where does import find code?

When you write import httpx, Python walks a list of directories, sys.path, in order and takes the first match. That list typically contains the directory of the script you ran, any directories in the PYTHONPATH environment variable, the standard library, and a directory called site-packages, where installed third-party packages live. Every packaging tool ultimately exists to put the right files, at the right versions, into the right site-packages.

One kitchen per recipe book

Imagine several cooks sharing one pantry. One recipe needs a particular brand of flour; another needs a different one; swapping the flour for one cook ruins the other's cake. The fix is to give each project its own pantry. A virtual environment is exactly that: a directory with its own site-packages and a python that uses it. Install packages "into the project" and they go into that pantry, leaving other projects and the operating system's Python untouched.

python -m venv .venv                 # create
.venv\Scripts\activate               # Windows   (macOS/Linux: source .venv/bin/activate)
python -m pip install httpx          # installs into .venv's site-packages
python -c "import sys; print(sys.prefix != sys.base_prefix)"   # True inside a venv

Two habits follow immediately: never type pip install without knowing which Python it belongs to (use python -m pip or a project tool), and never share an environment between projects.

Recipes and shopping receipts

A project describes what it needs in pyproject.toml, the way a recipe says "flour, about 500 g, any plain wheat flour". Those are ranges: httpx>=0.27,<1. When you install, a resolver chooses one exact version of every package — including the packages your dependencies depend on, the transitive dependencies — that satisfies all the ranges at once. A lockfile is the shopping receipt from that resolution: exact versions and file hashes for everything. Libraries publish recipes; applications keep receipts, so every build buys exactly the same ingredients.

Three layers of reproducibility

It helps to see the whole problem as three nested layers, each answering a different question. The virtual environment answers "which packages can this project see?" — only its own. The lockfile answers "exactly which versions and files are they?" — the same ones every time. The container image (or a pinned machine image) answers "on which interpreter, operating system and system libraries?" — the same ones in development, CI and production. Most packaging incidents are a missing layer: packages installed globally, versions resolved fresh at deploy time, or a production operating system that differs from the one the wheels were tested on. The rest of this lesson builds each layer properly.

Where the pantry analogy breaks: a virtual environment does not copy Python itself. It links to an existing interpreter (the "base" Python) and only isolates the installed packages. That is why a venv is tied to one Python version and to the machine it was created on, and why you recreate environments from the lockfile rather than copying the directory around.
body:
1. The import system and sys.path

When Python executes import x, it first checks sys.modules, a dict of every module already imported in this process; if x is there, it simply binds the name (imports run a module's code only once). Otherwise it asks a series of finders, the main one of which searches each directory in sys.path for a package directory x/ (with an __init__.py) or a module file x.py or a compiled extension. The first match is loaded, executed, stored in sys.modules and bound.

The order of sys.path is the source of many surprises. Its first entry is the directory of the script being run — or, for python -c and the interactive prompt, the empty string meaning the current directory. That entry comes before site-packages. So a folder in your current directory named like an installed package wins:

# flat/tinystats/__init__.py contains a stub whose mean() returns "LOCAL COPY"
cd flat
python -c "import tinystats; print(tinystats.mean([1]), tinystats.__file__)"
# LOCAL COPY  ...\flat\tinystats\__init__.py        ← not the installed package
python -c "import sys; print(repr(sys.path[0]))"
# ''

The same mechanism makes a file called random.py, json.py or requests.py in your project break unrelated imports. python -m package.module runs a module with the current directory on the path and correct package context, which is the right way to run code inside a package.

2. Virtual environments

python -m venv .venv creates a directory containing a pyvenv.cfg file (pointing at the base interpreter), a Scripts (Windows) or bin directory with a python that uses the environment, and an empty Lib/site-packages. When that python starts, it sees pyvenv.cfg, sets sys.prefix to the environment, and puts the environment's site-packages on sys.path instead of the system one. "Activating" only puts that Scripts/bin directory first on your shell's PATH for convenience; running .venv/Scripts/python directly works identically.

Rules that avoid most trouble: one environment per project, created inside the project directory and excluded from version control; always install with python -m pip (or uv) so you use the pip belonging to the Python you mean; never install into the system Python — many Linux distributions now enforce this with PEP 668's "externally managed" marker, which makes pip refuse; and treat environments as disposable, rebuilt from the lockfile. For command-line tools you want globally (Ruff, httpie), pipx or uv tool install give each tool its own hidden environment.

3. pyproject.toml: describing a project

Here is a complete, real project file for a small library, tinystats, with a src/ layout (section 6):

[build-system]
requires = ["hatchling"]
build-backend = "hatchling.build"

[project]
name = "tinystats"
version = "0.1.0"
description = "Tiny statistics helpers"
requires-python = ">=3.10"
dependencies = ["httpx>=0.27,<1"]
license = "MIT"

[project.optional-dependencies]
plot = ["matplotlib>=3.8"]

[project.scripts]
tinystats = "tinystats.cli:main"

The [build-system] table (PEP 517/518) names the build backend — the tool that knows how to turn this source into installable artefacts — and what must be installed to run it. Swapping hatchling for setuptools, flit, pdm-backend, or maturin (for Rust extensions) changes nothing else. The [project] table (PEP 621) is standard metadata every tool understands: name, version, supported Python versions, runtime dependencies as version ranges, optional dependencies ("extras", installed as tinystats[plot]), and [project.scripts] entry points that become command-line programs. Tool configuration lives in [tool.ruff], [tool.pytest.ini_options], [tool.mypy] and so on, so one file configures the whole project. Development-only dependencies such as pytest go in [dependency-groups] (PEP 735), which are never published as part of the package.

4. Building: sdists and wheels

Running the standard front end python -m build asks the backend for two artefacts:

python -m build
# Successfully built tinystats-0.1.0.tar.gz and tinystats-0.1.0-py3-none-any.whl

The sdist (.tar.gz) is the source plus metadata; installing it requires building it first, which may run code and need compilers. The wheel (.whl) is the built result, and it is just a zip file. Listing this one shows everything an installer needs:

['tinystats/__init__.py', 'tinystats/cli.py', 'tinystats/core.py',
 'tinystats-0.1.0.dist-info/METADATA', 'tinystats-0.1.0.dist-info/WHEEL',
 'tinystats-0.1.0.dist-info/entry_points.txt', 'tinystats-0.1.0.dist-info/RECORD']

# METADATA (excerpt)
Metadata-Version: 2.5
Name: tinystats
Version: 0.1.0
License-Expression: MIT
Requires-Python: >=3.10
Requires-Dist: httpx<1,>=0.27
Provides-Extra: plot
Requires-Dist: matplotlib>=3.8; extra == 'plot'

# entry_points.txt
[console_scripts]
tinystats = tinystats.cli:main

The filename encodes compatibility tags: py3-none-any means any Python 3, no compiled ABI, any platform. A compiled wheel looks like numpy-2.x-cp312-cp312-manylinux_2_17_x86_64.whl: CPython 3.12, its ABI, Linux on x86-64 with glibc 2.17 or newer (section 9). Note also Requires-Dist with an environment marker (extra == 'plot'); markers such as python_version < "3.11" and sys_platform == "win32" let one package declare platform-specific dependencies.

5. Installing: what pip and uv actually do

Installing the wheel into a fresh environment shows the whole flow. The installer reads the wheel's Requires-Dist, resolves compatible versions for httpx and everything httpx needs, downloads wheels, verifies them, unzips each into site-packages, writes a RECORD of installed files (used for uninstalling), and generates a small executable for each console script:

pip install dist/tinystats-0.1.0-py3-none-any.whl
tinystats 1 2 3 4                 # the generated console script
# 2.5
pip list
# anyio 4.15.1, certifi 2026.7.22, h11 0.16.0, httpcore 1.0.9, httpx 0.28.1,
# idna 3.20, pip 25.0.1, tinystats 0.1.0, typing_extensions 4.16.0

One requested dependency brought six others. That is the transitive dependency tree, and it is where version surprises come from: the application declared a range for httpx but said nothing about h11 or certifi.

During development you want code changes to take effect without reinstalling. An editable install (pip install -e ., which uv sync does for your own project by default) installs a small pointer in site-packages to your source directory instead of a copy.

6. The src/ layout

If the package directory sits at the repository root, running pytest or a script from the root puts the root first on sys.path (section 1), so tests import the working copy, not the installed package. They pass even when the wheel is broken — a data file missing from the build, a module excluded by mistake, a dependency not declared. Putting the package in src/tinystats/ means nothing importable sits at the root; tests can only import the package once it is installed (editable in development), so they exercise what users will actually receive. That is why the packaging guide and most modern templates use it.

7. Ranges versus locks

This distinction is the heart of dependency management. A library — code other people install — should declare the broadest ranges it genuinely supports, because it will be installed next to other libraries with their own constraints, and every unnecessary pin is a potential conflict for someone's application. An application — something you deploy — should install from a lockfile: the exact version, source URL and hash of every package in the resolved tree. uv lock on the tinystats project resolved 26 packages (the plot extra and different dependency sets for Python 3.10, 3.11 and 3.12+ included) into uv.lock, with entries like:

[[package]]
name = "anyio"
version = "4.15.1"
source = { registry = "https://pypi.org/simple" }
dependencies = [
    { name = "exceptiongroup", marker = "python_full_version < '3.11'" },
    { name = "idna" },
    { name = "typing-extensions", marker = "python_full_version < '3.15'" },
]
wheels = [
    { url = "https://files.pythonhosted.org/.../anyio-4.15.1-py3-none-any.whl",
      hash = "sha256:6152fdbbf9a77fdec97731721bebf7c4c44f7c29b424b0065826173efc7ed101", ... },
]

Installs from the lock are identical every time, and the hashes mean a tampered or substituted file is rejected. Upgrades then become explicit changes: uv lock --upgrade-package httpx, reviewed and tested, usually opened automatically by Renovate or Dependabot. Other tools produce equivalent locks: Poetry's poetry.lock, PDM's pdm.lock, and pip-tools' pip-compile --generate-hashes, which writes a fully pinned requirements.txt. PEP 751 (Final) standardised a tool-neutral lock format, pylock.toml; uv export --format pylock.toml produced one from the same project, and newer pip versions can install from it.

Why is pip freeze > requirements.txt not a lockfile? The pip freeze output from the test environment lists exact versions — but only for this one environment on this platform and Python version, without hashes, without distinguishing what you asked for from what came along, and it even records the local wheel as a file:// path. It is a snapshot, not a reproducible resolution.

8. The modern toolchain

  • uv (Astral, written in Rust) replaces pip, pip-tools, virtualenv, pipx and pyenv-style Python management with one fast tool: uv init, uv add httpx (edits pyproject.toml and the lock), uv sync (makes the environment match the lock), uv run pytest, uv python install 3.14, and uv run script.py for single-file scripts that declare their dependencies in a comment header (PEP 723). Its speed comes from a global cache, parallel downloads and hard-linking files instead of copying.
  • Poetry and PDM are established project managers with their own lock formats; pip plus pip-tools remains a solid minimal combination; conda/mamba/pixi manage non-Python binaries too (CUDA toolkits, GDAL, compilers), which is why scientific and GPU environments often use them.
  • Ruff lints and formats in one very fast tool, replacing flake8, isort, pyupgrade and black in many projects, configured in [tool.ruff].
  • Type checkers (py10) and pytest (py12) run in CI across the supported Python versions.
  • pre-commit runs formatters, linters and checks on staged files before each commit, so problems are fixed before review.

Which should you choose? For a new application or library in 2026, uv is the default recommendation of many teams: one tool, standard pyproject.toml, a universal lockfile and very fast CI. Existing Poetry or pip-tools setups work well and need no migration unless speed or workflow is a problem. Choose conda, mamba or pixi when the environment must include non-Python binaries that are hard to get as wheels, such as specific CUDA toolkits or geospatial libraries. Whatever the tool, the principles are the same: declare ranges, lock exactly, install from the lock, and update deliberately.

9. Compiled packages and platform wheels

Packages with C, C++ or Rust code — NumPy, pandas, PyTorch, Pydantic's core, cryptography — must be compiled for each platform. To spare users a compiler, maintainers build a wheel per combination of Python version, operating system and architecture, usually with cibuildwheel in CI. Linux wheels follow the manylinux standard: built against an old glibc and bundling other shared libraries (via auditwheel), so they run on most distributions; Alpine uses musl libc and needs musllinux wheels. The installer picks the most specific wheel whose tags match; if none match, it falls back to the sdist and tries to compile, which is the classic cause of slow or failing installs on new Python versions and unusual platforms. The stable ABI (abi3; an ABI, application binary interface, is the binary-level contract between compiled code and the interpreter) lets one wheel serve several Python versions for extensions that restrict themselves to it. The free-threaded builds (py8) have their own tags such as cp314t and need their own wheels.

A related convenience: python -m pip install --dry-run --report report.json httpx shows what a resolution would install without changing anything, and uv tree prints the resolved dependency tree, which is the fastest way to answer "why is this package here?" when an unfamiliar transitive dependency appears in a lockfile diff.

10. Security: the supply chain

Installing a package runs other people's code on your machine, and installing an sdist can run arbitrary build code before you ever import it. Threats include typosquatting (reqeusts), compromised maintainer accounts publishing malicious releases, and dependency confusion, where an attacker publishes a public package with the name of your private internal one and a higher version, so an installer configured with both indexes picks theirs. Defences: lockfiles with hashes; index pinning so internal names can only come from the internal index; a vetted mirror or proxy for production; pip-audit or similar scanners against vulnerability databases; minimal dependencies; and, for publishing your own packages, PyPI's trusted publishing, which lets CI upload via short-lived OpenID Connect tokens instead of long-lived API tokens.

11. Version numbers and specifiers

Python versions follow PEP 440, and dependency ranges are written with specifiers. The ones you meet daily, with what the packaging library (the reference implementation installers use) accepted in a test over a set of sample versions:

SpecifierMeaningAccepted from the samples
>=0.27,<1at least 0.27, below 1.00.27.2, 0.99
~=2.31compatible release: >=2.31, ==2.*2.31.5, 2.32.0
~=2.31.0>=2.31.0, ==2.31.*2.31.5
==3.*any 3.x release3.0, 3.2
!=1.5.0,>=1.4exclude one known-bad release1.4, 1.6 and later

Versions compare numerically per segment (1.10 is newer than 1.9) and pre-releases such as 2.0.0rc1 sort before the final release; installers skip pre-releases unless you ask for them or pin one explicitly. Many projects use semantic versioning (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH, where a major bump signals breaking changes), others use calendar versioning (2026.7.22, as certifi does). Neither is a guarantee, which is why the lock-and-test workflow matters more than the numbering scheme.

12. Single-file scripts with inline dependencies

Not everything is a project. For a one-off script — a data export, an evaluation run — PEP 723 lets the script declare its own requirements in a special comment block, and a runner such as uv run creates a cached, isolated environment for it on the fly:

# /// script
# requires-python = ">=3.11"
# dependencies = ["httpx>=0.27"]
# ///
import httpx, sys
print("httpx", httpx.__version__, "on Python", sys.version.split()[0])

# uv run report.py
# Installed 7 packages in 56ms
# httpx 0.28.1 on Python 3.12.10

The script is self-describing and reproducible to share (add uv lock --script to lock it too), without polluting any other environment or requiring a requirements.txt next to it.
deep:
Inside the import system

sys.meta_path holds finders; CPython's default list contains finders for built-in modules, frozen modules and the path-based finder. The path-based finder consults sys.path_hooks to get a finder for each sys.path entry (a directory, or a zip file via zipimport) and caches them in sys.path_importer_cache. A finder returns a module spec describing how to load the module; the loader then creates the module object, inserts it into sys.modules before executing its code (which is how circular imports partially work), and executes it. Packages have a __path__ that sub-imports search. Directories without __init__.py are namespace packages (PEP 420), which can be split across several directories — useful for plugin namespaces, confusing when created by accident. Editable installs are implemented with .pth files or custom finders in site-packages, which is why some tools resolve editable packages differently from regular ones.

Circular imports

When module A imports B at the top and B imports A, the second import finds A already in sys.modules but only partly executed, so names defined later in A do not exist yet, producing ImportError: cannot import name 'x' from partially initialized module. Fixes, in order of preference: move the shared code to a third module both can import; import the module rather than names from it (import a then use a.x at call time); defer the import into the function that needs it; and for type annotations only, use if TYPE_CHECKING: imports (py10).

How resolution works and why it can be slow

Choosing versions that satisfy every constraint is NP-hard in general. pip uses a backtracking resolver (since 20.3): it picks candidate versions, and when it hits a conflict, backtracks and tries older ones, which can take a long time for large trees with loose constraints. uv uses PubGrub, a conflict-driven algorithm that learns from each conflict to prune the search and produces readable explanations of unsolvable constraints. uv's lock is universal: it resolves once for every supported Python version and platform, recording markers (as in the anyio entry), so one lockfile serves Windows developers and Linux production. Metadata is fetched without downloading whole wheels using PEP 658 metadata files and HTTP range requests.

Wheel tags in detail

A wheel filename is {name}-{version}(-{build})?-{python tag}-{abi tag}-{platform tag}.whl. The Python tag (cp312, py3) says which interpreter; the ABI tag (cp312, abi3, none) says which binary interface compiled code expects; the platform tag (manylinux_2_28_aarch64, macosx_11_0_arm64, win_amd64, any) says where it runs. python -m pip debug --verbose lists the tags your interpreter accepts, in priority order. Understanding tags explains most "no matching distribution" errors: the package simply has not published a wheel for that combination yet.

GPU packages: an AI-engineering special case

PyTorch and similar libraries ship different builds for different accelerator stacks (CUDA versions, ROCm, CPU-only). Because standard wheel tags do not describe CUDA versions, these builds are published on separate indexes (https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu128-style URLs), and projects must direct the installer to the right index per platform, which uv supports through per-package index configuration and markers. The wheels are several gigabytes, which dominates Docker build times and image sizes, so teams cache them aggressively and separate the heavy dependency layer from application code. Work on "wheel variants" aims to let installers select accelerator-specific builds automatically.

Reproducibility beyond Python packages

A lockfile pins Python packages but not the interpreter build, the operating system libraries, the compilers used for sdists, or the CUDA driver. Fully reproducible environments pin those too: a base image by digest, the Python version exactly (uv's .python-version or the image tag), system packages at fixed versions, and for ML, the driver and CUDA toolkit. Conda-based lockfiles (conda-lock, pixi) and Nix go further by pinning native dependencies, at the cost of more complex tooling.

What "installed" means: dist-info and uninstalling

Each installed distribution leaves a name-version.dist-info directory in site-packages containing its METADATA, the RECORD of every file it installed (with hashes), entry_points.txt, INSTALLER (which tool installed it) and optionally direct_url.json for packages installed from a path or URL. importlib.metadata.version("httpx") and importlib.metadata.entry_points() read these at runtime, which is how plugin systems such as pytest's discover installed plugins. Uninstalling removes exactly the files in RECORD. Mixing installers in one environment — conda and pip, or pip and a system package manager — causes trouble precisely because each keeps its own records and may overwrite the other's files.
prod:
Docker images for Python services

A good image builds fast and runs small. Structure: a builder stage that copies only pyproject.toml and the lockfile and installs dependencies (uv sync --frozen --no-install-project), so that layer is cached until dependencies change; then copy the source and install the project; then a final stage from a slim base with the same Python version and libc, copying only the environment and the application, running as a non-root user. Set PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 so logs appear immediately. Prefer Debian-slim over Alpine unless every dependency publishes musllinux wheels. Pin the base image by digest and rebuild regularly to pick up security patches.

Dependency updates as a routine

Teams that update rarely face painful "big bang" upgrades across dozens of breaking changes. Teams that let Renovate or Dependabot open small, frequent update pull requests, each run through the full test suite, keep the lock current with little effort and get security fixes quickly. Group low-risk updates (patch releases of development tools) to reduce noise, and pin a schedule so updates do not land on Friday afternoons.

Private packages and monorepos

Internal libraries are published to a private index (Artifactory, AWS CodeArtifact, Google Artifact Registry, a self-hosted devpi) or consumed directly from Git. Configure installers so internal names resolve only from the private index. In monorepos, uv workspaces let several packages share one lockfile and depend on each other by path, so a change to a shared library is tested against all its consumers in one pull request.

CI speed

Dependency installation is often the slowest part of CI. Cache the installer's download cache keyed by the lockfile hash, use uv (typically an order of magnitude faster than pip for cold installs, more with a warm cache), avoid building sdists by preferring versions with wheels, and install only the dependency groups a job needs (no GPU packages for the linting job).

Notebooks and research code

Data-science and ML work often starts in notebooks with packages installed ad hoc into whatever kernel is running, and months later nobody can reproduce a result. The cheap discipline that fixes most of it: one project directory per piece of work with a pyproject.toml and lockfile, a Jupyter kernel registered from that project's environment, random seeds and data versions recorded alongside results, and the lockfile committed with the notebook. When a model moves to production, the same lock becomes the starting point for the serving image instead of a fresh, untested resolution.

Upgrading the Python version itself

New Python releases arrive every October. Upgrading is usually worthwhile (py11's free speed-ups, security support), but the blockers are compiled dependencies without wheels for the new version and deprecated APIs removed after their warning period. The routine: add the new version to the CI test matrix early, with warnings as errors, watch which dependencies fail, and switch production once the lockfile resolves cleanly with wheels for everything. Python versions receive bug fixes for about two years and security fixes for five, per PEP 602, so plan upgrades before the end-of-life date rather than after.

Incidents and responses

Recurring incident types: an unpinned transitive dependency releases a breaking change (the MarkupSafe story); a package is yanked or deleted from the index and builds fail (lockfiles with a vetted mirror protect against this); a malicious release of a popular package is published for a few hours (hash-pinned locks and delayed adoption help — some teams only accept versions older than a few days); and a new Python version ships before key compiled dependencies publish wheels for it, so upgrades wait. Each has the same lesson: control exactly what gets installed, and change it deliberately.
myths: pip freeze > requirements.txt is a lockfile.

It records the versions installed in one environment, without hashes, without marking which packages you asked for versus which came along, and without variants for other platforms or Python versions. A real lockfile (uv.lock, poetry.lock, pip-compile output with hashes, pylock.toml) is produced by a resolver from your declared dependencies and can be reproduced and updated deliberately.
Libraries should pin exact versions to be safe.

A library is installed alongside other libraries in someone else's application. If it pins requests==2.31.0 and another dependency needs 2.32, the application cannot be installed at all. Libraries declare the widest range they actually support; applications lock exact versions.
Installing packages into the system Python is fine for small scripts.

Different projects need different versions of the same package, and the operating system's own tools may depend on the system Python's packages. Many Linux distributions now mark their Python as externally managed (PEP 668), so pip refuses to install into it. Use a virtual environment per project, or a tool like uv or pipx that manages one for you.
A version number that follows semantic versioning guarantees minor upgrades are safe.

Semantic versioning is a promise from the maintainer, not a check. Minor releases regularly break someone through changed defaults, removed deprecated features or new transitive dependencies. Tests on every upgrade, driven by automated update pull requests, are what make upgrades safe.
setup.py is how you define a Python package.

Since PEP 517, 518 and 621, packages are declared in pyproject.toml: metadata in a standard [project] table and a pluggable build backend (hatchling, setuptools, flit, pdm-backend, maturin). setup.py still works with setuptools but executing arbitrary code to describe a package is legacy.
If it works on my machine, the Docker image will work the same.

Only if the image installs exactly the same versions. Without a lockfile, building the image later resolves whatever versions are newest that day. And compiled packages need wheels matching the image's platform: a slim Alpine image uses musl libc and needs musllinux wheels, or builds from source.
lab:
About 30 minutes on Python 3.10+. Everything happens in a scratch directory with its own virtual environments, so nothing touches your system Python. Outputs are from CPython 3.12.10 with build, hatchling and uv 0.12; versions of downloaded packages will be newer for you.

  1. Look at sys.path. Run python -c "import sys; print(*sys.path, sep='\n')" and identify the script-directory entry, the standard library and site-packages. Then create a venv and run the same command with its python; site-packages now points inside the venv.
  2. Create the project. Make tinystats/pyproject.toml as in body section 3, plus src/tinystats/__init__.py (importing mean from .core), src/tinystats/core.py (def mean(xs): xs = list(xs); return sum(xs) / len(xs)) and src/tinystats/cli.py (a main() that prints the mean of sys.argv[1:] as floats).
  3. Build it. In a venv with pip install build, run python -m build. Then inspect the wheel: 
    python -c "import zipfile; z = zipfile.ZipFile('dist/tinystats-0.1.0-py3-none-any.whl'); print(z.namelist()); print(z.read('tinystats-0.1.0.dist-info/METADATA').decode())"

    Find Requires-Dist, the extra and the entry point.

  4. Install and use it. In a second, fresh venv, pip install dist/tinystats-0.1.0-py3-none-any.whl, run tinystats 1 2 3 4 (expect 2.5), and pip list to see the transitive dependencies httpx brought.
  5. Trip over shadowing. Make a directory flat/tinystats/ with an __init__.py defining mean that returns "LOCAL COPY". From inside flat, run the installed venv's python with -c "import tinystats; print(tinystats.mean([1]), tinystats.__file__)". The local copy wins, because sys.path[0] is ''.
  6. Lock it. If uv is available (pip install uv in the scratch venv works), run uv lock in the project and open uv.lock: find httpx, its dependencies, the environment markers and the hashes. Then uv export --format pylock.toml and compare the standard format. Compare both with pip freeze from step 4.
  7. Break and fix a circular import. Create a.py with from b import g and def f(): return 1, and b.py with from a import f and def g(): return f(). Run python -c "import a" and read the "partially initialized module" error. Fix it by changing b.py to import a and calling a.f() inside g.
recap: import searches the directories in sys.path in order: the script's directory (or the current directory), PYTHONPATH, the standard library, then site-packages, where installed packages live.
A virtual environment is a directory with its own site-packages and a python that uses it, so each project has isolated dependencies without touching the system Python.
pyproject.toml declares a project: metadata and dependencies in the [project] table, the build backend in [build-system], and tool settings in [tool.*] tables.
A build backend turns the source into an sdist (a source archive that must be built on install) and a wheel (a ready-to-install zip containing the code and its metadata).
Installing a wheel unpacks it into site-packages, records the files, and creates console scripts from its entry points.
Libraries declare compatible version ranges; applications lock every direct and transitive dependency to exact versions with hashes, and update deliberately through tested pull requests.
uv combines virtual environments, dependency resolution, lockfiles, Python version management and script running in one fast tool; pip, pip-tools, Poetry, PDM and conda remain common.
A src/ layout stops tests from accidentally importing the working directory instead of the installed package.
Compiled packages ship platform-specific wheels (manylinux, musllinux, macOS, Windows) so users do not need compilers; the wheel filename's tags say where it runs.
Supply-chain defences include lockfiles with hashes, pinned index URLs to prevent dependency confusion, vulnerability scanning, and trusted publishing for releases.
glossary: Build backend
The tool named in [build-system] that turns a project's source into an sdist and a wheel, such as hatchling, setuptools or maturin.
Console script
A command-line program created on install from an entry point, which imports a module and calls a function.
Dependency confusion
An attack in which a public package with the same name as a private internal one is installed instead of it.
Editable install
An installation that points at your source directory, so code changes take effect without reinstalling.
Entry point
Metadata in a package that names an object (such as a function for a console script) for tools or plugins to find.
Lockfile
A generated file recording the exact version, source and hash of every package in the resolved dependency set.
manylinux
A family of wheel platform tags for Linux built against old enough glibc versions to run on most distributions.
PEP 668
The standard that lets a distribution mark its Python as externally managed so pip refuses to install into it.
pyproject.toml
The standard configuration file for a Python project: metadata, dependencies, build system and tool settings.
Resolver
The algorithm that chooses one version of every package so that all declared version constraints are satisfied.
sdist
A source distribution: an archive of the project's source that must be built into a wheel during installation.
site-packages
The directory where installed third-party packages live for a given Python environment.
sys.path
The list of directories Python searches, in order, when importing a module.
Transitive dependency
A package you did not ask for directly but that one of your dependencies requires.
Virtual environment
A self-contained directory with its own Python executable link and site-packages, isolating one project's dependencies.
Wheel
A built distribution: a zip file with a .whl extension containing ready-to-install code and metadata, tagged with the Python versions and platforms it supports.
drill:
Diagnose it

A deploy on Friday breaks production with ImportError: cannot import name 'soft_unicode' from 'markupsafe'. Nothing in your code changed; your requirements.txt lists flask and jinja2==2.11.3 without other pins. What happened, and how do you prevent it permanently?

Answer

What happened: a transitive dependency moved. Jinja2 2.11 depends on MarkupSafe with only a lower bound; MarkupSafe 2.1.0 (released in February 2022) removed the long-deprecated soft_unicode, which old Jinja2 still imported. The fresh image build resolved the newest MarkupSafe allowed by the ranges, so an unchanged codebase broke. You would confirm it by comparing pip freeze from the last good image and the broken one: only MarkupSafe's version differs.

Immediate fix: pin markupsafe<2.1 (the last working version) or upgrade Jinja2 and Flask to releases that no longer use soft_unicode, redeploy, then investigate calmly.

Permanent fix: keep only direct dependencies, as ranges, in pyproject.toml; generate a lockfile pinning every transitive dependency with hashes (uv lock, or pip-compile --generate-hashes); build images only from the lock (uv sync --frozen or pip install --require-hashes) so the same commit always produces the same environment; and let Renovate or Dependabot propose upgrades as pull requests that run the full test suite. Upgrades then happen on purpose, tested, on a weekday — not by accident during a deploy. Add a CI job that fails if the lockfile is out of date with pyproject.toml (uv lock --check), so nobody forgets to re-lock.
qa: E
Why should applications pin exact dependency versions but libraries should not?

Applications need reproducible deployments, so they lock every direct and transitive version and upgrade deliberately. Libraries are installed alongside other packages in someone else's environment, so declaring the broadest compatible ranges avoids impossible version conflicts for the applications that depend on them. The application's lockfile then chooses exact versions within everyone's ranges.
Follow-up: Should a library set upper bounds like <3? — Only when there is a known incompatibility; speculative caps cause unsolvable conflicts later, which is why many maintainers now avoid them.
E
What is a virtual environment and why use one?

A directory containing its own site-packages and a python executable (or link) that uses it, created with python -m venv .venv or uv venv. Packages installed while it is active go there, so each project has its own dependency versions, nothing leaks into the system Python, and the environment can be deleted and recreated from the lockfile at any time.
E
What is pyproject.toml?

The standard configuration file for a Python project. The [build-system] table names the build backend; the [project] table holds name, version, Python requirement, dependencies, optional extras and entry points; and [tool.*] tables configure tools such as Ruff, mypy and pytest. It replaced setup.py, setup.cfg and many separate config files.
M
What is the difference between an sdist and a wheel?

An sdist is a source archive that must be built during installation, which can require compilers, headers and running the project's build code. A wheel is a pre-built zip that installation simply unpacks into site-packages — faster, more reliable, and essential for compiled extensions. Its filename tags (for example cp312-cp312-manylinux_2_17_x86_64) say which Python versions and platforms it supports; a pure-Python wheel is tagged py3-none-any.

Follow-up: What happens if no wheel matches your platform? — pip or uv falls back to the sdist and builds it locally, which fails if compilers or system libraries are missing, a common problem on Alpine images and new Python versions.
M
What does a lockfile protect you from?

Unintended changes in transitive dependencies between builds, where a new upstream release breaks an unchanged app, and, with hashes, tampered or substituted packages. The same lock always produces the same environment, so builds are reproducible and upgrades become deliberate, reviewed changes. It also makes vulnerability scanning precise, because you know exactly which versions are deployed.
M
How does Python find a module when you import it?

It checks sys.modules for an already-imported module, then asks each finder in sys.meta_path, which searches the directories in sys.path in order: the directory of the script being run (or the current directory for python -c and the REPL), directories in PYTHONPATH, the standard library, and site-packages. The first match wins, which is why a local file named requests.py or a flat project directory can shadow an installed package.
M
Why use a src/ layout?

With the package at the top level of the repository, running tests or scripts from the repository root puts that directory first on sys.path, so imports pick up the working copy rather than the installed package. Tests then pass even when packaging is broken (a missing file or dependency in the wheel). Putting the package under src/ means it can only be imported once installed (usually editable), so tests exercise what users will actually get.
M
What does uv do, and why has it become popular?

uv is a Rust-based tool that replaces pip, pip-tools, virtualenv, pipx and pyenv-style Python version management, and adds project management with a cross-platform lockfile (uv.lock), workspaces and running scripts with inline dependency metadata (PEP 723). Its resolver and installer are much faster than pip thanks to parallel downloads, a global cache and hard-linking, which matters in CI and Docker builds. It follows the packaging standards, so projects stay portable.
M
What are optional dependencies (extras) and when do you use them?

Extras are named groups of additional dependencies declared under [project.optional-dependencies], installed with pip install 'tinystats[plot]'. Use them for features that need heavy or platform-specific packages most users do not want, such as plotting, a GPU backend or a specific database driver. Development tools (pytest, Ruff) belong in dependency groups (PEP 735) or the tool's dev dependencies rather than extras, since users never need them.
H
How would you build a small, reproducible Docker image for a Python service?

Use a multi-stage build: in the builder stage, copy only pyproject.toml and the lockfile, install dependencies from the lock (uv sync --frozen --no-install-project, or pip install --require-hashes from compiled requirements) so this layer is cached until dependencies change, then copy the source and install the project. The final stage starts from a slim base with the same Python and libc, copies only the virtual environment and the application, runs as a non-root user, and sets PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE and PYTHONUNBUFFERED. Pin the base image by digest and rebuild regularly for security patches.

Follow-up: Why not Alpine? — It uses musl libc, so it needs musllinux wheels; when a package has none it builds from source, which is slow and needs compilers. A Debian-slim base is usually simpler for Python.
H
What is dependency confusion and how do you defend against it?

If a company uses an internal package named, say, acme-auth from a private index, an attacker can publish acme-auth with a higher version number on PyPI. An installer configured with both indexes (for example pip's --extra-index-url) may pick the public, malicious one. Defences: install internal packages only from the private index (index pinning per package, as uv's index configuration supports), register your internal names on PyPI, use a proxy that serves a curated set, and use lockfiles with hashes so any substituted file fails verification.
H
How do compiled packages like NumPy install without a compiler?

Maintainers build wheels for each supported combination of Python version, operating system and CPU architecture, typically with cibuildwheel in CI, and upload them all. Linux wheels follow the manylinux (or musllinux) standards: they are built against an old glibc and bundle their other shared-library dependencies (via auditwheel) so they run on most distributions. The installer picks the wheel whose tags match the current interpreter and platform; the free-threaded build (cp313t, cp314t) and new Python versions need their own wheels, which is why adoption lags on release day.

Follow-up: What is the stable ABI? — A subset of the C API (abi3) whose binary interface does not change between Python versions, so one wheel tagged cp312-abi3 works on 3.12 and later; it is not yet available for the free-threaded build.
H
A deploy breaks with an ImportError though no code changed. How do you investigate?

Compare the installed versions between the last good and the broken build (pip freeze from both images, or the lockfile diff). Without a lockfile, a transitive dependency has almost certainly moved: find which package's new release removed the imported name, usually via its changelog. Pin it or upgrade the dependent package to restore service, then fix the process: resolve into a lockfile, build only from it, and let automated update pull requests with tests move versions forward.

t: Python in production: web services and data work
sum: How a Python web service actually runs (WSGI and ASGI, gunicorn and uvicorn workers, reverse proxies), choosing Django, Flask or FastAPI, the production essentials — configuration, logging, timeouts, connection pools, background jobs, health checks and graceful shutdown — and the pandas pitfalls that bite data and ML pipelines.
prereq: py8
The GIL, processes versus threads, memory growth and worker recycling.
py9
Threads, processes and asyncio; a blocking call in async code stalls the event loop.
py10
Type hints and Pydantic models that validate data at runtime.
py13
Virtual environments, lockfiles and building Docker images from them.
why:
A team launches an LLM-backed support assistant as a FastAPI service. In testing it is fast. On launch day, response times climb from 800 ms to 30 seconds, and the health check starts failing, so the orchestrator restarts pods, which makes things worse. The cause turns out to be one helper that calls an internal user-profile service with the synchronous requests library from inside an async def endpoint. Each call blocks the event loop for its duration, and with no timeout set, a few slow profile lookups stall every request on the worker, including the health check.

Meanwhile the analytics team's nightly job that computes customer features has started taking four hours. It iterates over a 20-million-row DataFrame with iterrows, and a well-meaning fix, df[df.active]["score"] = 0, silently does nothing, so the model is trained on unfiltered scores for a week.

Both teams wrote correct Python. What they lacked was knowledge of how Python behaves in production: how a web server actually runs your code, what a worker is, why an innocent blocking call can take a service down, what must surround every outbound call, how logs and configuration should work across a hundred containers, and which pandas idioms are thousands of times slower or silently wrong. This lesson is where the earlier topics — concurrency (py9), memory (py8), types and validation (py10), packaging (py13) — meet in running systems.

It starts with how a Python web service runs: the WSGI and ASGI interfaces, servers such as gunicorn and uvicorn, worker processes and the reverse proxy in front. It compares Django, Flask and FastAPI and shows, with real measurements, the def versus async def trap. It then covers the production essentials: configuration validated at startup, structured logging with request ids, timeouts and connection pools, background jobs, health checks and graceful shutdown. The second part turns to data work with pandas: vectorisation, chained assignment and copy-on-write in pandas 3.0, dtypes and memory, missing values and time zones. Examples were run on CPython 3.12.10 with FastAPI 0.141, uvicorn 0.54, Pydantic 2.13 and pandas 3.0.6.
primer:
The restaurant model of a web service

Picture a restaurant. The reverse proxy or load balancer is the host at the door: it greets every guest (terminates TLS, the encryption layer covered in net9), turns away troublemakers, and seats people at whichever section has room. The application server is the kitchen manager, and the workers are the cooks. Each cook follows the same recipes (your application code). How many dishes a cook can handle at once depends on the kind of cook: a synchronous cook works on one order from start to finish, even while it sits in the oven; an asynchronous cook starts many orders and moves between them while each is waiting.

Two contracts: WSGI and ASGI

How does a server like gunicorn call your Flask or FastAPI code? Through a standard contract, so any server works with any framework. WSGI (Web Server Gateway Interface, PEP 3333) is the synchronous contract: your application is a function that receives the request and returns the response, and the worker is busy until it returns. ASGI (Asynchronous Server Gateway Interface) is the async contract: your application is a coroutine that receives and sends messages, so one worker can juggle thousands of requests while they wait, and can keep connections open for WebSockets and streamed responses such as LLM tokens.

What production adds

Code that works on a laptop needs a few more things to survive in production. It must get its configuration from the environment and refuse to start if it is wrong. It must log in a form that can be searched across many instances, tagged with a request id. Every call it makes to another service needs a timeout, because in a distributed system something is always slow. Slow work must move to background jobs. And it must report its health and shut down gracefully, because orchestrators restart and move processes constantly. None of this is glamorous, and all of it is what separates a demo from a service.

Following one request

Trace a single request through that picture. A browser sends POST /orders. The load balancer terminates TLS and forwards plain HTTP to one instance. On that instance, the operating system hands the connection to one of the worker processes waiting on the shared socket. The worker parses the request, the framework matches the route, validates the JSON body into a typed object, and calls your handler. Your handler takes a connection from the worker's database pool, runs two queries, calls a pricing service through a pooled HTTP client with a timeout, logs a line tagged with the request id, and returns. The framework serialises the result, the worker writes the response, and the connection returns to the pool. Every production concern in this lesson attaches to one of those steps.

Where the restaurant analogy breaks: cooks in a kitchen share one pantry, but worker processes share nothing. Each has its own copy of the application's memory, caches, loaded ML model and database connections, which is why "add more workers" costs memory and connections, not just CPU.
body:
1. WSGI: the synchronous contract

A complete WSGI application is a callable that takes the request environment (a dict of CGI-style variables plus the request body stream) and a start_response callback, and returns an iterable of bytes:

def app(environ, start_response):
    body = f"hello from {environ['PATH_INFO']}".encode()
    start_response("200 OK", [("Content-Type", "text/plain"),
                              ("Content-Length", str(len(body)))])
    return [body]

# called by a test harness with PATH_INFO="/users":
# 200 OK [('Content-Type', 'text/plain'), ('Content-Length', '17')]
# [b'hello from /users']

Flask and Django (in its classic mode) produce exactly such a callable. The server — gunicorn, uWSGI, mod_wsgi — handles sockets and HTTP parsing, then calls it for each request in a worker. The key property: the worker is occupied until the call returns. If the handler waits two seconds on a database, that worker serves nothing else for two seconds. Concurrency therefore comes from running many workers (processes) or threads.

2. ASGI and the event loop

An ASGI application is async def app(scope, receive, send): it receives events ("request body chunk arrived", "client disconnected") and sends events ("response start", "body chunk"). Because it is a coroutine, a worker running an event loop (uvicorn, Hypercorn, Granian) can have thousands of requests in progress, switching whenever one awaits I/O (py9). ASGI also covers WebSockets and server-sent events, and it is what makes token-by-token streaming of LLM output efficient: an open stream costs a small coroutine rather than a whole worker. FastAPI and Starlette are ASGI frameworks; Django supports ASGI for async views.

3. Servers and workers

gunicorn is a pre-fork process manager. Its master process binds the listening socket, forks N workers that all accept connections from it, monitors them, restarts any that crash or exceed --timeout, and reloads them gracefully on signals. Worker classes determine concurrency inside each process: sync (one request at a time), gthread (a thread pool per worker), or uvicorn.workers.UvicornWorker for ASGI apps (an event loop per worker). uvicorn can also run on its own with --workers. gunicorn's documentation suggests (2 × cores) + 1 sync workers as a starting point; the right number comes from load testing while watching CPU, memory per worker, latency percentiles and database connections. In Kubernetes, many teams instead run one or two workers per container and scale the number of pods.

Useful gunicorn settings: --max-requests with --max-requests-jitter recycles workers after a number of requests, capping slow memory leaks (py8); --preload imports the application in the master before forking so read-only memory is shared copy-on-write (combine with gc.freeze(), py8); --timeout kills workers stuck longer than the limit, a safety net, not a substitute for timeouts in your code.

4. Frameworks: Django, Flask, FastAPI

  • Django: batteries included — ORM with migrations, admin interface, authentication, forms, templating, security middleware. The fastest route to a complete product around a relational database, with strong conventions.
  • Flask: a minimal core (routing, request and response objects, templates) and extensions for everything else. Flexible and easy to understand; you assemble and maintain the stack.
  • FastAPI: built on Starlette (ASGI) and Pydantic. Handler parameters and return types, declared with type hints (py10), drive request parsing, validation, serialisation and automatically generated OpenAPI documentation. Async-first, which makes it the common choice for JSON APIs, LLM backends and model serving.

5. The def versus async def trap, measured

FastAPI runs an endpoint declared with async def directly on the event loop, and one declared with plain def in a thread pool. That design is convenient but produces the most common production bug in FastAPI services. Three endpoints, each waiting one second, hit with ten concurrent requests through uvicorn:

@app.get("/async-sleep")
async def async_sleep():
    await asyncio.sleep(1)       # non-blocking wait
    return {"ok": True}

@app.get("/sync-sleep")
def sync_sleep():
    time.sleep(1)                # blocking, but runs in FastAPI's thread pool
    return {"ok": True}

@app.get("/async-blocking")
async def async_blocking():
    time.sleep(1)                # blocking call ON the event loop
    return {"ok": True}

# measured, 10 concurrent requests each:
# /async-sleep     1.19 s
# /sync-sleep      1.05 s
# /async-blocking 10.04 s

The rule: in async def endpoints use only async libraries (httpx.AsyncClient, asyncpg, async SQLAlchemy, async Redis clients); if an endpoint must call blocking code, declare it with plain def or wrap the call in await asyncio.to_thread(...). Also note the thread pool is finite (40 threads by default in the underlying AnyIO library), so many slow def endpoints can still saturate it.

6. Configuration validated at startup

Configuration belongs in the environment, not in code, so the same image runs in development, staging and production (the twelve-factor principle), and secrets are injected by the platform or a secrets manager. The common failure is reading variables lazily with os.environ.get scattered through the code, so a missing value surfaces as None in the middle of a request. Instead, declare all settings once and validate them when the process starts, for example with pydantic-settings:

from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings

class Settings(BaseSettings):
    database_url: str          # required
    workers: int = 4
    debug: bool = False

settings = Settings()          # reads DATABASE_URL, WORKERS, DEBUG from the environment

# with WORKERS=8 and DEBUG=true but no DATABASE_URL:
#   1 validation error for Settings
#   database_url  Field required [type=missing, ...]
# with DATABASE_URL set: settings.workers == 8 (an int), settings.debug is True
# with WORKERS=eight:
#   workers  Input should be a valid integer, unable to parse string as an integer

A bad deploy now fails immediately with a precise message, and the rest of the code receives typed values.

7. Logging that works across a fleet

Use the logging module, not print. Each module gets a logger with logging.getLogger(__name__), the application configures handlers and formats exactly once at startup, and libraries never configure logging themselves. In production, emit structured records — JSON with level, logger, message and context — so a log platform can filter and aggregate them. The most valuable piece of context is a request id, generated (or taken from an incoming header) by middleware and stored in a contextvars variable, which is automatically separate per thread and per asyncio task (py9):

import logging, json, contextvars
request_id = contextvars.ContextVar("request_id", default="-")

class JsonFormatter(logging.Formatter):
    def format(self, record):
        return json.dumps({"level": record.levelname, "logger": record.name,
                           "msg": record.getMessage(), "request_id": request_id.get()})

# after middleware sets request_id to "req-7f3a":
# {"level": "INFO", "logger": "app.orders", "msg": "creating order 1001", "request_id": "req-7f3a"}
# {"level": "WARNING", "logger": "app.orders", "msg": "inventory low for sku-42", "request_id": "req-7f3a"}

Pass the id to downstream services in a header so logs and traces from different services join up (OpenTelemetry does this automatically as trace context). Log exceptions once, where handled, with logger.exception (py7), and keep secrets, tokens and personal data out of logs.

8. Outbound calls: timeouts, pools and retries

Every call to another service can hang, and the defaults will not save you: requests has no default timeout at all. Against a local socket that accepted connections and never replied, requests.get(url, timeout=(3.05, 2)) raised ReadTimeout ... (read timeout=2) after 2.02 s; without a timeout it would have waited forever, holding a worker. The first number is the connect timeout, the second the maximum wait between bytes of the response. httpx defaults to a 5-second timeout, which is better but still worth setting deliberately.

Create one client per process and reuse it — requests.Session or httpx.Client/AsyncClient — so TCP and TLS connections are pooled rather than re-established per call (net13 covers connection pools). Retry only idempotent operations, with exponential backoff and jitter, at one layer (py4). For dependencies that fail for long periods, a circuit breaker stops calling them and fails fast, and a bulkhead (a separate, bounded pool) keeps one slow dependency from consuming all workers. The same logic applies to databases: a connection pool per worker process means total connections are pool size × workers × instances, which must stay within the database's limit; poolers such as PgBouncer help at scale.

9. Background jobs, health checks and shutdown

Work that is slow, retryable or not needed for the response — sending email, generating a report, re-embedding a document — goes to a task queue. The handler enqueues a job (with ids, not large objects) and returns, often 202 Accepted with a job id; worker processes run jobs from a broker such as Redis or RabbitMQ with retries and visibility. Celery is the long-established option; RQ, Dramatiq and arq are simpler; workflow engines such as Temporal handle long multi-step processes. Jobs must be idempotent, because delivery is at-least-once.

Orchestrators need two signals. A liveness check asks "is the process healthy enough to keep running?" and should be cheap and not depend on other services, or a database blip makes every instance restart at once. A readiness check asks "should traffic be sent here now?" and can include loaded models and reachable dependencies. On shutdown the platform sends SIGTERM, waits a grace period (30 s by default in Kubernetes), then SIGKILL. A graceful shutdown stops accepting new work, finishes in-flight requests and the current job, closes pools, and exits; gunicorn and uvicorn implement this for their workers, and the Dockerfile must use the exec form of CMD so the signal reaches Python rather than a shell.

10. pandas in pipelines: speed

pandas stores each column as an array (NumPy or Arrow), so column operations run in compiled code, while row-by-row iteration builds Python objects for every row. Computing quantity × price over 200,000 rows with pandas 3.0.6:

[row["qty"] * row["price"] for _, row in df.iterrows()]   # 6.13 s
df.apply(lambda r: r["qty"] * r["price"], axis=1)          # 1.06 s
[r.qty * r.price for r in df.itertuples()]                 # 0.165 s
df["qty"] * df["price"]                                    # 1.18 ms

That is over 5,000 times between the first and last line. iterrows is slowest because it builds a Series (with an index and a dtype) for every row; apply(axis=1) is a Python loop in disguise (py11). Conditional logic uses np.where or Series.where, lookups use merge or map, and aggregation uses groupby(...).agg(...).

11. pandas in pipelines: correctness

Chained assignment. df[df["qty"] > 5]["price"] = 0 selects rows (producing a new object) and then assigns into that object. Under copy-on-write, the default and only mode in pandas 3.0, it can never modify df: in the test it raised a ChainedAssignmentError warning and changed zero rows. The correct form is a single .loc call, df.loc[df["qty"] > 5, "price"] = 0, which updated 88,906 rows. Copy-on-write also means modifying a subset (sub = df[df.country == "IN"]; sub["qty"] = -1) never changes the original, which makes pipelines predictable (py1 discussed views versus copies).

Missing values and dtypes. A NumPy integer column cannot hold a missing value, so pd.Series([1, 2, None]) silently becomes float64 with nan, and ids like 1234567890123456789 can lose precision as floats. The nullable Int64 dtype keeps integers and uses <NA> for missing values. Decide explicitly how each stage treats missing data, because NaN propagates through arithmetic and is excluded by most aggregations by default.

Memory. Repeated strings are expensive: a 200,000-row country column used 10.2 MB as strings (pandas 3.0's default str dtype, or the old object dtype) and 0.2 MB as category. Read only needed columns (usecols, or columnar Parquet), downcast numeric types, and process large files in chunks or with Polars or DuckDB, which are multi-threaded and can work out of core.

Time zones. Store timestamps in UTC and convert at the edges. Daylight saving produces surprising arithmetic: adding one hour to 01:30 on 29 March 2026 in Europe/Berlin gives 03:30+02:00, because 02:00 to 03:00 does not exist that night. Naive (zone-less) timestamps compared with aware ones raise errors, and mixing them silently in groupbys by date is a classic cause of off-by-one-day reports.

12. Testing a service without its infrastructure

Web services are tested at the HTTP level with a test client that calls the application in-process, no server needed, and with real dependencies replaced through the framework's dependency injection (py12). In FastAPI, app.dependency_overrides swaps a dependency for a fake:

from fastapi import FastAPI, Depends
from fastapi.testclient import TestClient
from pydantic import BaseModel, PositiveInt

app = FastAPI()
class Order(BaseModel):
    sku: str
    qty: PositiveInt
def get_repo():
    raise RuntimeError("real database")
@app.post("/orders", status_code=201)
def create(order: Order, repo=Depends(get_repo)):
    repo.append(order)
    return {"sku": order.sku, "qty": order.qty}

fake = []
app.dependency_overrides[get_repo] = lambda: fake
client = TestClient(app)
client.post("/orders", json={"sku": "A1", "qty": 2})   # 201 {'sku': 'A1', 'qty': 2}, fake now holds 1 order
client.post("/orders", json={"sku": "A1", "qty": 0})   # 422 'Input should be greater than 0' at ['body', 'qty']

The second call shows validation doing its job before any of your code runs: the request never reached the handler. Tests like these cover routing, validation, status codes and serialisation quickly; a smaller set of integration tests then runs against a real database and the real server process.
deep:
How FastAPI turns type hints into an API

At startup FastAPI inspects each endpoint's signature (py3, py10): parameters that match path segments become path parameters, simple types become query parameters, Pydantic models become the JSON body, and Depends(...) parameters are resolved through a dependency-injection graph (database sessions, the current user). Pydantic validates incoming data and serialises return values according to the declared response_model, which also filters out fields you did not intend to expose. The same metadata generates the OpenAPI schema and interactive docs. Because behaviour comes from signatures, decorators that erase them (py4) or annotations that cannot be resolved break the API at import time rather than at runtime.

Sizing: Little's law in practice

The number of requests in progress equals arrival rate × time each spends in the system (Little's law). A service receiving 200 requests per second with 250 ms average latency has about 50 requests in flight. With sync workers, you need at least 50 workers or threads across the fleet, plus headroom for latency spikes, because when a dependency slows to 2 s the same traffic needs 400. With async workers, in-flight requests cost little memory, but the downstream pools (database connections, API rate limits) still bound concurrency. This arithmetic explains why a slow dependency without timeouts exhausts a sync service: in-flight requests grow until every worker is waiting.

Process models and memory

Each worker imports the whole application: frameworks, ORM models, and for ML services, model weights. A 2 GB model with eight workers is 16 GB, unless it is loaded before fork with --preload and stays shared copy-on-write (py8 explains why reference counting and GC erode that sharing, and gc.freeze()). For GPU inference, several workers cannot share one GPU's memory safely without a model server. That is why ML serving often uses one process per GPU with dynamic batching (vLLM, Triton), with the Python web tier as a thin, async gateway.

contextvars and request-scoped state

Thread-local storage fails under asyncio, where many requests share one thread. contextvars.ContextVar values belong to a context that asyncio copies into each task when it is created, so setting a request id in middleware makes it visible to everything that request's task calls, and invisible to other requests. Threads started with threading.Thread did not inherit the context before 3.14; 3.14's thread_inherit_context flag makes new threads start with a copy of the caller's context (on by default in the free-threaded build), and asyncio.to_thread copies the current context into the worker thread, whereas loop.run_in_executor does not: in a test, a request id set before the call was visible through to_thread but read as the default through run_in_executor, unless the call is wrapped as contextvars.copy_context().run(fn).

Copy-on-write in pandas 3.0, mechanically

Under copy-on-write, operations that produce a new DataFrame or Series from an existing one may share the underlying arrays instead of copying them, which saves memory and time. pandas tracks references to each array; the first write to an object whose data is shared with another triggers an actual copy of just that data. So derived objects behave like copies while costing like views until written. Chained assignment cannot work in this model because the intermediate object is a temporary whose data would be copied on write, which is why pandas 3.0 turns it into a warning rather than silently doing nothing. The same release made a dedicated string dtype the default for text columns.

Choosing between pandas, Polars and DuckDB

pandas remains the most widely used and best integrated with plotting, statistics and ML libraries. Polars, written in Rust on Arrow memory, is multi-threaded, has a lazy API that optimises the whole query (pushing filters down, selecting only needed columns) and handles larger-than-memory data in streaming mode; it is often several times to an order of magnitude faster on large transformations. DuckDB is an in-process analytical SQL database that queries Parquet, CSV and even pandas or Polars frames directly with a vectorised, parallel engine. A common production pattern is to do heavy joins and aggregations in DuckDB or Polars and hand the smaller result to pandas or scikit-learn.

Threads inside WSGI workers

gunicorn's gthread worker runs a thread pool inside each process, so one process can handle several requests at once while they wait on I/O, sharing that process's memory and pools. Because the GIL is released during socket waits (py8), this gives much of async's concurrency benefit for I/O-heavy Flask or Django apps without rewriting them, at the cost of thread-safety concerns in application code and the GIL's serialisation of any CPU work. A common configuration is a few processes (for CPU parallelism and fault isolation) each with a modest number of threads (for I/O overlap). On the free-threaded build (3.14), threads could also run CPU work in parallel, if every extension in the stack supports it.
prod:
Incident pattern: the slow dependency that takes everything down

A dependency slows down; requests waiting on it pile up; worker pools or event loops fill; health checks start failing; the orchestrator restarts instances, which lose their warm caches and connection pools and make things worse. The defences are layered: timeouts on every call, bounded pools and concurrency (bulkheads), circuit breakers that fail fast, liveness checks that do not depend on other services, load shedding (returning 503 early when queues are long), and retry budgets so clients do not multiply the load. The scale track's sc12 covers these resilience patterns in depth.

Observability for Python services

OpenTelemetry has automatic instrumentation for the common frameworks, database drivers and HTTP clients, producing traces with spans for each request and each outbound call, which answers "where did the time go?" across services. Pair traces with structured logs carrying the trace or request id, metrics for request rate, error rate and latency percentiles per endpoint (the RED method), worker and pool saturation, and event-loop lag for async services. Continuous profiling (py11) catches CPU regressions that metrics only hint at.

Capacity and cost for LLM backends

Services that call LLM APIs have unusual profiles: requests last seconds rather than milliseconds, responses are often streamed, and cost is per token. That favours ASGI workers (a streamed response holds a cheap coroutine, not a whole process), strict per-request token and time budgets, semaphores sized to the provider's rate limits (py9), caching of repeated prompts or embeddings, and metrics per endpoint for tokens, cost and time to first token alongside the usual latency and error rates. The AI-engineering track's ae1 and ae2 go into architecture and cost modelling.

Deploying safely

Build one immutable image from the lockfile (py13), promote the same image through environments, run database migrations as a separate step that is backward-compatible with the previous code version (add columns before using them, remove them after), and roll out gradually with automated rollback on error-rate or latency regressions. Readiness probes should only pass once the application, caches and models are loaded, or users hit cold instances during every deploy.

Data pipelines in production

Pipelines fail quietly more often than services fail loudly. Guard them with schema and data-quality checks at the boundaries (column presence and types, null rates, value ranges, row counts versus yesterday), using Pandera, Great Expectations or plain assertions; make each step idempotent and re-runnable for a given date partition; write outputs atomically (to a temporary location, then rename or commit) so consumers never read half-written data; and alert on freshness, not just failures. The ML track's ml14 covers the training/serving skew that follows when the online feature code and the batch pipeline compute features differently.

Security basics every Python service needs

Validate all input with typed models; use parameterised queries or the ORM, never string-formatted SQL; keep dependencies patched from the lockfile; never log or return secrets and stack traces to clients (disable debug modes in production — Flask's and Django's debug pages execute code or leak settings); set request size limits and timeouts at the proxy; and run containers as a non-root user with a read-only file system where possible. The SWE track's swe13 goes further.
myths: An async def endpoint is always faster.

Only if everything it awaits is truly asynchronous. In this lesson's measurement, ten concurrent requests to an async def endpoint that called blocking time.sleep(1) took 10.04 s, because each blocked the event loop; the same work in a plain def endpoint took 1.05 s, because FastAPI runs those in a thread pool.
HTTP client libraries time out by default.

requests has no default timeout: a server that accepts the connection and never answers blocks the call forever, holding a worker. Every outbound call needs an explicit timeout; in the lesson's test, timeout=(3.05, 2) turned a hung server into a ReadTimeout after 2.02 s.
More gunicorn workers always means more throughput.

Workers are processes, each with its own memory and connection pools. Past the point where CPU or the database is saturated, more workers add memory pressure, database connections and context switching. The starting formula (2 × cores + 1) is a guess to be tuned by load testing.
df[df.qty > 5]['price'] = 0 updates the DataFrame.

It is chained assignment: the first indexing produces a new object and the assignment modifies that. With pandas 3.0's copy-on-write it never modifies df and emits a ChainedAssignmentError warning; in the test, zero rows changed. Use df.loc[mask, 'price'] = 0.
Logging with print is fine in containers.

print output has no level, logger name, timestamp or structure, cannot be filtered or routed, and is block-buffered when not attached to a terminal, so it can appear late or be lost on a crash. The logging module with a JSON formatter and request ids is what makes logs searchable across hundreds of instances.
Background work can just run in a thread started from the request handler.

Threads started in a web worker die when the worker is recycled or the deploy restarts it, have no retries or visibility, and compete with request handling. Durable work belongs in a task queue (Celery, RQ, Dramatiq, arq) whose jobs are persisted, retried and monitored.

    import socket, threading, time, requests
