recap: WSGI is the synchronous interface between Python web servers and applications, where one request occupies one worker until it returns; ASGI is the asynchronous successor that supports many concurrent requests per process and long-lived connections.

gunicorn is a pre-fork process manager whose master starts worker processes; uvicorn is an ASGI server; production often runs gunicorn managing uvicorn workers behind a reverse proxy or load balancer.
Each worker process has its own memory, connection pools and caches, so capacity is workers × concurrency per worker, and database connections are pool size × workers × instances.
Django is batteries-included, Flask is minimal, and FastAPI is typed and async-first with automatic validation and OpenAPI docs, which makes it common for APIs and ML serving.
Configuration comes from the environment and is validated at startup, so a missing or malformed setting fails the deploy rather than a request.
Logs are structured, emitted through the logging module with one configuration at startup, and carry a request id propagated with contextvars.
Every outbound call has a timeout, reuses a pooled client, and retries only idempotent operations with backoff.
Durable background work goes to a task queue; services expose health and readiness endpoints and shut down gracefully on SIGTERM.

In pandas, vectorised column operations are thousands of times faster than iterrows, .loc replaces chained assignment, and copy-on-write (default in pandas 3.0) makes every derived object behave as a copy.
Data pipelines save memory with categorical and nullable dtypes and by loading only needed columns, and handle missing values and time zones deliberately.
glossary: ASGI
Asynchronous Server Gateway Interface: the standard interface between async Python web servers and applications, supporting HTTP, WebSockets and streaming.
Bulkhead
Isolating resources (separate worker pools or connection pools) so a failing dependency cannot exhaust capacity needed by everything else.
Circuit breaker
A wrapper that stops calling a failing dependency for a while after repeated errors, failing fast instead of piling up waiting requests.
Connection pool
A set of reusable open connections to a database or HTTP host, so requests do not pay connection setup each time.
contextvars
A standard-library module for values that are local to the current thread or asyncio task, used for request ids and similar context.
Copy-on-write (pandas)
pandas' model, default from 3.0, in which derived DataFrames and Series behave as independent copies and are only physically copied when modified.
gunicorn
A pre-fork WSGI HTTP server: a master process manages several worker processes; it can also run uvicorn's ASGI workers.
Graceful shutdown
Stopping a service by ceasing to accept new work, finishing in-flight requests within a deadline, then exiting.
Health check
An endpoint an orchestrator calls to decide whether an instance is alive (liveness) or ready to receive traffic (readiness).
Idempotent
An operation that has the same effect whether performed once or several times, which makes it safe to retry.
Reverse proxy
A server such as nginx or a cloud load balancer in front of the application that terminates TLS, buffers slow clients and distributes requests.
Structured logging
Emitting log records as machine-readable key-value data, usually JSON, rather than free text.
Task queue
A system where web processes enqueue jobs into a broker (Redis, RabbitMQ) and separate worker processes execute them with retries.
Twelve-factor app
A set of practices for cloud services, including configuration in the environment, logs as event streams and disposable processes.
uvicorn
A fast ASGI server for running async Python web applications such as FastAPI and Starlette.
WSGI
Web Server Gateway Interface (PEP 3333): the standard synchronous interface between Python web servers and applications.
drill:
Diagnose it

A Flask API on gunicorn with 4 sync workers serves 200 requests/s normally. Every few days, requests start timing out and all 4 workers show as busy, but CPU is near zero. A handler calls a partner API with requests.get(PARTNER_URL). What is happening, and what do you change?

Answer

What is happening: requests has no default timeout. When the partner API hangs — accepts the connection and never responds — each request to that handler blocks a sync worker indefinitely. With only 4 workers, 4 hung calls take the entire service down: every other endpoint queues behind them, and the health check may fail too, triggering restarts. Near-zero CPU confirms the workers are waiting, not working; py-spy dump on a worker would show it stuck in a socket read inside requests. Little's law explains why it only happens sometimes: at 200 requests/s even a few seconds of partner slowness needs far more than 4 workers in flight.

Changes:

  • Always pass a timeout: session.get(url, timeout=(3.05, 5)) (connect, read), using one shared requests.Session per process for connection pooling.
  • Wrap the partner in a circuit breaker with a fallback or a fast 503 when it is failing, so its outage does not consume your capacity.
  • Isolate it: if the call is slow by nature, move it to a background job, or give it its own bounded worker pool (a bulkhead) so it cannot starve other endpoints.
  • Consider an async stack (FastAPI with httpx.AsyncClient) if many requests wait on I/O, since one worker can then hold hundreds of in-flight calls — but the missing timeout is the actual bug, and an async service without timeouts fails the same way.
  • Keep gunicorn's own --timeout as a safety net that kills stuck workers, and add alerts on worker saturation and on the partner's latency and error rate.
qa: E
What is the difference between WSGI and ASGI?

WSGI (PEP 3333) is the synchronous Python web interface: the server calls the application as a function with the request environment, and the request occupies a worker thread or process until the function returns. ASGI is its asynchronous successor: the application is an async callable that receives and sends events, so one process can hold many concurrent requests on an event loop and support long-lived connections such as WebSockets and streamed responses. Flask and classic Django are WSGI; FastAPI, Starlette and Django's async views are ASGI.

Follow-up: Can a WSGI app stream responses? — It can return an iterator of chunks, but each open stream still occupies a worker for its whole duration, which is why token streaming at scale uses ASGI.
E
Why is requests.get(url) without a timeout a production bug?

requests has no default timeout, so a server that accepts the connection but never responds blocks the call forever. In a sync web server each hung call permanently occupies a worker, and a handful of them exhaust the pool and take the whole service down while CPU sits at zero. Always pass timeout=(connect, read), reuse a Session, and alert on dependency latency.
E
Why configure services with environment variables validated at startup?

Environment variables keep configuration out of the code and image, so the same artefact runs in every environment (the twelve-factor approach), and secrets can be injected by the platform. Validating them once at startup, for example with a pydantic-settings class, means a missing DATABASE_URL or a malformed WORKERS value fails the deploy immediately with a clear message, instead of failing on the first request that needs it at 3 a.m.
M
How do you choose between Django, Flask and FastAPI?

Django is batteries-included — ORM, migrations, admin, authentication, forms — so it is the fastest path to a full product with a relational database. Flask is minimal and lets you choose every component, suiting small services and teams with strong preferences. FastAPI builds on type hints and Pydantic for request validation, serialisation and automatic OpenAPI docs, and is async-first, which makes it the common choice for JSON APIs and ML model serving. The deciding factors are usually the data model's complexity and whether you need async.

Follow-up: Is FastAPI faster than Flask? — For I/O-heavy workloads with async libraries it handles more concurrent requests per process; for CPU-bound handlers the framework matters little, and the database usually dominates.
M
How does gunicorn work, and how many workers should you run?

gunicorn's master process binds the socket, forks a configured number of worker processes, restarts any that die or exceed the timeout, and handles signals for graceful reloads. Each sync worker handles one request at a time, so capacity is roughly workers × 1; threaded or async (uvicorn) workers handle many. The documented starting point is 2 × cores + 1 for sync workers, then load-test, watching CPU, memory per worker, latency percentiles and database connections.
M
What happens if you call a blocking function inside a FastAPI async def endpoint?

The endpoint runs on the event loop, so the blocking call stops the loop and every other request on that worker waits. Measured: ten concurrent requests to an async def endpoint that called time.sleep(1) took 10.04 s, versus about 1 s for a plain def endpoint doing the same, because FastAPI runs def endpoints in a thread pool. Use async libraries in async def endpoints, declare endpoints that must call blocking code as plain def, or wrap the call with asyncio.to_thread.
M
How do you make logs useful across many instances?

Configure logging once at startup, emit structured JSON with level, logger name, timestamp and message, and attach a request id to every record, stored in a contextvars variable set by middleware and added by a filter or formatter. Propagate the id to downstream services in a header so traces join up, log exceptions with logger.exception once where they are handled, and never log secrets or full request bodies. Libraries should only create loggers, never configure handlers.
M
How do you make a slow pandas transformation faster?

Replace row-wise Python (iterrows, apply with axis=1) with vectorised column operations, np.where, groupby aggregations or merges; in the lesson, iterrows took 6.13 s and the vectorised product 1.18 ms for 200,000 rows. Reduce memory with categorical dtypes for repeated strings (10.2 MB to 0.2 MB in the test), smaller numeric types and loading only needed columns from Parquet. For data larger than memory or needing many cores, use chunking, Polars or DuckDB.
M
Where should long-running or background work go in a web service?

Into a task queue: the request handler validates input, enqueues a job to a broker such as Redis or RabbitMQ, and returns quickly (often 202 Accepted with a job id); separate worker processes (Celery, RQ, Dramatiq, arq) execute jobs with retries, timeouts and monitoring. Jobs must be idempotent because they will sometimes run twice, and their arguments should be ids rather than large objects. Threads spawned from the request lose work on restarts and have no visibility.
H
Your API times out under load but CPU is near zero. How do you investigate?

Zero CPU with timeouts means workers are waiting, not working. Check worker saturation and the latency of every dependency in traces; take py-spy dump of a worker to see what it is blocked on — typically a socket read to a slow dependency without a timeout, a database connection pool wait, or a lock. Fix with explicit timeouts, pool sizing that matches the database's limits, circuit breakers and bulkheads for flaky dependencies, and moving slow work off the request path.

Follow-up: What if the pool wait is the bottleneck? — Compare pool size × workers × instances with the database's max_connections and its real capacity; often the answer is fewer connections via a pooler such as PgBouncer and faster queries, not a bigger pool.
H
How do you serve an ML model from a Python web service?

Load the model once per worker process at startup, not per request, and account for memory: each worker holds its own copy, so worker count is bounded by RAM or GPU memory. Keep inference off the event loop — plain def endpoints or a thread pool for native code that releases the GIL, a process pool for pure-Python pre-processing. Validate inputs with Pydantic, batch requests if throughput matters, set timeouts, and expose readiness only after the model has loaded. At scale, use a dedicated model server (vLLM, Triton, TorchServe) that does dynamic batching and GPU scheduling, with the Python API as a thin gateway.
H
What does graceful shutdown require in a containerised Python service?

When the orchestrator sends SIGTERM, the service must stop accepting new connections, let in-flight requests finish within the grace period (30 s by default in Kubernetes), finish or re-queue the current background job, close pools, and exit; SIGKILL follows if it does not. gunicorn and uvicorn handle SIGTERM for their workers; the application must honour cancellation, avoid very long requests, and set a readiness probe to fail first so the load balancer stops sending traffic. Running the server as PID 1 without a proper init or exec form in the Dockerfile often means signals never reach Python.
H
What changed in pandas 3.0 that affects production pipelines?

Copy-on-write became the default and only mode: any derived DataFrame or Series behaves as an independent copy, so modifying a subset never changes the original, chained assignment never works and raises a ChainedAssignmentError warning, and SettingWithCopyWarning is gone. Strings default to a dedicated str dtype instead of object. Pipelines that relied on views being modified in place, or on object dtype for strings, need updating; the payoff is predictable semantics and fewer defensive copies.

When to use def versus async def, and how FastAPI runs each.

Why chained assignment was ambiguous and how copy-on-write fixes it.
Configuration, logs, processes and disposability for cloud services.

sum: The classic Python trick questions grouped by the few rules that explain them — references, evaluation time, floating point, truthiness, iteration and scope — plus a version-by-version tour of what changed from 3.8 to 3.14: the walrus, pattern matching, exception groups, the 3.12 generic syntax, the free-threaded build, deferred annotations and template strings.

Names refer to objects; mutation versus rebinding; is versus ==; shallow and deep copies.
py3
Defaults are evaluated once; closures bind late; LEGB scoping.
py5
Iterators are single-pass; modifying a list while iterating skips items.
py7
Exceptions, finally, and exception groups with except*.
why:
Two kinds of questions come up in almost every Python interview. The first is the snippet: "What does this print?" — a loop that removes items from the list it is iterating, a default argument that remembers values, round(2.5), a match statement with a constant in it. The second is "what's new?": "Have you used pattern matching? What are exception groups for? What changed in 3.12? What are t-strings?" Candidates who answer the first kind from memory stumble on the next variation; candidates who can't answer the second sound like they stopped learning Python years ago.

Both kinds matter outside interviews too. The snippet puzzles are distilled production bugs. A configuration loader that writes cfg.get("port") or 8080 silently overrides a deliberate port 0. A report that rounds with round surprises finance with 2.5 becoming 2. A cleanup loop that removes items while iterating skips every second one. A match on HTTP status codes that uses a bare constant name treats every status as OK. And the version features are the tools you are expected to reach for: TaskGroup instead of loose tasks, tomllib instead of a third-party parser, the 3.12 generic syntax, and in 3.14 lazily evaluated annotations and template strings that make safe HTML and SQL construction possible.

This lesson is the capstone of the Python track. Its first half regroups the classic gotchas by the handful of rules that explain them — several taught in earlier topics (py1, py3, py5, py7) — and adds the ones not covered elsewhere: floating point, rounding and division, truthiness, comparisons and datetimes. Its second half is a version-by-version tour from Python 3.8 to 3.14, with working examples of the features you should recognise and use, and a deeper look at pattern matching and t-strings. It ends with how teams manage Python upgrades. The gotchas were run on CPython 3.12.10; features that exist only in 3.13 or 3.14 are shown as documented in the official release notes and PEPs and are labelled with their version.
primer:
Six rules behind almost every gotcha

Python's surprising behaviours are not a random list. Nearly all of them follow from six rules, and once you can name the rule, you can predict the output instead of remembering it.

  1. Names are references. Assignment never copies; mutation is visible through every name bound to the object (py1). This explains aliasing, [[0] * 3] * 3, shared class attributes and caches that return shared objects.
  2. Some things are evaluated once. Default arguments are evaluated when def runs; class bodies run once; module code runs once on first import (py3, py6).
  3. Closures look names up late. A function reads an enclosing variable's value when called, not when created (py3).
  4. Floats are binary approximations. Most decimal fractions cannot be stored exactly, so arithmetic and rounding produce surprises (this lesson).
  5. Truthiness conflates "empty" with "missing". 0, "", [] and None are all false in an if (this lesson).
  6. Iteration and mutation don't mix. Iterators are single-pass and track positions, so changing a collection while looping over it goes wrong (py5).

Python keeps changing — on a schedule

Since 2019, CPython releases a new minor version every October (PEP 602). Each gets about two years of bug-fix releases and security fixes until five years after release. So in late 2026, 3.10 through 3.14 are supported (3.10 reaching end of life in October 2026), and 3.15 is due. Each release adds language features and library improvements and removes things that were deprecated two releases earlier.

What "modern Python" means in practice

Knowing the feature list is less important than knowing which features change how you write everyday code. From 3.8 to 3.14 those are: f-strings everywhere (with = for debugging), | for unions and dict merges, match for dispatching on data shapes, dataclasses and typed signatures with the built-in generic syntax, TaskGroup and asyncio.timeout for async code, exception groups for concurrent failures, and, from 3.14, t-strings for safe templating and forward references without quotes. A codebase that uses these reads as current; one full of Optional[List[Dict]], %-formatting and loose create_task calls reads as a decade old.

How to answer a "what does this print?" question

In an interview, narrate the rule, not just the answer: "The default list is created once when def runs, so both calls append to the same list, and it prints [1, 2] [1, 2]. The fix is a None default." That shows the interviewer you can handle the next variation. Then mention how you would catch it in practice — a linter rule or a test — because that is what a senior engineer does with a known trap.

Where the "six rules" framing breaks down: some behaviours are CPython implementation details rather than language rules — small-integer caching that makes is seem to work, or the exact moment a generator's cleanup runs. Name them as implementation details when they come up, and never rely on them.
body:
1. References and evaluation time: the classics, briefly

These were taught in detail earlier; here is the one-line explanation for each, as you would give it in an interview.

def f(x, acc=[]):                  # default evaluated once (py1, py3)
    acc.append(x); return acc
f(1); f(2)                         # [1, 2] — the same list both times

fns = [lambda: i for i in range(3)]
[fn() for fn in fns]               # [2, 2, 2] — closures read i when called (py3)

grid = [[0] * 3] * 3
grid[0][0] = 1                     # [[1, 0, 0], [1, 0, 0], [1, 0, 0]] — one inner list, three times (py1)

t = (1, [2])
t[1] += [3]                        # raises TypeError AND leaves t == (1, [2, 3]) (py1)

Two more in the same family. A mutable class attribute (members = [] in the class body) is shared by every instance (py6). And except SomeError as e: deletes e at the end of the block — after the except in the test, print(e) raised NameError: name 'e' is not defined — because keeping it would create a reference cycle through the traceback's frames (py7, py8).

2. Floating point

Python's float is an IEEE 754 64-bit binary number: 53 bits of precision in base 2. Fractions whose denominator is a power of two (0.5, 0.25, 0.375) are exact; most decimal fractions, like 0.1, are repeating fractions in binary, the way 1/3 is 0.333... in decimal, so they are stored as the nearest representable value.

0.1 + 0.2                  # 0.30000000000000004
0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3           # False
math.isclose(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3)   # True — compare with a tolerance
decimal.Decimal(0.1)       # 0.1000000000000000055511151231257827021181583404541015625 (the float's true value)
decimal.Decimal("0.1") + decimal.Decimal("0.2")   # Decimal('0.3') — exact decimal arithmetic

Python prints floats with the shortest decimal string that converts back to the same binary value, which is why 0.1 displays as 0.1 even though it is not exactly 0.1 — the error only shows when operations accumulate it. Rules of thumb: never compare floats with == after arithmetic; use math.isclose (relative tolerance) or an absolute tolerance appropriate to the domain; for money, use integer minor units (cents) or Decimal constructed from strings, never from floats; for summing many floats accurately, math.fsum.

3. Rounding and integer division

round(x) uses round-half-to-even ("banker's rounding"): round(2.5) is 2 and round(3.5) is 4. Rounding halves always upwards would bias sums and averages upwards; alternating by evenness cancels out. Floating-point representation adds a second layer: round(2.25, 1) is 2.2 (2.25 is exact in binary, so the even rule applies), but round(2.35, 1) is 2.4, because 2.35 is actually stored as slightly more than 2.35. For financial rounding rules, use Decimal.quantize with an explicit rounding mode such as ROUND_HALF_UP.

The // operator is floor division: it rounds towards negative infinity, so -7 // 2 is -4, and % is defined to match (-7 % 2 is 1), keeping (a // b) * b + a % b == a true. int(-3.5) and math.trunc(-3.5) truncate towards zero instead, giving -3. C, Java and JavaScript truncate integer division, so ported code can silently change behaviour for negative numbers.

4. Truthiness, None and defaults

In a boolean context, False, None, numeric zero (0, 0.0), empty strings and empty containers are false; almost everything else is true, including "0", " " and [0]. This makes if items: a clean "non-empty" test, and makes "missing" checks dangerous:

cfg = {"port": 0}
cfg.get("port") or 8080      # 8080 — the deliberate 0 is lost
cfg.get("port", 8080)        # 0    — default only when the key is missing
port = cfg.get("port")
if port is None:              # explicit "missing" test
    port = 8080

Also remember [] == False is False even though not [] is True: truthiness and equality are different questions. When None is itself a meaningful value, use a private sentinel object as the "not provided" marker (py1).

5. Comparisons and chaining

Comparison operators chain: 1 < x < 10 means 1 < x and x < 10, which is convenient. The same rule produces puzzles: False == False in [False] is True, because it means (False == False) and (False in [False]). is compares identity and must not be used for values (py1). Sorting mixed types raises: sorted([3, "a"]) gives TypeError: '<' not supported between instances of 'str' and 'int'. And string sorting is by code point, so sorted(["b", "B", "a"]) is ['B', 'a', 'b']; pass key=str.lower (or str.casefold for full Unicode case folding) for human ordering.

6. Iteration, slicing and strings

Removing from a list while iterating over it skips elements; mutating a dict's size while iterating raises RuntimeError; a generator can be consumed once (py5). Slicing never raises for out-of-range bounds — [1, 2, 3][10:20] is [] — while indexing does (IndexError: list index out of range), so a slice can hide an off-by-one bug that an index would have exposed. str.split() with no argument splits on runs of whitespace and drops empty strings, but split(" ") keeps them: "a b c".split(" ") is ['a', 'b', '', 'c']. str.strip("abc") strips any of those characters, not the substring; for a prefix or suffix use removeprefix/removesuffix (3.9).

7. Datetimes and time zones

A naive datetime has no time zone and means whatever the programmer assumed; an aware one carries a tzinfo. datetime.utcnow() returns a naive value that merely happens to hold UTC time, which then gets treated as local time elsewhere; it is deprecated since 3.12 and emitted a DeprecationWarning in the test. Use datetime.now(datetime.UTC) (the UTC alias is 3.11+; timezone.utc before), store and compute in UTC, convert to local zones with zoneinfo (3.9) only for display, and remember that daylight-saving transitions create non-existent and repeated local times (py14).

8. Features by version: 3.8 to 3.10

  • 3.8: the walrus operator, :=, assigns inside expressions: if (n := len(items)) > 1: or while (chunk := f.read(8192)):. Positional-only parameters with / (py3). f-string debugging with =: f"{x=}" prints x=10. typing.Protocol, Literal, TypedDict and Final.
  • 3.9: dict union, d1 | d2 (right side wins: {'a': 1, 'b': 3, 'c': 4}) and |=; built-in generics in annotations, list[int]; str.removeprefix/removesuffix; the zoneinfo module; functools.cache; the relaxed decorator grammar (py4).
  • 3.10: structural pattern matching (section 10); union types written int | None; zip(..., strict=True); parenthesised context managers across lines; itertools.pairwise; and much clearer error messages for syntax errors, missing brackets and misspelled names.

9. Features by version: 3.11 to 3.14

  • 3.11: roughly 25% faster on average from the specialising adaptive interpreter (py11); exception groups, except* and add_note (py7); asyncio.TaskGroup and asyncio.timeout (py9); tracebacks that underline the failing expression; tomllib for reading TOML; typing.Self, LiteralString and variadic generics.
  • 3.12: the type parameter syntax def first[T](xs: Sequence[T]) -> T, class Box[T] and type Vector = list[float] (py10); f-strings that can reuse the enclosing quote character and contain any expression (f"{'nested' + "quotes"}" works); immortal objects and a per-interpreter GIL (py8); comprehension inlining (py3); itertools.batched; @typing.override; sys.monitoring; and deprecation of datetime.utcnow.
  • 3.13: a new interactive interpreter with multi-line editing, history and colour; defined locals() semantics (PEP 667, py3); copy.replace; TypeIs, ReadOnly and type parameter defaults; warnings.deprecated; the experimental free-threaded build and JIT (py8, py11); batched(strict=True); queue.Queue.shutdown; and removal of 19 legacy "dead battery" standard-library modules such as cgi, telnetlib and crypt (PEP 594).
  • 3.14 (released 7 October 2025): deferred evaluation of annotations and the annotationlib module (py10); template strings (section 11); except A, B: without brackets when there is no as (PEP 758); a SyntaxWarning for return/break/continue leaving finally (PEP 765, py7); the free-threaded build officially supported (PEP 779); concurrent.interpreters and InterpreterPoolExecutor (PEP 734); a compression package with Zstandard support (compression.zstd, PEP 784); attaching a debugger to a running process with python -m pdb -p PID (PEP 768); REPL syntax highlighting and import completion; map(..., strict=True); uuid.uuid7(); forkserver as the default multiprocessing start method on Linux (py9); and asyncio introspection with python -m asyncio ps. The incremental garbage collector introduced in 3.14.0 was reverted in 3.14.5 (py8).

10. Structural pattern matching in depth

match (3.10) compares a subject against case patterns in order and runs the first that matches, binding parts of the subject to names as it goes. It is designed for dispatching on the shape of data:

def classify(ev):
    match ev:
        case {"type": "click", "x": int(x), "y": int(y)}:
            return f"click {x},{y}"
        case {"type": "key", "key": "q" | "Q"}:
            return "quit"
        case [first, *rest] if rest:
            return f"batch {first}+{len(rest)}"
        case str() as s:
            return f"text {s}"
        case _:
            return "unknown"

classify({"type": "click", "x": 1, "y": 2, "extra": 9})   # 'click 1,2' — extra keys are ignored
classify({"type": "key", "key": "Q"})                      # 'quit'
classify([1, 2, 3])                                        # 'batch 1+2'
classify("hi")                                             # 'text hi'
classify(3.0)                                              # 'unknown'

Key semantics: mapping patterns match if the listed keys are present and ignore extra keys (use **rest to capture them); sequence patterns match lists and tuples but deliberately not strings; class patterns call isinstance and then read attributes, with positional sub-patterns mapped through the class's __match_args__ (dataclasses define it automatically); int(x) is a class pattern that checks the type and binds. And the trap: a bare name is a capture pattern that matches anything. Compiling a match with case OK: followed by case _: fails with SyntaxError: name capture 'OK' makes remaining patterns unreachable; with no later case it compiles and silently matches everything. Compare against constants with dotted names (HTTPStatus.OK), literals, or a guard.

11. Template strings (3.14)

f-strings are convenient but dangerous for building HTML, SQL or shell commands, because by the time a library sees the result, user input has been merged into the string and cannot be told apart from the trusted parts. PEP 750 adds t-strings: the same syntax with a t prefix, but the result is a string.templatelib.Template, not a str. According to the 3.14 documentation:

# Python 3.14
variety = "Stilton"
template = t"Try some {variety} cheese!"
type(template)      # <class 'string.templatelib.Template'>
list(template)
# ['Try some ', Interpolation('Stilton', 'variety', None, ''), ' cheese!']

Iterating a template yields the literal strings and Interpolation objects, each carrying the evaluated value, the source expression text, and any conversion (!r) and format spec. A processing function can therefore treat the two differently — escape every interpolated value for HTML, turn each into a bound SQL parameter, or quote each for a shell — and then assemble the result. Because a Template is not a str, an API that accepts only templates makes unsafe concatenation a type error rather than a code-review item. The standard library supplies the types; escaping functions come from libraries built on them.

12. Everyday traps not covered elsewhere

Methods that mutate return None. xs = xs.sort() leaves xs as None, because list.sort, list.append, dict.update and random.shuffle change the object in place and return None by convention (py1). The functional counterparts — sorted(xs), xs + [item], {**d, **other} — return new objects. The opposite trap applies to immutable types: name.strip() on its own line does nothing, since strings cannot change; the result must be assigned (name = name.strip()).

Strings are sequences of code points, not characters. "café" typed with a precomposed é has length 4, but the visually identical "café" (e followed by a combining accent) has length 5 and compares unequal; unicodedata.normalize("NFC", ...) makes them equal. An emoji with a skin-tone modifier has length 2 in Python and takes 8 bytes in UTF-8. Case-insensitive comparison needs casefold, not lower: "Straße".lower() == "strasse" is False, while "Straße".casefold() == "strasse" is True. Text from users, files and LLM output should be normalised before comparing, deduplicating or counting length limits.

Dict views are live. k = d.keys() followed by d["b"] = 2 gives list(k) == ['a', 'b']: views reflect later changes (py2). Snapshot with list(d) when you need a fixed set.

Shadowing modules. A file in your project named random.py, email.py, json.py or test.py is found before the standard library's module of the same name, because the script's directory comes first on sys.path (py13), producing baffling AttributeErrors in unrelated imports. Similarly, a variable named list, dict, id or type shadows the built-in for the rest of its scope (py3).
deep:
How floats are stored and printed

A 64-bit float has a sign bit, an 11-bit exponent and a 52-bit fraction with an implicit leading 1, giving 53 significant bits — about 15 to 17 significant decimal digits. Every float is exactly a fraction with a power-of-two denominator; (0.1).as_integer_ratio() reveals it as 3602879701896397 / 36028797018963968. Since Python 3.1, repr prints the shortest decimal string that round-trips to the same float, which hides the error until arithmetic accumulates it. Special values follow IEEE 754 too: float("inf"), -0.0 (which equals 0.0 but has a sign), and NaN, which is unequal to itself (py1). math.fsum uses extra precision internally and returns the correctly rounded sum, which matters when adding many values of different magnitudes, a common case in metrics and ML.

Pattern matching implementation details

The compiler turns a match statement into a sequence of type checks, length checks, key lookups and comparisons; there is no special runtime "matcher" object. Class patterns use isinstance and getattr; positional sub-patterns rely on __match_args__, a tuple of attribute names that dataclasses and named tuples generate. Mapping patterns use the mapping's get method for listed keys, so they work with any collections.abc.Mapping. Sequence patterns reject str, bytes and bytearray on purpose, since treating a string as a sequence of characters is rarely what dispatch code wants. Guards are evaluated after bindings, so names bound by a failed guard may still be set, which is why case-bound names should not be relied on outside their block.

How t-strings are evaluated

At runtime a t-string evaluates each interpolated expression eagerly, left to right, exactly like an f-string, but does not call format or str: it stores the values, the source text, the conversion and the format spec. Template exposes strings (the literal parts, always one more than the interpolations), interpolations and values, and supports concatenation with other templates but not with plain strings. This design lets processors apply different policies — HTML escaping, SQL parameter binding, structured logging that keeps values as fields rather than formatting them into the message — while keeping the familiar f-string syntax and its compile-time checking.

Deferred annotations and what they change

Before 3.14, annotations were evaluated when a function or class was defined, costing time at import and failing on forward references (py10). Under PEP 649 and 749, the compiler generates an __annotate__ function and evaluates it only when someone asks for annotations, in one of three formats (values, forward references or strings) via annotationlib. For ordinary code nothing changes except that forward references work without quotes. For frameworks that read annotations — dataclasses, Pydantic, FastAPI, ORMs — the details of when and how they ask matter, which is why their 3.14 support landed with specific releases.

The release cycle and supporting several versions

PEP 602 fixed an annual October release. Each version receives regular bug-fix releases for about two years (extended from 18 months for 3.13 and later) and then source-only security fixes until five years after its first release. Libraries typically support all non-end-of-life versions; the Scientific Python community's SPEC 0 recommends supporting Python versions for three years after release, which is why NumPy and pandas drop old versions sooner. Supporting several versions in one codebase means writing to the oldest syntax you support, using typing_extensions for newer typing constructs, gating library features with sys.version_info >= (3, 12) checks, and testing on every version in CI.

Where CPython is heading

The two big long-term projects are visible in 3.13 and 3.14. The free-threaded build removes the GIL at a small single-thread cost and is officially supported but still opt-in; its success depends on the extension ecosystem publishing compatible wheels. The JIT compiler, experimental and off by default, builds on the specialising interpreter; its gains are modest so far and workload-dependent. Sub-interpreters offer isolated parallelism within one process. None of these change how you write ordinary Python, but they change the answers to "how do I use all my cores?" (py8, py9) over the next few releases.

Why Python strings are code points

Since Python 3, str is a sequence of Unicode code points, and CPython stores each string in the narrowest fixed-width form that fits its largest code point — 1, 2 or 4 bytes per code point (PEP 393) — so indexing is O(1) and len counts code points. What users perceive as one character, a grapheme cluster, can be several code points: a base letter plus combining marks, an emoji plus a skin-tone modifier, or flags made of two regional-indicator symbols. That is why truncating a string at a code-point index can split a visible character, and why UI and database length limits (often in bytes, or in UTF-16 units in JavaScript) disagree with len. Libraries such as regex with \X, or grapheme segmentation packages, handle user-perceived characters when it matters.
prod:
Catching gotchas automatically

Most of this lesson's traps can be caught before review. Ruff (or flake8-bugbear) flags mutable default arguments (B006), function definitions in loops that use the loop variable (B023), mutable class attributes without ClassVar (RUF012), bare except (E722), and datetime.utcnow and naive datetimes (the DTZ rules). The compiler itself warns about is with literals, rejects unreachable capture patterns, and since 3.14 warns about return in finally. Type checkers catch None handling and many truthiness bugs. Enabling these in CI is cheap insurance.

Money, measurements and ML metrics

Financial code uses integer minor units or Decimal with explicit quantisation and rounding modes, and rounds once at defined points rather than repeatedly. Scientific and ML code accepts floating point but compares with tolerances (math.isclose, numpy.allclose), sums carefully (math.fsum, pairwise summation in NumPy), and watches for precision loss when using float32 or bfloat16. Evaluation reports that print metrics to many decimal places invite false precision; round for display only.

Upgrading Python in production

Upgrades are routine for teams that treat them as such. Keep the newest Python in the CI matrix from its first release candidate, with deprecation warnings turned into errors for your own code, so incompatibilities surface months early. Use Ruff's pyupgrade rules (UP) to modernise syntax once the oldest supported version allows it — Optional[X] to X | None, List[int] to list[int], old-style formatting to f-strings. Re-resolve the lockfile for the new version to confirm every dependency publishes wheels, benchmark (behaviour such as the 3.14 garbage collector changed within a release series), and roll out gradually. Track end-of-life dates: 3.10 stops receiving security fixes in October 2026, so services still on it need a plan now.

Text normalisation in data and LLM pipelines

Deduplication, search indexes, evaluation metrics and prompt caches all compare strings, and invisible differences — Unicode normalisation forms, non-breaking spaces, different quote characters, trailing whitespace — make equal-looking text compare unequal. Pipelines that ingest documents or model output normalise once at the boundary (NFC or NFKC, whitespace collapsing, casefold where case is irrelevant) and record which normalisation was applied, so that training data, retrieval indexes and evaluation all see text the same way.

Adopting new features responsibly

New syntax is only usable when every environment that runs the code supports it: a library that uses match cannot support Python 3.9, and one that uses def f[T] requires 3.12. Applications that control their runtime can adopt features as soon as they upgrade; libraries lag by the length of their support window. Some features are worth a version bump on their own — TaskGroup and asyncio.timeout make async code markedly safer, and 3.14's t-strings enable safe templating APIs — while others are conveniences that can wait.

Knowing which Python you are actually running

A surprising number of "this feature doesn't work" reports come from code running on a different interpreter than the developer assumed: a system Python in a cron job, an old base image in CI, a notebook kernel pointing at another environment. Log sys.version and sys.executable at service start-up, declare requires-python in pyproject.toml so installers refuse unsupported versions (py13), pin the interpreter in Docker images and .python-version files, and fail fast with a clear message if a script needs newer features (if sys.version_info < (3, 11): sys.exit("needs Python 3.11+")). On 3.13 and later, sys._is_gil_enabled() also tells you whether a free-threaded interpreter is running with the GIL disabled, which matters when diagnosing concurrency behaviour (py8). These checks cost seconds to add and save hours of confusion.

Interview technique for snippet questions

When given a snippet, read it aloud line by line, name the rule at the line where it bites ("the default is evaluated once here"), state the output, and then propose the fix and how you would prevent recurrence (a lint rule, a test, a type). If unsure, say which rule you are applying; interviewers value the reasoning over instant recall, and a clearly reasoned wrong answer is often corrected in one exchange.
myths: Gotcha questions test obscure trivia.

Almost every classic Python puzzle is one of six rules in disguise: names are references, some things are evaluated once at definition time, closures look names up late, floats are binary, truthiness conflates 'empty' with 'missing', and iterators and containers change under you when mutated. Know the rules and you can derive the answers instead of memorising them.
round(2.5) is 3.

Python's round rounds exact halves to the nearest even number (banker's rounding) to avoid a systematic upward bias, so round(2.5) is 2 and round(3.5) is 4. And many values that look like halves are not exact in binary: round(2.35, 1) gives 2.4 because 2.35 is stored as slightly more than 2.35.
if not value: checks whether a value is missing.

It checks whether the value is falsy, and 0, 0.0, empty strings and empty containers are all falsy along with None. cfg.get('port') or 8080 replaces a deliberate port 0 with 8080. When 'missing' is what you mean, test is None or use dict.get(key, default).
case OK: in a match statement compares against the constant OK.

A bare name in a pattern is a capture pattern: it binds the subject to a new variable named OK and always matches. Python 3.10+ even refuses to compile such a case when later cases follow ('name capture makes remaining patterns unreachable'). Compare against constants with dotted names such as HTTPStatus.OK, or a guard.
t-strings are just f-strings with a different letter.

An f-string immediately produces a str. A t-string (Python 3.14) produces a Template object that keeps the literal parts and the interpolated values separate, so a library can escape the values safely for HTML or SQL before combining them. It is a tool for safe string processing, not a formatting shortcut.
The newest Python version is always the right one for production.

New releases bring speed and features, but compiled dependencies may not have wheels for them on release day, and some features (the free-threaded build, the JIT) are opt-in and still maturing. Teams usually adopt a new version a few months after release, once their lockfile resolves with wheels for everything, and stay within the supported window.

recap: Mutating an object is visible through every name that refers to it, while rebinding a name affects only that name; list multiplication and shared class attributes create hidden aliases.
Default arguments are evaluated once when the def runs, and closures read variables when called, which explains the mutable-default and late-binding traps.

Floats are binary approximations: 0.1 + 0.2 is 0.30000000000000004, so compare with math.isclose and use Decimal or integer cents for money; round uses round-half-to-even and // floors towards negative infinity.
Truthiness treats 0, empty strings and empty containers like None, so test is None when you mean missing.
Iterators are single-pass, and modifying a list while iterating over it skips elements; build a new collection instead.
3.8 added the walrus operator, positional-only parameters and f-string = debugging; 3.9 added dict union and built-in generics; 3.10 added structural pattern matching and X | Y unions.
3.11 was much faster and added exception groups, except*, TaskGroup, asyncio.timeout and tomllib; 3.12 added the def f[T] generic syntax, type aliases, flexible f-strings and per-interpreter GILs.
3.13 added a new interactive REPL, defined locals() semantics, copy.replace and experimental free-threaded and JIT builds, and removed the 'dead battery' modules.

glossary: Banker's rounding
Rounding exact halves to the nearest even digit (round-half-to-even), which Python's round uses to avoid bias.
Capture pattern
A bare name in a match-case pattern; it matches anything and binds the subject to that name.
Decimal
The decimal module's exact base-10 number type, suitable for money when constructed from strings.
Deferred annotations
Python 3.14's evaluation of annotations only when requested (PEP 649/749), instead of when the def or class runs.
End of life (EOL)
The date after which a Python version receives no more fixes, including security fixes.
f-string
A string literal prefixed with f whose {expressions} are evaluated and formatted immediately into a str.
Floor division
The // operator, which divides and rounds down towards negative infinity.
Free-threaded build
A CPython build without the GIL (PEP 703), experimental in 3.13 and officially supported in 3.14.
Guard
An if condition attached to a case in a match statement, which must be true for the case to match.
IEEE 754
The standard for binary floating-point numbers used by Python floats (64-bit doubles).
Structural pattern matching
The match/case statement (3.10+) that compares a value against patterns describing its shape and binds parts of it.
t-string
A template string literal prefixed with t (3.14) that evaluates to a string.templatelib.Template holding literal parts and interpolations separately.
Truthiness
How a value behaves in a boolean context; zero, empty containers, empty strings and None are falsy.
Walrus operator
The := assignment expression (3.8+), which assigns a value to a name inside an expression and returns it.
drill:
Predict and explain 
items = [1, 2, 3, 4]
for x in items:
    if x % 2 == 0:
        items.remove(x)
print(items)

print(0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3, round(2.5), round(3.5), -7 // 2)

def get_port(cfg):
    return cfg.get("port") or 8080
print(get_port({"port": 0}))

OK = 200
def check(code):
    match code:
        case OK:
            return "ok"
        case _:
            return "error"
print(check(404))
Answer

It does not run at all. The whole file fails to compile with SyntaxError: name capture 'OK' makes remaining patterns unreachable, because Python compiles a module before executing any of it, so none of the earlier prints appear. case OK: is a capture pattern — it binds a new local variable named OK to whatever the subject is and always matches — so the case _: after it could never run, and the compiler rejects it. Without the trailing case _ it would compile and return "ok" for 404, silently. Compare against constants with a dotted name such as HTTPStatus.OK, a literal, or a guard (case c if c == OK:).

With the match fixed, the other lines print:

[1, 3] — correct only by luck. The list iterator advances by index; removing 2 shifts 3 into the current index, which is then skipped, and 4 is removed next. With [2, 4] it prints [4]. Never mutate a list you are iterating over: items = [x for x in items if x % 2].

False 2 4 -4 — 0.1 and 0.2 are binary approximations whose sum is 0.30000000000000004; round sends exact halves to the even neighbour; floor division rounds towards negative infinity.

8080 — 0 or 8080 is 8080 because 0 is falsy, so a deliberately configured port 0 (meaning "pick any free port") is silently replaced. Use cfg.get("port", 8080) or an explicit is None check.
qa: E
Why does 0.1 + 0.2 not equal 0.3 in Python?

Python floats are IEEE 754 64-bit binary numbers, and 0.1 and 0.2 have no exact binary representation, just as 1/3 has none in decimal. Each is stored as the nearest representable value, and their sum is 0.30000000000000004, which is not the stored value of 0.3. Compare with math.isclose, and use Decimal constructed from strings, or integer cents, for money.

Follow-up: Why does Decimal(0.1) print a long number? — Constructing from the float copies its exact binary value, 0.1000000000000000055511151231257827021181583404541015625; construct from the string '0.1' to get exact decimal 0.1.
E
What does round(2.5) return, and why?

2. Python rounds exact halves to the nearest even integer (round-half-to-even, or banker's rounding), so round(3.5) is 4 and round(2.5) is 2. Averaged over many values this avoids the upward bias of always rounding halves up. Many decimal 'halves' are not exact in binary, so round(2.35, 1) is 2.4 while round(2.25, 1) is 2.2.
E
What does the walrus operator do, and when is it useful?

The assignment expression := (3.8+) assigns a value to a name and returns it inside a larger expression. It removes duplicated work or an extra line: while (chunk := f.read(8192)): processes a file in chunks, and [y for x in data if (y := expensive(x)) is not None] filters on a computed value without computing it twice. Overuse hurts readability, so reserve it for these patterns.
M
In a match statement, why does case SOME_CONSTANT: not compare against the constant?

A bare name in a pattern is a capture pattern: it binds the subject to a new variable with that name and always matches. Python even rejects it at compile time if more cases follow, with 'name capture makes remaining patterns unreachable'. Compare against constants with dotted names (an Enum member or module attribute, such as HTTPStatus.OK), literals, or a guard clause (case c if c == OK).
M
What will this print, and why? items = [1, 2, 3, 4]; for x in items: if x % 2 == 0: items.remove(x); print(items)

[1, 3], by luck. The list iterator advances by index; removing 2 shifts 3 into index 1, and the iterator moves on to index 2, which is now 4, skipping 3. 4 is removed too. With [2, 4] the same code leaves [4]. The fix is to build a new list, items = [x for x in items if x % 2], or iterate over a copy.
Follow-up: What happens with a dict? — Changing a dict's size during iteration raises RuntimeError: dictionary changed size during iteration, so the bug is loud rather than silent.
M
Explain structural pattern matching with an example.

match compares a subject against case patterns in order and runs the first that matches, binding parts of the subject to names. Patterns can be literals, captures, wildcards (_), sequences ([first, *rest]), mappings ({'type': 'click', 'x': int(x)} which matches any dict with those keys and ignores others), class patterns (Point(x=0, y=0)), alternatives ("q" | "Q") and guards (if rest). It shines for dispatching on the shape of parsed data, such as JSON events, AST nodes or command tuples.
M
What did Python 3.11 change that matters in practice?

Speed: the specialising adaptive interpreter and cheaper frames made typical code about 25% faster (10-60% depending on workload). Error handling: exception groups and except*, add_note, and tracebacks that point at the exact failing expression. Async: TaskGroup and asyncio.timeout for structured concurrency. And tomllib for reading TOML, plus typing additions such as Self.
M
What are the headline changes in Python 3.12 and 3.13?

3.12: the PEP 695 type parameter syntax (def first[T](xs: Sequence[T]) -> T, class Box[T], type Alias = ...), f-strings that can reuse quotes and contain any expression, immortal objects, per-interpreter GILs for sub-interpreters, itertools.batched and @override, and deprecation of datetime.utcnow. 3.13: a new interactive REPL with multi-line editing and colour, defined locals() semantics (PEP 667), copy.replace, TypeIs and warnings.deprecated, the experimental free-threaded build and JIT, and removal of 19 legacy 'dead battery' modules such as cgi and telnetlib (PEP 594).
M
What is new in Python 3.14?

Deferred evaluation of annotations (PEP 649/749) with the annotationlib module; template strings (t-strings, PEP 750); except and except* without brackets for multiple types (PEP 758); a SyntaxWarning for return, break or continue leaving finally (PEP 765); official support for the free-threaded build (PEP 779); concurrent.interpreters and InterpreterPoolExecutor (PEP 734); compression.zstd (PEP 784); a safe external debugger interface with python -m pdb -p PID (PEP 768); REPL syntax highlighting; and forkserver as the default multiprocessing start method on Linux. 3.14.0 shipped an incremental garbage collector that 3.14.5 reverted.
H
How do t-strings work and why do they matter for security?

A t-string literal, t'Hello {name}', evaluates the expressions like an f-string but returns a string.templatelib.Template instead of a str. The template exposes the static string parts and a sequence of Interpolation objects, each with the evaluated value, the expression text, and any conversion and format spec. A library function such as html(template) or sql(template) can then escape or parameterise each value before assembling the result, so user input can never be interpreted as markup or SQL. With f-strings the values are already merged into one string by the time any library sees it.

Follow-up: Can you pass a t-string where a str is expected? — No; a Template is not a str and has no automatic conversion, which is deliberate: an API that accepts only Template makes unsafe string building a type error.
H
Why is if not value a bug-prone way to check for missing data?

It tests truthiness, and 0, 0.0, '', [], {} and None are all falsy. A configuration port of 0, a balance of 0.0, an intentionally empty list of recipients, or an empty string meaning 'clear this field' all get treated as missing. value or default has the same problem: {'port': 0}.get('port') or 8080 returns 8080. Use is None checks, dict.get(key, default), or a sentinel object when None is itself a valid value (py1).
H
How do you manage upgrading a large codebase to a new Python version?

Check the support windows first: each version gets about two years of bug fixes and five of security fixes (PEP 602), and 3.10 reaches end of life in October 2026. Add the target version to the CI matrix early, run with warnings as errors to surface deprecations, and let tools such as Ruff's pyupgrade rules rewrite syntax automatically. Confirm every dependency publishes wheels for the new version by re-resolving the lockfile, run performance benchmarks because behaviour such as GC changes between releases, and roll out gradually with the old image ready for rollback.

Follow-up: Would you enable the free-threaded build during an upgrade? — Not as part of the same change; it is a separate build with different trade-offs and needs its own compatibility and race-condition testing.
H
Why does except ZeroDivisionError as e: ... make e undefined after the block?

Python implicitly deletes the as-target at the end of the except clause, as if with try/finally: del e. The exception's traceback references the frame, and the frame references e, so keeping e would create a reference cycle keeping every local variable in the frame alive until the garbage collector runs (py8). If you need the exception later, assign it to another name inside the block, knowing that you keep the traceback's frames alive too.
